questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A 25-year-old male came with complaints of acute abdominal pain. A plain X-ray abdomen erect was taken which is shown below. What is your diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Pneumoperitoneum

The above X-ray clearly shows the presence of subdiaphragmatic free gas in the right upper quadrant. This indicates pneumoperitoneum.

Causes of pneumoperitoneum include:

1. Bowel perforation

1. Peptic ulcer
2. Ischemic bowel
3. Necrotizing enterocolitis.

2. Small bowel perforation

1. Trauma
2. Penetrating injuries

3. During surgery / laparoscopy

Signs of pneumoperitoneum:

• Bowel-related signs

• Double wall sign (also known as Rigler's sign or gas-relief sign)
• Telltale triangle sign (also known as triangle sign)

• Peritoneal ligament-related signs

• Football sign
• Falciform ligament sign
• Lateral umbilical ligament sign (also known as inverted "V" sign)
• Urachus sign

• Right upper quadrant signs

• Cupola sign
• Fissure for ligamentum teres sign
• Hepatic edge sign
• Lucent liver sign
• Morison's pouch sign (doge cap sign)
• Periportal free gas sign

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A 30-year-old female came to OPD with complaints of backache. On examination, Schober test was positive and her eyes and nose were hyperpigmented. Probable diagnosis is
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Ochronosis

Given X-ray shows intervertebral disc calcification and hyperpigmentation of nose and eyes are present. Both features are indicative of ochronosis as diagnosis.

• Ochronosis also known as alkaptonuria is an autosomal recessive disorder.
• It is due to deficiency of homogentisic acid oxidase leading to accumulation of homogentisic acid.

• Clinical features: Triad of

• Homogentisic aciduria (urine turns dark color on standing due to oxidation or alkalinisation)
• Eumelanin like pigmentation of skin, sclera, cartilages etc.
• Degenerative chronic arthropathies especially of spine, hip, knees.

Option a: Hypoparathyroidism doesn't explain hyperpigmentation and other clinical features of hypoparathyroidism aren't mentioned.

Option b: Fluorosis - dental symptoms are not mentioned and osteoporosis will be marked in case of fluorosis. Also, hyperpigmentation is not a typical feature of fluorosis.

Option d: Ankylosing spondylitis – females are unlikely to be affected and it doesn’t explain hyperpigmentation.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A 45-year-old woman comes to the emergency department with severe back pain, vomiting, and hypotension. CT findings are given below. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Renal angiomyolipoma

The given CT image shows well-circumscribed lesions with low attenuation (black in colour) that indicate fatty tissue. This is suggestive of renal angiomyolipomas.

Angiomyolipomas (AMLs) are benign tumours that occur sporadically or in association with tuberous sclerosis. It is commonly seen in adults between 30 and 50 years of age, with a female predilection. AMLs predominantly affect the kidneys, though they can occur in other sites such as the liver (a common extra-renal location) and less frequently in the ovary, fallopian tube, spermatic cord, palate, and colon.

Histologically, angiomyolipomas consist of perivascular epitheloid cells with varying proportions of vascular, immature smooth muscle cells, and fat cells. Patients with AMLs present with flank pain, a palpable mass, hematuria, recurrent urinary tract infections, hypertension, or renal failure. Larger tumours increase the risk of complications, such as spontaneous retroperitoneal hemorrhage, which can manifest as sudden-onset abdominal or flank pain, along with symptoms like nausea, vomiting, and hypotension.

Everolimus is used for the treatment of angiomyolipomas. Treatment should be considered for asymptomatic, growing AMLs measuring >3 cm in diameter. Angiomyolipomas do not normally require surgery unless life-threatening bleeding is present.

Other options:

Renal cyst is a broader term that includes the cystic lesions of the kidney. They can be simple cysts that are benign. Complex or complicated cystic lesions need evaluation and can be malignant. Bosniak classification is used for renal cysts. Cysts appear as hypodense lesions (greyish) with a thin wall, with or without septations.

CT image showing a simple renal cyst:

Renal cell carcinoma (RCC) is the most common malignant tumour of the kidney. It usually occurs in the age group 50-70 years and macroscopic hematuria is seen in about 60% of the cases. It is a differential for angiomyolipoma but it is important to note that macroscopic fat is almost always associated with ossification or calcification.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A thin, 34-year-old male, presents with sharp pain and sudden onset dyspnea. Chest X-ray was performed and is shown below. What is the most probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Pneumothorax

The given chest radiograph clearly depicts the presence of pneumothorax, which represents air in the pleural space.

• The right hemithorax shows blackening (depicts area of low density) due to the presence of air.
• The visceral pleural line has separated from the chest wall by a transradiant zone devoid of vessels.
• The collapsed lung can be seen with a clear border.
• There is a mediastinal shift to the left side (contralateral), which is typically seen with cases of tension pneumothorax.

All the above features are suggestive of pneumothorax.

Note: Pleural effusions signify the presence of fluid accumulation in the pleural space. The fluid may have varying degrees of mobility depending on the nature of effusion (free-flowing or loculated).

While a small amount of free fluid is usually hard to detect on an erect PA chest x-ray, a significant pleural effusion (200-500 mL) is represented by obscured lateral and posterior costophrenic angles and the hemidiaphragm affected. Subsequently, homogenous opacification of the lower lung field develops, associated with concave superior margin relative to the lung. This margin is higher laterally than medially.

A massive pleural effusion cause dense opacification usually associated with a contralteral mediastinal shift.

Here is an image of a left-sided pleural effusion representing the homogenous opacification of the left lower and middle lung fields. There is associated blunting of the left sided costophrenic angle. The superior border of the effusion is concave and is higher laterally than medially.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: Based on the given image, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Pseudoaneurysm of internal carotid artery

The given image is a digital subtraction angiogram(DSA) and it shows a pseudoaneurysm of the internal carotid artery.

The right ICA injection anteroposterior view shows the neck of the pseudoaneurysm originating from the transverse segment of the cavernous portion of the ICA.

Option A: Carotico-cavernous fistula is characterized by the premature filling of the veins as shown in the image below:

Option C: Angiofibroma is characterised by tumour blush. It is the radiological enhancement of a tumour that reveals opacification of the well-vascularized tumours.

Option D: Hemangioma can be differentiated from other vascular malformations by the presence of well-circumscribed mass demonstrating intense tissue staining, usually in a lobular pattern.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: Which of the following will have reduced uptake on FDG PET scan?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Typical carcinoid

Typical carcinoid is more likely to have reduced uptake on FDG PET scan than an atypical carcinoid.

The low metabolic rate of tumors makes the tumor negative (show reduced uptake) on an FDG PET scan.

Typical examples are:

• Bronchoalveolar carcinoma ( Adenocarcinoma in situ)
• Carcinoid tumour (Typical > Atypical)

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A 39-year-old male patient presented with complaints of fever and cough. His chest radiograph shows air bronchogram sign. The probable diagnosis is :
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Consolidation

The radiograph shows air bronchogram sign in a lung with consolidation, seen in pneumonia, which is supported by the clinical history of this patient.

An air bronchogram is a tubular outline of an airway made visible when there is filling of the surrounding alveoli by fluid or inflammatory exudates.

The causes of air bronchogram are as follows:

• Lung consolidation
• Pulmonary edema
• Nonobstructive pulmonary atelectasis
• Severe interstitial disease
• Neoplasm
• Normal expiration

Pleural effusion is seen as a homogenous opacity on chest radiograph.

The given radiograph shows peribronchial thickening and air bronchogram sign:

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A child presented with a history of road traffic accident. The axial CT image of the child, shown below, is suggestive of _________
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Extradural Hemorrhage

The given CT image shows the typical bi-convex hyperdense lesion not crossing cranial sutures, characteristic of an extradural hemorrhage.

As the dura mater tends to adhere to the skull, the hematoma collecting between the skull and this dura is seen on CT sections as a biconvex dense area immediately beneath the skull vault, convex towards both the brain and the vault. They tend not to cross the suture lines.

The temporoparietal convexity is the most common site. The hematoma usually lies beneath a fracture of the squamous part of the temporal bone. The underlying brain is displaced but often appears intrinsically normal.

Monitoring an extradural hemorrhage and immediate intervention if necessary is an important step in management since the brain can herniate with increased bleeding that is causing raised ICP.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A child presents with history of having ingested a button battery. What is your next course of action?
options: Reassure and to check whether passed in stools
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Remove endoscopically

This case should be managed by removing the button battery endoscopically after confirming its position on X-Ray.

Button battery ingestion causes alkaline caustic injury, more in the areas surrounding the negative pole.

Management :

• The child is to be kept NPO until the oesophageal position of the battery is ruled out by X-ray scan. Vomiting should never be induced since the battery, which has passed through the esophagus, might lodge back again into it. Reassurance can be done only if the position of the battery is confirmed and if there are no symptoms.
• Since the question does not mention that the child is asymptomatic, the management of choice would be removing the battery endoscopically.
• Management also depends on battery life. Fresh batteries need to be removed as soon as possible as they have a higher concentration of injurious substances.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A middle-aged female patient with a history of cholelithiasis, presented with vomiting and abdominal pain. The abdominal radiograph showed Rigler’s triad. Which of these is not a component of Rigler’s triad?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Large bowel obstruction

Rigler’s triad is seen in gallstone ileus and consists of

• Pneumobilia
• Small bowel obstruction
• Ectopic gall stone (usually in the right iliac fossa)

This should not be confused with Rigler’s sign and Rigler's notch sign.

Rigler's Sign:

Seen in pneumoperitoneum. Here, the air is seen on both sides of the bowel wall unlike normally, where the air is seen only in the intraluminal side of the bowel.

Rigler's notch sign:

Refers to indentation seen in the border of a solid lung mass, which is thought to represents a feeding vessel, thus suggesting the presence of bronchial carcinoma. But, this is not specific and can also be seen in granulomatous infections.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: All among the following are ionizing radiations except:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. MRI

MRI is a technique that produces topographic images by means of magnetic fields and radiofrequency waves.

The ionizing radiations

• Alpha
• Beta
• Gamma
• X-Rays

The non-Ionizing radiations are:

• Radiofrequency waves
• UV rays
• Microwaves

Alpha and beta rays are particulate radiation (particles) whereas gamma and x-rays are electromagnetic rays. All electromagnetic waves have a constant velocity of 3×108 m/s and no mass. The electromagnetic spectrum, from low frequency to high frequency consists of:

Radiowaves < Microwaves < Infrared < Visible light < Ultraviolet < X-rays < Gamma rays

Note: W. C. Roentgen is the father of X-ray and the first medical X-ray by Roentgen was of his wife Anna Bertha's left hand. Physicists Peter Mansfield and Paul Lauterbur developed MRI-related imaging techniques in medicine and they were awarded the Nobel prize in 2003.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: From the X-ray given, pick out the probable diagnosis:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Pneumoperitoneum

The above X-ray clearly shows the presence of subdiaphragmatic free gas in the right upper quadrant. This indicates pneumoperitoneum.

Pneumoperitoneum is the presence of free gas within the peritoneal cavity but outside the viscera. The most common cause of pneumoperitoneum is bowel perforation.

• Gastric and posterior duodenal perforations are seen in long-standing cases of peptic ulcers.
• Intestinal perforations are seen with ischemia, inflammation, diverticula, or obstruction.
• Other causes also include iatrogenic, penetrating injuries, prolonged mechanical ventilation, peritoneal dialysis, etc.

Signs of pneumoperitoneum:

• Bowel-related signs

• Double wall sign/Rigler's sign/gas-relief sign- Air is seen on both sides of the bowel wall.
• Telltale triangle sign/triangle sign - Triangle of gas formed between three loops of the bowel or between the abdominal wall and two loops of the bowel.

• Peritoneal ligament-related signs

• Football sign- Air outlines the confines of the peritoneal cavity
• Falciform ligament sign-  Air outlines the falciform ligament
• Lateral umbilical ligament sign/inverted "V" sign- Air outlines the lateral umbilical ligament
• Urachus sign - Air outlines the urachus

• Right upper quadrant signs

• Cupola sign- Air outlines the median subphrenic space
• Fissure for ligamentum teres sign- Air outlines the ligamentum teres
• Hepatic edge sign- Cigar-shaped free-air pocket in the subhepatic region. It tracks superomedial following the contours of the liver
• Lucent liver sign - Reduction of hepatic radiodensity due to accumulation of free gas anterior to the liver
• Morison's pouch sign / Doge cap sign - Triangular/ crescentic gas lucency bound by the 11th rib
• Periportal free gas sign.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: Identify the procedure.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Myelography

The procedure depicted in the image represents myelography.

Myelography is a procedure used to evaluate spinal conditions. X-ray myelography can be used to evaluate the spinal canal in patients with spondylolisthesis. While MRI has largely replaced X-ray myelography it is done when there is a contraindication to MRI (Eg; non-compatible pacemaker, severe claustrophobia).

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: The Doppler waveform of the venous blood flow in lower limb DVT is _____.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Monophasic

The Doppler waveform of the venous blood flow in lower limb DVT is monophasic proximal to the level of obstruction.

The normal venous waveform shows a variation (phasicity) secondary to respiration referred to as respirophasic waveform. Loss of this phasic variation results in a monophasic waveform suggestive of venous obstruction proximal to the level of interrogation.

A normal artery has a triphasic signal. The waveform becomes biphasic in mild-moderate stenosis and monophasic in severe stenosis.

The image given below shows the normal triphasic signal from an artery.

Monophasic waveform:

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: What is the diagnosis shown in the image below?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Cervical rib

The given X-ray shows cervical rib.

Patients with a cervical rib usually show a lump and tenderness in the supraclavicular fossa. The pallor and paresthesias are due to vascular and neural compressions respectively. A radiograph of the neck is useful in detecting a cervical rib.

However, the absence of a rib on the x-ray does not rule out the possibility of a cervical rib. CT and MRI are more sensitive.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: All lung carcinomas for diagnosis requires CECT thorax but MRI is useful in which of the following:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Pancoast tumor

MRI is useful in Pancoast tumor because of the associated soft tissue infiltration, extent of which can be best visualised using an MRI

Pancoast syndrome/superior sulcus tumor results from a local extension of a tumor growing in the apex of the lung, with the involvement of C8, T1, and T2 nerve roots.

It presents with pain that radiates to the ulnar distribution of the arm, often with the destruction of the 1st and 2nd ribs. Patients with the central or endobronchial growth of the primary tumor may present with a cough, hemoptysis, wheeze, stridor, dyspnea, or post-obstructive pneumonitis.

Regional spread can cause

• Tracheal obstruction,
• Esophageal compression with dysphagia
• Recurrent laryngeal paralysis with hoarseness
• Phrenic nerve palsy with the elevation of the hemidiaphragm and dyspnea
• Sympathetic nerve paralysis with Horner’s syndrome (enophthalmos, ptosis, miosis, and anhydrosis).

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: An 8-year old child presents with the history of cough for 7 months. He also gives a history of haemoptysis for 1 month and fever for 4 days. The X-ray is given below. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Consolidation

The given X-ray shows opacities in the right middle lobe and history of fever, cough and haemoptysis suggesting consolidation due to lobar pneumonia.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: The following image of a FAST scan in a trauma patient suggests:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Positive fast

The image of FAST in a trauma patient suggests Positive FAST as there is a fluid collection in the abdominal cavity. The thin anechoic area located between the liver(on the left) and the Kidney(on the right) is a collection of fluid visualized in this RUQ Sonogram image.

FAST stands for Focused assessment with sonography for trauma. It is a rapid diagnostic examination to assess patients with potential thoracoabdominal injuries. It is performed within 2-4 minutes.

Technique:

• Patient in the supine position
• 3.5-5.0 MHz convex transducer
• Following regions are scanned :

• Subxiphoid: assess for pericardial effusion and left lobe liver injuries
• Right upper quadrant: assess for right liver injuries, right kidney injury, and Morison pouch
• Left upper quadrant: assess for splenic injury and left kidney injury
• Suprapubic region: assess the bladder and pouch of Douglas

An "extended FAST or eFAST" scan may be performed: left and right thoracic views to assess for pneumothorax and haemothorax.

Sequentially order of FAST is:- pericardial sac, the Right Upper Quadrant (RUQ), Left Upper Quadrant (LUQ), and pelvis.

4 ‘Ps’ are evaluated in sequence: Pericardial sac → Perihepatic region → Perisplenic region → Pelvis.

Note:-

In Pneumoperitoneum, air is collected in the peritoneal cavity which is usually hyperechoic not anechoic and would appear white in the ultrasound image.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: The given USG of lung shows:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Sea shore sign

The given image shows the seashore sign seen in M-mode imaging of the normal lung.

M-mode is defined as the time-motion display of the ultrasound wave along a chosen ultrasound line. With M-Mode, even rapid motions can be displayed, measured, and recorded.

In the M-mode of USG, the motionless portion of the chest above the pleural line creates horizontal ‘waves', and the sliding below the pleural line creates a granular pattern, the ‘sand’. The resultant picture is one that resembles waves crashing in onto the sand and is therefore called the ‘seashore sign’ and is present in a normal lung.

Option A: Stratosphere sign or barcode sign is a finding in the M-mode seen as parallel horizontal lines above and below the pleural line. This is seen in pneumothorax.

Option C: There is no named sign called troposphere sign.

Option D: Mirror image artifact is seen when there is a highly reflective surface (eg: Diaphragm) in the path of the primary beam.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A 22-year-old male was brought to the emergency room following a road traffic accident. On examination, his GCS was E2M2V3. He had no fractures and no hydrocephalus or raised intracranial pressure. Non-contrast CT was performed and was found to be normal. The likely diagnosis is
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Diffuse axonal injury

The given clinical scenario of an RTA with no imaging abnormality along with a disproportionate clinical manifestation suggests diffuse axonal injury.

It is caused due to stretching of axons in subcortical white matter due to sudden deceleration injuries. It is usually associated with mild nonspecific changes in NCCT. It is visualized on T2 MRI characterized by multiple lesions showing microbleeds or linear hypointensities. It may also show disruption of white matter tracts on tractography.

Other options

Post-concussion syndrome usually follows mild traumatic brain injury. It does not have a severe clinical status as seen in this patient.

Extradural hemorrhage is produced usually results secondary to trauma to head. The bleeding is usually arterial and blood collects between outer dura and inner table of the skull. It can very well be visualized on CT.

A cerebral herniation is defined as a shift of cerebral tissue in an adjacent space. Intracranial brain herniation can be classified into 3 types - subfalcine, transtentorial and tonsillar. A distinct clinical picture can be produced as a result of compression of neurovascular structures by the herniating part. CT is the imaging modality of choice because it can be done rapidly.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A 25-year-old male with Marfanoid features presented with sudden onset breathlessness. The chest X-ray is given below. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Pneumothorax

The chest X-ray demonstrating tracheal deviation and displacement of the heart away from the affected side along with the partial collapse of the left lung in the above condition points to a diagnosis of left-sided pneumothorax.

Marfan's syndrome is one of the causes for seconday spontaneous pneumothorax in adults.

Pneumothorax refers to the collection of air in the pleural space.

Chest radiograph in spontaneous pneumothorax demonstrates:

• Thin, sharp white line, demarcating the visceral pleural edge
• Absence of lung markings seen peripheral to this line
• Peripheral space radiolucent compared to adjacent lung
• Complete lung collapse, as well as subcutaneous emphysema and pneumomediastinum, may be seen
• Deep sulcus sign (on supine chest radiograph)

Deep sulcus sign: On a supine position(common in the ICU), air collects anteriorly and basally, within the non-dependent portions of the pleural space, abnormally deepening the costophrenic angle. This sign is indicative of pneumothorax in such patients and may be the only visible clue, especially when patient can not be imaged upright.

The image below is plain chest x-ray showing pneumothorax with deep sulcus sign (shown by arrow):

When there is a progressive accumulation of air intrapleurally in the thoracic cavity (caused by a valve effect during inspiration and expiration), it is called Tension pneumothorax. It can result in compression of mediastinal structures and compromise cardiopulmonary function. It is life-threatening and requires emergency intervention.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A 46-year-old male presented with chronic back pain and neck stiffness. X-ray cervical spine is given below. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Diffuse idiopathic skeletal hyperostosis

The given clinical scenario and the radiograph showing ossification of the anterior longitudinal ligament, in front of the C2 to C7 cervical vertebral bodies, point towards a diagnosis of Diffuse Idiopathic Skeletal Hyperostosis (DISH). It is also referred to as Forestier disease.

DISH is a common disorder characterized by bone and calcium formation at the sites of ligamentous insertions. It occurs in the middle-aged or elderly. The radiograph shows calcification of anterior and sometimes posterior longitudinal ligaments appearing as flowing or dripping-like candle wax. It is usually asymptomatic but the calcification might cause compression of the spinal cord and can be better visualized on CT and MRI. In contrast to ankylosing spondylitis, the sacroiliac joints are usually spared.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: An 18-year-old girl presented with seizures and her radiological image is as given below. Knowing that the MR spectroscopy of the lesion showed elevated choline, alanine, and lactate, what is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Neurocysticercosis

The given radiological image and history of seizures suggests a diagnosis of neurocysticercosis.

Neurocysticercosis presents with seizures, hydrocephalus, raised ICP, and may even cause signs of chronic meningitis. The given image shows multilobulated cystic lesions (with scolex) in the subarachnoid space, typical parenchymal brain calcifications are suggestive of neurocysticercosis caused by T. solium (Cysticercosis cellulose).

• Cyst with a dot sign: seen in both MRI and CT and the dot represents the eccentrically placed scolex of the parasite.

MR Spectroscopy features of neurocysticercosis include elevated lactate, alanine, succinate, and choline levels and reduced levels of N -acetyl aspartate and creatine. Escobar's pathological stages describe 4 stages - vesicular, colloidal vesicular, granular nodular, and nodular calcified.

Other options

• Solid or ring enhancement is typical in the post-contrast images of tuberculoma. A central focus of calcification with a ring of peripheral enhancement (the "target sign") is also described in tuberculosis but is not specific to it.
• Cerebral toxoplasmosis appears as multiple hypodense regions predominantly in the basal ganglia and at the corticomedullary junction. It can be associated with ring enhancing lesions as well.
• Cryptococcosis is usually associated with normal scans but may show cerebral atrophy, hydrocephalus or mass lesions as well.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: Which of the following is a finding of large bowel obstruction?
options: Dilated loops of intestine with plica circularis
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Dilated loops with haustrations

Dilated bowel loops with haustrations is a feature of large bowel obstruction.

In large bowel obstruction, the colon is distended proximally with the distal portion collapsed. The colon is considered dilated if it is more than 6 cm in diameter while the cut off for caecum is 9cm.

Other options:

Dilated loops of the intestine with plica circularis (valvulae conniventes) and predominantly central loops are features of the small bowel obstruction. The small bowel is considered dilated if it is more than 3 cm in diameter.

The string of pearls sign is also a feature of small bowel obstruction seen in plain radiographs or CT. It represents a row of gas bubbles trapped between the valvulae conniventes.

Differences in small and large bowel obstruction on radiography are listed below:

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: Which of the following statements is false regarding acute radiation syndrome?
options: GI manifestations occurs at a lower radiation dose than bone marrow depression
Bone marrow suppression appear at doses greater than 1 Gy
Bone marrow suppression occurs earlier than neurovascular effects
GI manifestations occur at a lower radiation dose than neurovascular effects
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. GI manifestations occurs at a lower radiation dose than bone marrow depression

GI manifestations do not occur at a lower radiation dose than bone marrow depression.

Stages of Acute Radiation Syndrome (ARS)

The prodromal phase manifests with non-specific symptoms like nausea, vomiting, anorexia. Early and persistent symptoms predict severity.

Latent phase: The patient looks and feels generally healthy for a few hours or even up to a few weeks. In severe cases, this phase may be absent.

Manifest illness phase: Symptoms are seen as per the radiation dose. Tissues with greater rates of cellular division are most radiosensitive, and hence the hematopoietic and gastrointestinal systems are the most affected.

Recovery phase or Death: The recovery phase will be seen after the manifest stage when the patient recovers from the acute exposure. The time taken for recovery will depend on the severity of the injury and the organ system affected.

Radiation dose
Sub-syndrome

~1-2 Gy

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: 8-month-old boy is brought to the emergency department due to respiratory distress. Severe cough and wheezing began an hour ago while the patient was playing at his cousin’s house. Chest radiograph is shown in the image below. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient’s symptoms?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Foreign body aspiration

Foreign body aspiration should be suspected in infants with sudden onset cough, wheeze, unilateral decreased breath sounds and respiratory distress, especially during play or eating. Chest X-ray may show unilateral hyperinflation (air trapping) due to a ball-valve obstruction, even if the foreign body is radiolucent.

• X-ray: unilateral hyperlucent lung, mediastinal shift, or collapse
• Most common site: Right main bronchus (more vertical and wider)

Diagnosis & management:

• High suspicion → Rigid bronchoscopy (gold standard)
• Both diagnostic and therapeutic

Why not other options?

A. Anaphylaxis: Would have urticaria, hypotension, bilateral wheeze — not unilateral hyperinflation.

B. Asthma: Recurrent episodes, bilateral wheeze; rare at 8 months and not sudden during play.

C. Bronchiolitis: Viral prodrome (fever, coryza), bilateral findings.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A 19-year-old college student who had a history of frequent respiratory infections as a child presents to the OPD. He has been experiencing recurrent episodes of coughing and shortness of breath over the past few months. He also complains of fatigue and chest pain, particularly on the left side. The CT scan reveals a mass in the lower lobe of his left lung as shown. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Sequestration

Pulmonary sequestration is a congenital anomaly characterized by non-functioning lung tissue that lacks normal communication with the tracheobronchial tree and receives arterial supply from the systemic circulation (usually aorta). It commonly presents in adolescents or young adults with recurrent localized lung infections, most often in the posterior basal segment of the left lower lobe.

Key Imaging Features (CT):

• Well-defined mass in lower lobe (usually left)
• Systemic arterial supply from aorta
• No communication with bronchial tree

Types:

• Intralobar sequestration (most common): within normal lung, recurrent infections
• Extralobar sequestration: separate pleural covering, seen in infants

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A 2-month-old infant presents with tachypnea, poor feeding, and recurrent lower respiratory tract infections. On examination, there is tachycardia, mild right-sided chest flattening, and a soft continuous murmur heard over the right lower lung field. SpO₂ is 92%. ECHO shows: Right pulmonary veins draining into the IVC Right lung smaller than left Evidence of left-to-right shunt Mild pulmonary hypertension What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Anomalous left coronary artery from pulmonary artery (ALCAPA)
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Scimitar syndrome

Scimitar syndrome is a form of partial anomalous pulmonary venous return where the right pulmonary veins drain into the IVC, often associated with a hypoplastic right lung, dextroposition of heart, and left-to-right shunt. On chest X-ray, a characteristic curved vascular shadow along the right cardiac border (“scimitar sign”) may be seen. Infants present with recurrent respiratory infections, tachypnea, and features of pulmonary hypertension due to increased pulmonary blood flow.

Why not others:

• TAPVR: All pulmonary veins drain abnormally; causes severe cyanosis early. Here only right pulmonary veins → IVC (partial).
• Pulmonary sequestration: Nonfunctioning lung tissue with systemic arterial supply; no anomalous pulmonary venous drainage.
• ALCAPA: Anomalous coronary artery → presents with heart failure/ischemia, not lung hypoplasia or anomalous pulmonary veins.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A 22-year-old male undergoes CT brain for evaluation of seizures. The scan (image shown) reveals a well-defined midline lesion along the corpus callosum with areas of fat attenuation and curvilinear calcifications along its margins. Which of the following statements regarding this condition is/are correct? A. It is a true neoplasm arising from neuroepithelial tissue B. It is commonly associated with agenesis or dysgenesis of the corpus callosum C. The calcification pattern described is characteristic and termed “bracket calcification” D. It shows intense contrast enhancement on CT E. It arises due to abnormal persistence and maldifferentiation of primitive meninx
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. B, C, E

• B is correct: Corpus callosum lipoma is frequently associated with callosal agenesis/dysgenesis
• C is correct: Curvilinear peripheral calcifications → “bracket sign”, classic imaging clue
• E is correct: It is a congenital malformation, arising from abnormal persistence of primitive meninx, not a true tumor
• A is incorrect: It is not a true neoplasm
• D is incorrect: Lipomas show fat density and do not enhance significantly

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A 24-year-old female comes to emergency with complaints of acute abdominal pain. The attending physician wants to get an abdominal X-ray done for the same. What does the “10 day rule” advise regarding x-ray exposure for women of child bearing age refer to?
options: A gap of less than 10 days between 2 successive X rays.
Avoid non urgent X-rays within 10 days post menstruation.
Perform X-rays during the first 10 days of the menstrual cycle.
X-rays should be avoided 10 days before menstruation.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Perform X-rays during the first 10 days of the menstrual cycle.

• The “10-day rule” recommends that non-urgent radiological examinations involving ionizing radiation in women of reproductive age should be performed within the first 10 days of the menstrual cycle (counting from the first day of menstruation).
• This timing minimizes the risk of irradiating an unrecognized early pregnancy, as ovulation and potential conception are unlikely during this period.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A 25-year-old male presents with progressive hearing loss in the right ear and occasional imbalance over the past year. MRI of the brain is shown below. Which of the following genetic mutations is most likely associated with this patient's condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Merlin

Vestibular schwannoma (acoustic neuroma) presents with progressive unilateral sensorineural hearing loss and imbalance and is strongly associated with mutation of the NF2 gene encoding merlin (schwannomin) on chromosome 22.

• Tumor arises from Schwann cells of vestibular division of CN VIII
• MRI: Cerebellopontine angle (CPA) enhancing mass

Differentiation:

• Neurofibromin → NF1 (cafe au lait macules, optic nerve gliomas, neurofibromas)
• Merlin (NF2) → Vestibular schwannoma
• GNAS → McCune-Albright syndrome, toxic thyroid nodule
• GNAQ → Uveal melanoma, storage weber syndrome.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A 25-year-old shepherd from Rajasthan presents with cough and mild chest pain for past few days. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Hydatid cyst

A well-defined rounded cystic lesion in the lung of a patient from an endemic rural area (e.g., shepherd with exposure to sheep/dogs) is characteristic of a pulmonary hydatid cyst caused by Echinococcus granulosus. Chest X-ray may show a solitary, spherical homogeneous opacity; if ruptured, signs like water-lily sign or air crescent sign may appear. Hydatid disease commonly involves liver and lungs and is associated with exposure to livestock and dogs.

Why not other options:

A. Lung abscess: Thick-walled cavity with air-fluid level and surrounding consolidation; usually with fever and toxicity.

B. Pneumatocele: Thin-walled air-filled cyst, typically post-staphylococcal pneumonia in children.

C. Tuberculoma: Solid round opacity, often in upper lobes ± calcification; not a large smooth cyst.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A 28-year-old man from rural area presents with painless hematuria and irritative voiding symptoms. Abdominal X-ray is shown below. This radiographic pattern is most characteristic of:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Schistosomiasis

Curvilinear or “eggshell” calcification outlining the urinary bladder on X-ray is characteristic of urinary schistosomiasis (Schistosoma haematobium).

Patients typically present with painless hematuria and irritative urinary symptoms, and chronic infection can lead to bladder wall fibrosis, calcification, and increased risk of squamous cell carcinoma of the bladder.

Why not others:

• GU tuberculosis: Thimble bladder, irregular calcification — not smooth rim.
• Neurogenic bladder: Trabeculated/distended bladder, no calcification.
• Pelvic abscess: Soft tissue mass, no bladder wall calcification.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A 28-year-old man presents with cough for 1 week and hemoptysis for 1 month. He has had fever for the last 14 days. Chest Xray PA is given below. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Left upper lobe (LUL) collapse

Left upper lobe collapse on chest X-ray is suggested by a veil-like opacity over the left lung with elevation of the left hilum and the classic Luftsichel sign (crescent of air adjacent to the aortic arch due to hyperinflated lower lobe).

On lateral view, anterior displacement of the oblique fissure confirms upper lobe collapse. Recognition of lobar collapse patterns helps localize disease and identify underlying causes such as endobronchial obstruction (e.g., TB, tumor, mucus plug).

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A 28-year-old man presents with the history of cough for one week. He also gives a history of hemoptysis for 1 month and fever for 4 days. The X-ray is given below. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. LLL consolidation

On chest X-ray, loss of the left hemidiaphragm silhouette with preserved left heart border indicates left lower lobe (LLL) consolidation due to the silhouette sign, which helps localize lung pathology.

Silhouette Sign Principle: Loss of normal border occurs when pathology is in anatomical contact with that structure.

Localization:

• LLL consolidation → Obscures left hemidiaphragm
• Lingular consolidation → Obscures left heart border
• RML consolidation → Obscures right heart border
• RLL consolidation → Obscures right hemidiaphragm

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A 3-day-old newborn baby boy is brought to the hospital with difficulty breathing, cyanosis and coughing whenever he is fed. The baby was born full-term via vaginal delivery, and his mother had an uneventful pregnancy. He had a birth weight of 2.8 kg and was discharged from the hospital after 48 hours of observation. On examination, the baby appears to be in respiratory distress, with increased work of breathing and decreased oxygen saturation levels. What would be the best contrast of choice for study?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Iohexol

A neonate with cyanosis, coughing, and respiratory distress during feeding suggests tracheoesophageal fistula (TEF)/esophageal atresia.

For contrast study in suspected TEF:

• Use a non-ionic, water-soluble contrast (e.g., Iohexol)
• It is less irritating to lungs if aspirated
• Safer than hyperosmolar agents like Gastrografin

Avoid:

• Barium → causes severe chemical pneumonitis if aspirated
• Gastrografin → hyperosmolar, risk of pulmonary edema

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A 3-month-old baby presents to you with jaundice. USG of the liver shows the following abnormality. What is the best investigation to confirm the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Intra-operative cholangiography

In infants with persistent jaundice and ultrasound features suggestive of biliary atresia (e.g., triangular cord sign, absent/atrophic gallbladder), the gold standard for confirmation is intra-operative cholangiography, which demonstrates absent or discontinuous extrahepatic bile ducts.

• Presents with prolonged neonatal jaundice, pale stools, dark urine
• USG: triangular cord sign, small/absent gallbladder
• Best confirmatory test: Intraoperative cholangiography
• Early diagnosis critical → Kasai portoenterostomy ideally before 6–8 weeks

Other investigations:

• HIDA scan → screening/supportive, not definitive
• MRCP → limited in infants
• Liver biopsy → supportive

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A 3-year-old boy presents with recurrent febrile urinary tract infections. Ultrasound shows mild hydronephrosis. A voiding cystourethrogram (VCUG) is shown below. Which of the following statements regarding is/are correct? A. It is most commonly due to a congenital short intravesical ureter B. Grade IV is characterized by ureteral tortuosity and calyceal blunting C. It predisposes to renal scarring predominantly due to sterile urine backflow D. Long-term prophylactic antibiotics are used to prevent recurrent UTIs in selected cases E. Surgical correction is indicated in cases of Grade I–II VUR
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. A, B, D

• A is correct: Primary VUR results from a short intramural ureter, leading to incompetence of the vesicoureteral junction.
• B is correct: Grade III VUR shows mild to moderate dilatation with calyceal blunting.
• C is incorrect: Renal scarring is mainly due to infected reflux (pyelonephritis), not sterile reflux.
• D is correct: Antibiotic prophylaxis is used in selected children to prevent recurrent UTIs and renal damage.
• E is incorrect: Low-grade VUR (Grade I–II) is usually managed conservatively, not surgically.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A 3-year-old child is brought to the emergency department after accidental ingestion of a metallic object. The child has mild drooling but is otherwise stable. A chest X-ray (image shown) demonstrates a round radio-opaque object in the upper mediastinum. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Reassure and observe for spontaneous passage
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Urgent endoscopic removal

The double ring (halo) sign on X-ray indicates a button battery, not a coin. This is due to the bilaminar structure of the battery producing two concentric rings.

Button batteries in the esophagus are a medical emergency because they can cause:

• Liquefaction necrosis
• Rapid mucosal injury (within hours)
• Risk of perforation and fistula (e.g., tracheoesophageal fistula)

Thus, urgent endoscopic removal is mandatory, even if the child is stable.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A 30-year-old HIV-positive man presents with fever for 3 weeks, dry cough, and significant weight loss. His HRCT thorax is given below. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia

This patient has the classic presentation of Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PJP), the most common opportunistic pneumonia in patients with advanced HIV infection (CD4 count <200 cells/mm³).

Key clues in the vignette:

• HIV-positive patient
• Subacute illness (weeks rather than days)
• Dry (nonproductive) cough
• Progressive dyspnea
• Fever and weight loss
• HRCT showing diffuse bilateral ground-glass opacities
• Hypoxemia out of proportion to chest auscultation findings

Characteristic imaging

Chest X-ray

• Bilateral diffuse perihilar interstitial infiltrates (may be normal early)

HRCT

• Diffuse bilateral ground-glass opacities (most characteristic)
• Relative subpleural sparing
• Thin-walled cysts or pneumatoceles may occur

Why the other options are incorrect?

A. Staphylococcal pneumonia

• Acute, severe illness with high fever
• Patchy bronchopneumonia, cavitation, lung abscesses, pneumatoceles
• Productive cough is common

B. Pneumococcal pneumonia

• Sudden onset of fever with productive cough
• Classically causes lobar consolidation
• Not diffuse bilateral ground-glass infiltrates

C. Tuberculosis

• Common in HIV but usually presents with upper lobe infiltrates, cavitary lesions (higher CD4), or miliary/disseminated disease (lower CD4)
• HRCT findings are not predominantly diffuse ground-glass opacities

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A 30-year-old male presents with chronic sinusitis and recurrent respiratory tract infections since childhood. CXR is shown below. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Kartagener syndrome

Kartagener syndrome is a subtype of primary ciliary dyskinesia characterized by the triad of:

• Chronic sinusitis
• Bronchiectasis with recurrent respiratory infections
• Situs inversus/dextrocardia on chest X-ray

It results from defective dynein arms causing impaired mucociliary clearance and recurrent infections since childhood.

Why not others?

A. Cystic fibrosis: Causes recurrent infections, but usually has pancreatic insufficiency, malabsorption, infertility, not situs inversus.

C. Primary ciliary dyskinesia: Broad term; Kartagener is its classic triad variant with situs inversus (seen on CXR).

D. Asthma: Causes wheeze, not chronic sinusitis + lifelong recurrent infections + bronchiectasis.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A 30-year-old multiparous woman presents with chronic lower back pain. The pain is non-radiating, worse with activity, and improves with rest. There are no neurological deficits. X-ray pelvis shows bilateral symmetric sclerosis of the iliac side of the sacroiliac joints, with joint spaces preserved. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Osteitis condensans ilii

Osteitis Condensans iliiis a benign condition

• Seen mostly in multiparous women
• Causes triangular sclerosis on iliac side
• SI joint space remains normal
• No joint erosions ,No fusion

To rule out Ankylosing spondylitis:

• Causes erosions
• Causes joint space narrowing
• Eventually leads to joint fusion
• Pain is inflammatory
• Pain worse in morning, better with activity.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A 32-year-old HIV-positive man with CD4 count of 60 cells/µL presents with headache, confusion, and focal seizures. MRI brain given below. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Cerebral Toxoplasmosis

• In HIV patients with CD4 <100 cells/µL, multiple ring-enhancing brain lesions with surrounding edema on MRI are most commonly due to cerebral toxoplasmosis.
• Lesions are typically multiple, involve basal ganglia or corticomedullary junction, and present with headache, seizures, and focal deficits.
• CNS lymphoma is usually solitary, while neurocysticercosis shows cysts with scolex and tuberculomas often have different clinical context.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A 32-year-old woman presents to the breast clinic with a painless lump in her left breast that she discovered during a self-examination. On examination, a well-defined, mobile, firm, and non-tender mass of 2 cm is palpated in the upper outer quadrant of the left breast. The overlying skin is smooth, and there is no nipple discharge or lymphadenopathy. Mammogram is shown below. Classify the following mammography lesion as per BIRADS staging:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. BIRADS 2

BI-RADS 2 (benign) lesions show classic benign features such as well-defined margins, coarse “popcorn” calcifications, simple cysts, or fibroadenoma, with no suspicious features. These findings have 0% malignancy risk and require routine screening only, not biopsy or short-interval follow-up.

BI-RADS Scoring System (Mammography):

• BI-RADS 0: Incomplete – need additional imaging
• BI-RADS 1: Negative (normal)
• BI-RADS 2: Benign lesion (0% malignancy) → routine screening
• BI-RADS 3: Probably benign (<2% risk) → short-interval follow-up (6 months)
• BI-RADS 4: Suspicious (2–95% risk) → biopsy required

o    4A: Low suspicion

o    4B: Moderate

o    4C: High
• BI-RADS 5: Highly suggestive of malignancy (>95%) → treat as cancer
• BI-RADS 6: Known biopsy-proven malignancy

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A 35-year-old man with a history of RTA with intense pain in the suprapubic region. On examination, abdominal distention was present. Heart rate and blood pressure was normal. Imaging is shown below. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Extraperitoneal bladder rupture

Bladder injury following blunt trauma (e.g., RTA) is classified as intraperitoneal or extraperitoneal rupture, and imaging findings on retrograde cystography/CT cystography help differentiate them.

Extrapertioneal bladder rupture (Most common; associated with pelvic fracture):

• Contrast extravasation confined to perivesical space
• “Flame-shaped” or irregular contrast around bladder
• Does not outline bowel loops
• Usually managed conservatively with catheter drainage

Intraperitoneal bladder rupture:

• Contrast outlines bowel loops
• Contrast seen in peritoneal cavity (paracolic gutters)
• Requires surgical repair

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A 38-year-old female presented to the emergency department with the sudden onset of severe epigastric pain. On physical exam, she had a temperature of 100.4°F, a pulse of 115 bpm and a blood pressure of 125/72 mmHg. Abdomen was tender & rigid. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Pneumoperitoneum

Pneumoperitoneum refers to free air within the peritoneal cavity, most commonly due to perforation of a hollow viscus (e.g., perforated peptic ulcer). On erect chest X-ray, it appears as air under the diaphragm, especially under the right hemidiaphragm.

• Sudden severe abdominal pain
• Board-like rigidity (peritonitis)
• Fever, tachycardia
• Surgical emergency

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A 4-month-old girl is diagnosed with a febrile urinary tract infection. A voiding cystourethrogram is shown in the image. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this infant's presentation?
options: Obstruction due to a renal stone
Presence of a posterior urethral valve
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Congenital short intravesical ureter length

In infants with recurrent febrile UTI, vesicoureteral reflux (VUR) is the most common underlying cause. It occurs due to a congenitally short intravesical ureter, leading to an incompetent ureterovesical junction and retrograde flow of urine from bladder to ureter and kidney.

Key Imaging (VCUG):

• Contrast refluxing from bladder into ureters ± kidneys
• May show dilated ureters and renal pelvis

Pathophysiology:

Short submucosal ureteric tunnel → Loss of flap-valve mechanism → Urine reflux → Recurrent UTI and renal scarring

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A 4-year-old unimmunized child presents with sudden onset high fever, dysphagia, drooling, and muffled “hot potato” voice. The child is anxious and sitting upright. Lateral neck X-ray image is shown below. Which of the following statements regarding this condition is/are correct? A. It is most commonly caused by Haemophilus influenzae type b B. Direct laryngoscopic examination should be performed immediately in the emergency room C. Lateral neck X-ray may show obliteration of the vallecula (“vallecula sign”) D. Securing the airway takes precedence over radiological confirmation E. It commonly presents with barking cough and responds to steroids alone
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. A, C, D

• A is correct: Classical cause is H. influenzae type b (though incidence reduced with vaccination)
• B is incorrect: Direct examination can precipitate complete airway obstruction
• C is correct: Vallecula sign (loss of normal air space) is an additional radiological clue
• D is correct: Airway management is the first priority
• E is incorrect: Barking cough suggests croup, not epiglottitis

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A 42-year-old man presents with acidity and abdominal pain for the past few months, not relieved by taking antacids. CECT abdomen is shown below. Which of the following is the next best investigation?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Secretin stimulation test

Refractory peptic ulcer disease with abdominal pain and imaging suggestive of a pancreatic/duodenal lesion should raise suspicion for gastrinoma (Zollinger–Ellison syndrome).

The secretin stimulation test is the most sensitive confirmatory test for gastrinoma — paradoxically, gastrin levels increase after secretin administration, unlike normal physiology.

Why not others?

A. Endoscopic ultrasound: For tumor localization after confirming gastrinoma.

C. H. pylori test: For routine peptic ulcer; does not explain refractory ulcers with pancreatic lesion.

D. Barium study: Shows ulcer only, not the cause.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A 42-year-old man presents with long-standing hypertension, recurrent flank pain, and intermittent hematuria. His father developed end-stage renal disease at the age of 55 years. A CT scan of the abdomen is performed, as shown in the accompanying video. Which of the following genetic mutations is associated with a more severe phenotype and earlier progression to end-stage kidney disease in this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. PKD1 mutation on chromosome 16

PKD1-associated ADPKD generally has a more severe phenotype, with earlier development of renal complications and progression to kidney failure compared with PKD2-associated ADPKD, which typically follows a milder course.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A 42-year-old woman presents with a severe, sudden-onset, throbbing headache and double vision for the past 30 minutes. She has a history of migraine and reports frequent headaches. She has not had her period for several months. On examination, her blood pressure is 95/61 mm Hg, and visual field testing reveals decreased visual acuity and loss of peripheral vision in both eyes. MRI of brain is shown below. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Pituitary apoplexy

Key clues:

• 42-year-old woman
• Sudden severe throbbing headache
• Loss of peripheral vision in both eyes → bitemporal hemianopia
• MRI shows a sellar/suprasellar mass
• Hypotensive (95/61 mmHg)

👉 Acute hemorrhage/infarction into a pituitary adenoma. Diagnosis: Pituitary apoplexy

Pituitary apoplexy = Acute hemorrhage or infarction of a pituitary tumor.

• It is a neurosurgical and endocrine emergency requiring urgent steroids and decompression.

Classic presentation:

• Sudden severe headache
• Visual field defects (optic chiasm compression → bitemporal hemianopia)
• Hypotension (acute ACTH deficiency → adrenal crisis)
• The MRI image shows a sellar mass consistent with this.

Transient ischemic attack:

• DOES NOT cause chiasmal compression pattern.
• Does not show sellar mass on MRI.

Sheehan syndrome:

• Postpartum pituitary infarction.
• No obstetric history here.

Migraine with aura: Can cause visual symptoms but: No chiasmal defect, No hypotension, No sellar mass

TAKEAWAY:

Sudden worst headache + bitemporal hemianopia + hypotension = Think pituitary apoplexy

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A 44-year-old man presents with intermittent dysphagia and episodes of retrosternal chest pain unrelated to exertion. A barium swallow study is performed (image shown). Which of the following is the most appropriate identification of the radiological finding?
options: Bird beak sign of achalasia cardia
Corkscrew esophagus of diffuse esophageal spasm
Feline esophagus due to transient transverse folds
Rat tail narrowing due to malignant stricture
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Feline esophagus due to transient transverse folds

The feline esophagus sign refers to multiple fine, closely spaced transverse mucosal folds seen on barium swallow due to transient, non-propulsive esophageal contractions.

• Represents early or mild esophageal motility disorder (often related to diffuse esophageal spasm)
• Folds are transient and subtle, unlike fixed structural abnormalities
• Caused by uncoordinated contraction of circular muscle layer

Important differentiation:

• Feline esophagus → fine transverse folds (early spasm)
• Corkscrew esophagus → multiple deep, irregular contractions (advanced spasm)
• Bird beak → achalasia (LES failure)
• Rat tail → malignancy (irregular narrowing)

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A 45 year old lady presents with acute abdominal pain and distension. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Large bowel obstruction due to fecolith
Small bowel obstruction due to bowel perforation
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Cecal volvulus

Cecal volvulus presents with acute abdominal pain and distension and shows a markedly dilated, displaced cecum (often in left upper abdomen) on X-ray with a single dilated loop > 9cm in diameter with the presence of haustrations and small bowel obstruction features.

Key distinction:

• Cecal volvulus: dilated cecum displaced upward/left, small bowel dilatation
• Sigmoid volvulus: massively dilated loop from pelvis with classic coffee-bean pointing to RUQ and no small bowel dilatation initially.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A 45-year-old male patient presents to their primary care physician with a complaint of dysphagia. He reports that he experiences a sensation of food getting stuck in his throat when he eats. He also reports some mild chest discomfort with exertion. The patient has a history of Down syndrome and congenital heart disease. Barium swallow is shown here. Which imaging modality should be performed next?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Computed tomography angiography

A barium swallow showing external compression of the esophagus with dysphagia and history of congenital heart disease suggests vascular compression (e.g., aberrant subclavian artery or vascular ring). The next best investigation is CT angiography, which clearly delineates vascular anatomy and confirms the diagnosis.

• Dysphagia + smooth extrinsic compression on barium swallow → suspect vascular cause
• Seen with:

• Aberrant right subclavian artery (dysphagia lusoria)
• Double aortic arch
• Other vascular rings

• Best next test: CT angiography (defines vessels and compression)

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A 45-year-old man is being evaluated for epigastric pain and burning sensation for the past few weeks. A barium study was done for the patient. Which of the following findings on barium study would indicate that the ulcer is benign?
options: Interruption of rugae at ulcer edge
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Hampton's line

On barium study, benign gastric ulcers show characteristic radiologic features that help differentiate them from malignant ulcers.

Benign ulcer features:

• Hampton’s line – a thin radiolucent line at the ulcer neck due to mucosal edema (highly suggestive of benign ulcer)
• Ulcer crater projects beyond the expected gastric contour
• Radiating mucosal folds extending up to the ulcer margin
• Smooth, regular margins

Malignant ulcer features:

• Carman meniscus sign
• Ulcer projecting into the lumen
• Irregular, nodular margins
• Abrupt interruption of rugal folds

Image showing Carman meniscus sign

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A 45-year-old man is evaluated in the emergency department for chest pain that developed while eating a piece of steak at a restaurant. He reports intermittent episodes of food (particularly meat) getting stuck in his lower chest over the past 3 years. Patient’s barium swallow image is shown below. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Schatzki's ring

Schatzki ring is a thin mucosal ring located at the gastroesophageal junction, causing intermittent solid food dysphagia, especially with poorly chewed meat (“steakhouse syndrome”). Symptoms may be long-standing and episodic

Barium swallow:

• Smooth, thin, circumferential narrowing at distal esophagus
• Located at the squamocolumnar junction

Differentiation:

A. Achalasia → Bird-beak tapering + dysphagia to solids & liquids

B. Esophageal adenocarcinoma → Progressive dysphagia + irregular narrowing

C. Plummer-Vinson syndrome → Upper esophageal web

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A 45-year-old woman with long-standing rheumatic mitral stenosis undergoes a chest X-ray. Which of the following is not a radiological feature of Left Atrial Enlargement (LAE)?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Double left heart border

Left atrial enlargement (LAE), commonly seen in mitral stenosis, produces characteristic chest X-ray findings due to enlargement of the left atrium. These include:

• Straightening of left heart border (prominent left atrial appendage)
• Splaying of carina (>90°)
• Posterior displacement of esophagus on barium swallow

A double right heart border (double density sign) is the true sign of LA enlargement, not a double left heart border. Therefore, “double left heart border” is not a feature of LAE.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A 46-year-old male presented to the clinic with a persistent cough, fatigue, weight loss. X-ray of the patient is as given below. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. TB

Chest X-ray in pulmonary tuberculosis typically shows upper lobe infiltrates, cavitation, fibrosis, and volume loss, often associated with systemic symptoms like chronic cough, weight loss, and fatigue.

Post-primary TB classically involves the apical and posterior segments of upper lobes due to higher oxygen tension, and cavitary lesions help distinguish it from other causes of chronic lung disease.

Why not other options:

• Aspergilloma: Shows a fungal ball within a pre-existing cavity with an air crescent sign and mobile intracavitary mass — not primary infiltrative upper lobe disease.
• Carcinoma lung: Usually presents as a solitary mass, irregular opacity, or collapse — not typical bilateral apical cavitary lesions.
• Sarcoidosis: Bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy ± reticulonodular pattern; cavitation is uncommon.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A 5-year-old child presents with episodic head-shaking movements since infancy, progressive gait instability, and mild cognitive impairment. There is no history of vomiting or macrocephaly. Neurological examination reveals truncal ataxia with relatively preserved limb coordination. MRI brain (coronal T2-weighted image shown) demonstrated below. Which of the following neuroanatomical abnormalities best explains the embryological basis of this condition?
options: Failure of dorsal induction leading to holoprosencephaly
Failure of segmentation of the rhombic lips causing midline fusion of cerebellar hemispheres
Abnormal neural crest migration affecting posterior fossa development
Defective canalization of the fourth ventricle leading to cyst formation
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Failure of segmentation of the rhombic lips causing midline fusion of cerebellar hemispheres

Rhombencephalosynapsis is a rare hindbrain malformation characterized by agenesis of the cerebellar vermis with fusion of the cerebellar hemispheres, resulting from failure of midline cleavage of the rhombic lips during embryogenesis.

• MRI hallmark: single-lobed cerebellum with absent vermis and fused hemispheres
• Associated structural feature: fusion of dentate nuclei and superior cerebellar peduncles
• Fourth ventricle: typically narrow, slit-like, or keyhole-shaped
• Clinical clue: persistent head-shaking stereotypies + truncal ataxia (very characteristic)

Differentiation:

• vs Dandy–Walker → enlarged posterior fossa + cystic dilation of 4th ventricle
• vs Joubert syndrome → molar tooth sign (not fusion)

This condition represents a failure of cerebellar midline patterning, not a cystic or obstructive posterior fossa anomaly.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A 5-year-old child was brought unconscious. NCCT of the head was performed and shown below. All of the following should be worked up except:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Karyotyping

In a child with intracranial hemorrhage suggestive of non-accidental injury (shaken baby syndrome), evaluation should include:

• Detailed physical examination
• Skeletal survey to detect fractures
• Ophthalmologic exam for retinal hemorrhages

These help confirm child abuse. Karyotyping is not part of routine workup, as the condition is traumatic, not genetic.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A 50-year-old female presents with a history of progressive vision loss in her right eye. An MRI of the orbit reveals a lesion with a characteristic appearance. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis based on the MRI findings?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Optic nerve glioma

Optic nerve glioma typically shows:

• Fusiform enlargement of the optic nerve
• Intrinsic expansion of the nerve
• No “tram-track” enhancement pattern

Ruling out other options:

A. Optic nerve sheath meningioma → Shows the classic “Tram-track” sign (enhancing sheath surrounding non-enhancing nerve), more common in middle aged females, dural based lesion.

C. Choroidal melanoma → intraocular mass, not optic nerve enlargement

D. Optic neuritis → inflammatory, no mass lesion

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A 50-year-old man presents after severe head trauma with rapidly deteriorating consciousness. Non-contrast CT brain (image shown) demonstrates a large hyperdense intracranial hemorrhage with irregular internal hypodense foci and significant surrounding mass effect with midline shift. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management based on this imaging finding?
options: Conservative management with serial CT scans
Observation as this represents resolving hemorrhage
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Urgent neurosurgical evacuation of hematoma

• The CT shows heterogeneous hematoma with hypodense areas indicating “swirl sign” which indicates active ongoing bleeding
• Associated mass effect and midline shift indicate raised intracranial pressure

This combination signifies:

• Unstable hematoma
• High risk of rapid expansion and herniation

Thus, urgent surgical intervention is required.

Other options:

• Conservative approach is inappropriate in unstable bleed
• Thrombolysis is contraindicated
• This is not resolving hemorrhage

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A 52-year-old man presents with a slowly enlarging lateral neck mass. CT angiography reveals a well-defined, intensely enhancing lesion at the carotid bifurcation producing splaying of the internal and external carotid arteries (lyre sign). The radiologist is asked to comment on tumor extent and surgical planning. Which of the following radiological classifications is most relevant for predicting surgical difficulty and risk of vascular morbidity in this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Shamblin classification

• Carotid body tumors (paragangliomas) are classified using the Shamblin classification, based on their relationship to carotid vessels:

o    Type I: Small, minimally attached

o    Type II: Partially surrounding vessels

o    Type III: Encasement of carotid arteries → highest surgical risk

• This classification is crucial for:

o    Predicting surgical complexity

o    Estimating risk of vascular injury and cranial nerve damage

Other options:

• Bismuth → biliary strictures
• DeBakey → aortic dissection
• Bosniak → renal cysts

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A 52-year-old man with long-standing cirrhosis undergoes a barium swallow. The image shows multiple serpiginous, worm-like filling defects along the distal esophagus, creating a “rosary-bead” appearance. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Esophageal varices

• Esophageal varices: is an important cause of upper GI bleed.
• On barium swallow, esophageal varices appear as multiple serpiginous, filling defects in the distal esophagus producing a classic “rosary-bead” or “string-of-beads” appearance.
• They occur due to portal hypertension (commonly from cirrhosis) causing dilated submucosal venous channels in lower esophagus
• Veins in lower esophagus dilate and bulge into the lumen.

Why not other options:

A. Esophageal webs: Thin, smooth shelf-like filling defect (usually upper esophagus), not serpiginous.

B. Candidiasis: Irregular shaggy mucosa with plaque-like filling defects (“feathery” appearance).

C. Diffuse esophageal spasm: “Corkscrew esophagus” due to multiple contractions, not worm-like filling defects.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A 55-year-old man with hypertension, hyperlipidemia and a history of smoking presents for a routine evaluation. He is asymptomatic at the moment but is concerned about his cardiovascular health due to a family history of heart disease. Which of the following scores is used to assess coronary artery disease risk based on calcification on NCCT?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Agatston score

• The Agatston score is used to quantify coronary artery calcification (CAC) on (NCCT) .
• it Assesses risk of coronary artery disease and future cardiovascular events.
• Higher calcium scores correlate with increased atherosclerotic burden and guide risk stratification and preventive therapy (e.g., statins).
• Other scores like CHA₂DS₂-VASc and Reynolds risk score assess clinical risk but are not based on CT coronary calcification.

Why not other options:

A. CHA₂DS₂-VASc score: Used to assess stroke risk in atrial fibrillation, not coronary calcification.

C. Reynolds risk score: Estimates cardiovascular risk using clinical and lab factors (CRP, lipids), not CT calcium score.

D. CARPREG score: Predicts cardiac risk in pregnant women with heart disease.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A 56-year-old male presents with sudden onset altered sensorium. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Pontine hemorrhage

• 56-year-old male
• Sudden onset altered sensorium
• Strongly suggests an acute intracranial bleed.

Imaging clue:

• The CT shows a hyperdense lesion in the pons (brainstem) — centrally located in the posterior fossa. The location is classic for pontine hemorrhage, most commonly due to chronic hypertension.

Pontine haemorrhage presents with:

• Sudden loss of consciousness
• Altered sensorium
• Pinpoint pupils
• Abnormal posturing

Other options:

• A. Hypertensive hemorrhage → Usually basal ganglia (putamen), thalamus, cerebellum — not specifically centered in the pons.
• B. Berry aneurysm rupture → Causes subarachnoid hemorrhage (blood in basal cisterns).
• D. EDH → Lens-shaped extra-axial bleed.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A 58-year-old man with a history of anterior wall myocardial infarction presents with exertional dyspnea. To assess myocardial viability and guide revascularization, multiple radionuclide imaging modalities are considered. On evaluation: • A perfusion scan using thallium-201 shows a fixed perfusion defect in the anterior wall. • A PET scan using 18-FDG shows increased uptake in the same region. Which of the following is the most accurate interpretation of these findings?
options: Transmural infarction with no viable myocardium
Normal myocardium with physiological tracer variation
Hibernating myocardium with preserved metabolic activity
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Hibernating myocardium with preserved metabolic activity

Thallium-201 assesses perfusion, where infarcted or poorly perfused areas appear as cold spots. FDG-PET assesses metabolic activity (glucose uptake).

A perfusion-metabolism mismatch (reduced perfusion but increased FDG uptake) indicates viable but ischemic myocardium (hibernating myocardium), which can recover function after revascularization.

• True infarction: both perfusion and metabolism decreased (matched defect)
• Normal myocardium: normal perfusion, low FDG uptake (fatty acid metabolism predominates)

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A 58-year-old man with a known bleeding disorder is brought to the emergency department after developing sudden-onset severe headache followed by vomiting and rapidly progressive alteration in sensorium. On arrival, his Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score is 9/15, which subsequently falls to 7/15. There is no history of recent head trauma. Neurological examination reveals reduced responsiveness with focal neurological deficits. In view of the acute neurological deterioration, an emergency non-contrast CT (NCCT) of the brain is performed, as demonstrated in the accompanying video. Based on the clinical presentation and imaging findings, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Intraparenchymal hemorrhage

The NCCT demonstrates an acute intraparenchymal hemorrhage, which typically appears as a hyperdense collection within the brain parenchyma in the acute phase. A pre-existing bleeding disorder significantly increases the risk of spontaneous intracranial hemorrhage.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A 58-year-old man with carcinoma of the oropharynx is planned for definitive radiotherapy. The radiation oncologist chooses intensity-modulated radiotherapy (IMRT). Which of the following best explains the fundamental principle?
options: Use of uniform radiation beams shaped only by static collimators
Forward planning with manual field shaping based on anatomical landmarks
Dynamic modulation of beam intensity across multiple small beamlets using inverse planning
Delivery of radiation using a single high-dose fraction with stereotactic accuracy
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Dynamic modulation of beam intensity across multiple small beamlets using inverse planning

Intensity-modulated radiotherapy (IMRT) is an advanced radiotherapy technique that uses inverse planning algorithms to modulate the intensity of multiple small beamlets, allowing precise dose sculpting around complex tumor volumes while sparing adjacent organs at risk (OARs).

Key high-yield points:

• Core principle: Inverse planning (desired dose → algorithm determines beam intensities)
• Technique: Dynamic multileaf collimator (MLC) movement creates non-uniform beam intensity
• Advantage over 3D-CRT: Sharper dose gradients and superior conformity
• Clinical importance: Parotid gland sparing in head & neck cancers reduces xerostomia
• Limitation: Higher monitor units → increased low-dose radiation “bath” to normal tissues

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A 58-year-old woman presents with progressive headaches and focal seizures. MRI brain shows a well defined extra axial, dural based mass with adjacent hyperostosis and a dural tail sign. An MR spectroscopy is done to further characterise the lesion. Which of the following spectral peaks is most characteristic of this tumor?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Prominent alanine peak.

A well-defined extra-axial, dural-based mass with hyperostosis and a dural tail on MRI is characteristic of meningioma.

On MR spectroscopy, meningiomas show a prominent alanine peak, -due to high alanine content in these tumors.

-Also demonstrate high choline and low N-acetylaspartate (NAA), reflecting high cellular turnover and non-neuronal origin respectively.

Why not other options:

A. Elevated myo-inositol: low-grade gliomas and Alzheimer disease

C. Lipid-lactate peak: Suggests high-grade tumors, necrosis, abscess, or metastasis, not benign meningioma.

D. Increased NAA: Marker of neuronal tissue; reduced in extra-axial tumors like meningioma.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A 6-month-old infant presents with a history of multiple seizures and developmental delay. On physical examination, you notice facial lesions, hypopigmented macules on the skin, and ungual fibromas. MRI brain is shown. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. TSC

Tuberous sclerosis complex (TSC) is an autosomal dominant neurocutaneous disorder characterized by seizures, developmental delay, and cutaneous lesions such as hypopigmented “ash-leaf” macules, facial angiofibromas, and ungual fibromas. MRI brain typically shows cortical tubers and subependymal nodules/giant cell astrocytoma.

Genetics:

• Mutation in TSC1 (hamartin) or TSC2 (tuberin)
• Leads to hamartomas in multiple organs

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A 60-year-old man presents with a 3-month history of recurrent, crampy abdominal pain occurring 20–30 minutes after meals. The pain typically lasts for about an hour and has led him to avoid eating because of the fear of triggering symptoms. He has unintentionally lost 8 kg over the past 3 months. His medical history is significant for long-standing diabetes mellitus, hypertension, dyslipidemia, and a 30-pack-year smoking history. Physical examination is unremarkable except for a faint epigastric bruit. Routine blood investigations, abdominal ultrasonography, and upper GI endoscopy are normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate investigation to confirm the diagnosis?
options: CT angiography of the abdominal vessels
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. CT angiography of the abdominal vessels

The patient has chronic mesenteric ischemia (intestinal angina) caused by atherosclerotic narrowing of the mesenteric arteries.

Key clinical clues

• Postprandial abdominal pain (20–30 minutes after meals)
• Pain lasting 1–2 hours
