• Food fear (sitophobia)
• Progressive weight loss
• Multiple atherosclerotic risk factors:

• Smoking
• Diabetes
• Hypertension

• Epigastric bruit
• Normal endoscopy despite persistent symptoms

Investigation of choice: ✅ CT Angiography (CTA)

• CTA is the investigation of choice to confirm chronic mesenteric ischemia because it:

• Demonstrates stenosis or occlusion of the:

• Celiac artery
• Superior mesenteric artery (SMA)
• Inferior mesenteric artery (IMA)

• Defines the severity and extent of disease
• Helps plan endovascular or surgical revascularization

• It has largely replaced conventional catheter angiography as the initial diagnostic test.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A 62 year old male with a history of smoking presents to the emergency department with shortness of breath and fever. A chest X-ray is performed as shown below. Which of the following radiological signs is seen in this case?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Golden S sign

The Golden “S” sign on chest X-ray indicates right upper lobe collapse due to a central obstructing mass (commonly bronchogenic carcinoma). It appears as an S-shaped contour of the minor fissure caused by a combination of lobar collapse and a hilar mass. This sign is an important radiological clue to underlying lung malignancy causing lobar atelectasis.

Why not other options:

A. Luftsichel sign: Seen in left upper lobe collapse, crescent of air near aortic arch.

B. Flat waist sign: Seen with lower lobe collapse.

D. Superior triangle sign: Seen in left lower lobe collapse behind cardiac shadow.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A 62-year-old man presents with chronic cough and weight loss. A chest radiograph is obtained. On the frontal film, the cardiac silhouette appears enlarged and there is apparent widening of the mediastinum. However, the patient is clinically stable with no features of cardiac disease. On reviewing the imaging details, it is noted that the scapulae project over the lung fields and the clavicles are more horizontal. Which of the following is the most likely explanation for these radiographic findings?
options: True cardiomegaly due to left ventricular enlargement
Expiratory film causing apparent mediastinal widening
Anteroposterior (AP) view causing magnification of cardiac silhouette
Rotation of patient leading to mediastinal shift
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Anteroposterior (AP) view causing magnification of cardiac silhouette

In AP view (portable X-ray):

• Heart is farther from the detector → appears magnified
• Scapulae overlie lung fields
• Clavicles are more horizontal

In PA view (standard):

• Heart size is more accurate
• Scapulae are rotated out of lung fields

Thus, apparent cardiomegaly and mediastinal widening are projectional artifacts, not true pathology.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A 62-year-old man with obstructive LUTS undergoes a Tc-99m MDP bone scan. Multiple hot spots are seen throughout the knee, ribs, and pelvis. His serum ALP is normal, PSA is normal, and MRI of the spine is unremarkable. Which of the following is the most likely cause of false-positive hot spots on the bone scan?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Degenerative joint disease

• Tc-99m MDP bone scan detects areas of increased osteoblastic activity, not specifically malignancy.
• Therefore, many benign conditions can produce false-positive hot spots, especially degenerative joint disease (osteoarthritis).
• Degenerative changes commonly cause increased tracer uptake in weight-bearing joints (spine, knees, ribs, pelvis) and may mimic metastasis.
• Correlation with clinical findings, PSA/ALP levels, and other imaging helps distinguish benign degenerative uptake from true skeletal metastases.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A 65-year-old male with a 40-pack-year smoking history presents with cough and unintentional weight loss. A contrast-enhanced CT scan reveals a mass in the right upper lobe of the lung suspicious for bronchogenic carcinoma. Which of the following organs must be evaluated to assess for common metastasis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Adrenals

Bronchogenic carcinoma commonly metastasizes hematogenously to the adrenal glands, liver, brain, and bones. Therefore, evaluation of the adrenals with CT or PET-CT is essential during staging of lung cancer, even in asymptomatic patients, as adrenal metastasis is frequent and may alter management and prognosis.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A 65-year-old man presents with hematuria and left flank pain. Imaging studies reveal a renal mass, and a subsequent biopsy confirms the diagnosis of papillary renal cell carcinoma. Which of the following cytogenetic abnormalities is most characteristic of papillary chromophilic renal cell carcinoma?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Trisomy 7/17

Renal cell carcinoma (RCC) subtypes are associated with characteristic cytogenetic abnormalities, which helps in diagnosis and correlates with tumor biology.

Papillary (chromophilic) RCC

This subtype commonly shows Trisomy of chromosomes 7 and 17 and often:

• loss of Y chromosome (in males)

• may be associated with activating alterations of MET proto-oncogene (esp hereditary type)

Differentiation from other RCC subtypes

• Clear cell RCC → loss of 3p, VHL gene inactivation

• Chromophobe RCC → multiple chromosomal losses (1,2,6,10,13,17)

• Xp11 translocation RCC → Xp translocations (TFE3 gene fusion), seen in children/young adults

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A 68-year-old man develops profound hypotension following massive blood loss. Despite successful resuscitation, prolonged tissue hypoxia results in ischemic injury to multiple organs. The treating physician explains that different cell types vary considerably in their susceptibility to oxygen deprivation. Which of the following correctly identifies the most and least hypoxia-sensitive cells?
options: Most sensitive – Hepatocytes; Least sensitive – Lymphocytes
Most sensitive – Bone marrow cells; Least sensitive – Neurons
Most sensitive – Retina; Least sensitive – Adipose tissue
Most sensitive – Neurons; Least sensitive – Fibroblasts
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Most sensitive – Neurons; Least sensitive – Fibroblasts

Different tissues have varying tolerance to hypoxia depending on their metabolic activity, oxygen requirement, and ability to survive anaerobic metabolism.

Most sensitive cells

Neurons are the most susceptible to hypoxic injury because they:

• Have a very high metabolic rate
• Depend almost exclusively on aerobic metabolism
• Possess negligible glycogen stores

Irreversible neuronal injury begins within 3–5 minutes of complete ischemia.

Least sensitive cells

Fibroblasts are among the most resistant cells because they:

• Have low metabolic demands
• Can survive prolonged periods of reduced oxygen supply
• Continue to function even in relatively hypoxic environments during wound healing

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A 7-year-old child presents with intermittent left-sided flank pain, episodes of vomiting after heavy fluid intake, and a palpable abdominal mass. USG finding is shown below What is the mangement of above condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Anderson Hynes Pyeloplasty

Intermittent flank pain after heavy fluid intake with ultrasound showing gross hydronephrosis in a child is characteristic of pelvi-ureteric junction (PUJ) obstruction. The definitive treatment for symptomatic PUJ obstruction with preserved renal function is Anderson–Hynes pyeloplasty, which relieves obstruction and preserves kidney function.

Why not other options:

A. Rovsing procedure: It is a historic surgical technique for Polycystic Kidney Disease (PKD) that involves puncturing and unroofing (deroofing) multiple renal cysts

• Rovsing sign: Used for appendicitis (pain in the RLQ on LLQ palpation)

B. Endoscopic dilation: Temporary or less effective; not definitive treatment in children with significant PUJ obstruction.

D. Partial nephrectomy: Done for non-functioning renal segment or tumors, not for PUJ obstruction with salvageable kidney.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A 70 year old male patient with a history of congestive heart failure presents with worsening shortness of breath and pleuritic chest pain. A chest X-ray is taken, which is shown below. Which of the following statements about the finding on the chest X-ray is most accurate?
options: It is most commonly seen with effusion occupying the oblique fissure.
It may be mistaken for a lung mass due to its appearance.
It will typically require surgical intervention to resolve.
It is mostly associated with exudative pleural effusion.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. It may be mistaken for a lung mass due to its appearance.

• There is a well-defined, lens-shaped opacity in the lung field.
• This is NOT a true lung mass, It is fluid trapped in a fissure.
• This is called: 👉 Pseudotumor (Vanishing tumor) / Interlobar pleural effusion.

PATHOPHYSIOLOGY:

In heart failure:

• Fluid accumulates and Sometimes it collects inside a lung fissure
• It forms a rounded opacity and starts looking like a tumor due to the rounded morphology.

👉It disappears when heart failure improves, because it is just fluid.

Hence called a vanishing tumor.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A 70-year-old man comes to the casualty after 3 episodes of sudden loss of vision in his right eye like a curtain falling down, each of which resolved spontaneously` after about 2 minutes. He has a history of hypertension and diabetes. Neurological examination of the patient is normal. What investigation would aid in the management of this patient?
options: MRI Diffusion-weighted imaging of the brain
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Doppler of the neck

That is Amaurosis Fugax. It is a transient ischemic attack (TIA) of the retina due to ipsilateral Carotid artery plaque sending emboli to the retinal artery.

Next best step: Doppler of the neck (Carotid Doppler)

Because:

• It detects carotid stenosis
• Helps decide if patient needs carotid endarterectomy.
• Prevents future stroke

Why not other options:

B. MRI DWI brain: Detects acute cerebral infarct; patient has transient monocular vision loss (amaurosis fugax) without persistent deficit.

C. Non-contrast CT head: Poor for detecting carotid plaques or TIA cause; mainly for acute hemorrhage/stroke.

D. Ocular B-scan: Evaluates intraocular pathology (retinal detachment, vitreous hemorrhage), not embolic carotid disease.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A lady was incidentally diagnosed with a 0.5 cm solid mass in her gall Bladder on USG as shown. What is the next step in the management?
options: Reassure the patient and follow up
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Reassure the patient and follow up

Gallbladder polyps <1 cm (especially <6 mm) detected incidentally on ultrasonography are usually benign (most commonly cholesterol polyps) and are managed with observation and periodic follow-up, not surgery.

Management based on size:

• <6 mm: Reassurance and periodic USG follow-up
• 6–9 mm: Serial follow-up (especially if risk factors present)
• ≥10 mm: Cholecystectomy due to malignancy risk
• Any size + symptoms/risk factors (PSC, age >50, sessile polyp) → consider surgery

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A nuclear medicine resident is comparing different radionuclides used in diagnostic imaging. Two nuclides are found to have the same mass number (A) but different atomic numbers (Z). These nuclides are best described as:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Isobars

Isobars are nuclides that have:

• Same mass number (A) ✅
• Different atomic numbers (Z) ✅

Since: Mass number (A) = Protons + Neutrons

Isobars have the same total number of nucleons but belong to different elements because their proton numbers differ.

Examples:

• ¹⁴C (Z = 6) and ¹⁴N (Z = 7)
• ⁴⁰Ar, ⁴⁰K, ⁴⁰Ca

Why the other options are incorrect?

A. Isotopes ❌

• Same atomic number (Z)
• Different mass number (A)
• Example: ¹²C, ¹³C, ¹⁴C

C. Isotones ❌

• Same number of neutrons
• Different atomic numbers and mass numbers
• Example: ¹⁴C (6p, 8n) and ¹⁵N (7p, 8n)

D. Nuclear isomers ❌

• Same Z and A
• Different nuclear energy states
• Example: ⁹⁹ᵐTc and ⁹⁹Tc

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A patient comes to you with an inoperable small cell lung carcinoma. He is posted for thoracic external beam radiotherapy. How will the respiratory movement be counteracted during this procedure?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Gating

Respiratory gating is used in thoracic radiotherapy to compensate for tumor movement caused by breathing. Radiation is delivered only during a specific phase of the respiratory cycle (usually end-expiration), ensuring accurate targeting of the tumor while minimizing radiation exposure to surrounding healthy tissues. This technique improves precision in treating lung and upper abdominal tumors during external beam radiotherapy.

Why not other options:

A. Arc modulation: Refers to rotational delivery of radiation (IMRT/VMAT) to improve dose distribution, not to control respiratory motion.

B. Fractionation: Dividing total radiation dose into multiple sessions to reduce toxicity; unrelated to breathing movement.

C. Afterloading: Used in brachytherapy where radioactive source is placed after applicator insertion; not for respiratory motion control.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A patient presents to emergency department with chronic ear discharge and head ache with ear pain. CT revealed the following findings. What is the most probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Cerebellar abscess

Chronic suppurative otitis media (CSOM), especially with cholesteatoma, can lead to intracranial complications via direct spread through bone or venous channels. The most common brain abscess from otogenic infection occurs in the cerebellum (posterior fossa) and may present with headache, ear discharge, fever, and signs of raised intracranial pressure.

Key Imaging Clue: Ring-enhancing lesion in posterior fossa/cerebellum on CT

Otogenic Intracranial Complications:

• Cerebellar abscess → most common
• Temporal lobe abscess
• Lateral sinus thrombosis
• Meningitis
• Extradural/subdural abscess

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A person at the airport with symptoms showing agitations showed following x- ray findings. He was carrying enema apparatus and laxatives. Which of the following is a wrong statement?
options: He is at risk of poisoning
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. He is malingering

History clue:

• Airport
• Agitation
• Carrying enema apparatus and laxatives

This screams drug smuggler trying to evacuate packets.

Other options:

A. Abdominal CT imaging is required

✔ True — CT is more sensitive and helps confirm number/location of packets.

C. He is body packer

✔ True — Radiograph is classic for this.

D. He is at risk of poisoning

✔ True — If a packet ruptures → acute drug toxicity → can be fatal.

B. He is malingering

• This is the wrong statement.
• This is not malingering.
• There is clear radiographic evidence of foreign bodies.
• This is a medical emergency and should not be mistaken for malingering.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A preterm neonate on mechanical ventilation develops sudden respiratory distress. A chest X-ray (image shown) reveals elevation and outlining of the thymus by lucent streaks of air, giving a characteristic “spinnaker sail sign.” Which of the following is the most accurate interpretation and underlying mechanism of this finding?
options: Pneumothorax due to alveolar rupture causing air in pleural space
Pneumomediastinum due to alveolar rupture with air tracking along perivascular sheaths
Pulmonary interstitial emphysema due to air trapping within lung parenchyma
Congenital diaphragmatic hernia with herniation of abdominal contents
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Pneumomediastinum due to alveolar rupture with air tracking along perivascular sheaths

Pneumomediastinum in neonates is classically identified by the spinnaker sail sign, where mediastinal air lifts and outlines the thymus, making it appear like a billowing sail on chest X-ray.

• Mechanism (Macklin effect):

o    Alveolar rupture → air dissects along perivascular sheaths → collects in mediastinum

• Common setting:

o    Positive pressure ventilation, RDS, or birth-related barotrauma

Important differentiation:

• Pneumomediastinum → thymus outlined/elevated (spinnaker sail sign)
• Pneumothorax → pleural air with lung collapse (no thymic elevation)
• Pulmonary interstitial emphysema → streaky lucencies within lung parenchyma

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A term baby with respiratory distress is intubated following CXR. Saturation remains 80% despite ventilation. What is the next best step?
options: Insert a nasogastric tube for decompression
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Insert a nasogastric tube for decompression

In a neonate with respiratory distress and CXR showing bowel loops in the thorax (suggestive of congenital diaphragmatic hernia), the immediate management is nasogastric tube insertion for gastric decompression. This reduces intrathoracic bowel distension and lung compression, improving ventilation and oxygenation before definitive surgical repair. Bag-mask ventilation and CPAP should be avoided as they worsen gastric distension.

Why not others:

• A. CPAP: Worsens gastric distension → more lung compression.
• C. Immediate surgery: Stabilize first, then operate.
• D. HFOV: Consider later if needed, not first step.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A woman has been diagnosed with endometrial carcinoma is undergoing radiotherapy. Choose the correct statement.
options: Intensity is inversely proportional to the square of the distance from the source
Small blood vessels are most radioresistant
Rapidly proliferating cells are most radioresistant
Small intestinal mucosa is most radio-resistant
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Intensity is inversely proportional to the square of the distance from the source

Radiation intensity follows the inverse square law, meaning the intensity of radiation exposure is inversely proportional to the square of the distance from the radiation source. Even small increases in distance significantly reduce radiation exposure.

Radiobiology Principles:

• Rapidly dividing, poorly differentiated cells → most radiosensitive (e.g., bone marrow, intestinal mucosa, germ cells)
• Well-differentiated, slowly dividing cells → radioresistant (e.g., muscle, nerve)
• Small blood vessels are radiosensitive and can be damaged

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: All of the following are considered radioprotectors, except:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Cisplatin

• Radioprotectors are agents that protect normal tissues from radiation-induced damage by scavenging free radicals or enhancing DNA repair.
• Examples: amifostine, melatonin, and zinc compounds which reduce radiation toxicity to healthy cells.
• Cisplatin is not a radioprotector; it is a radiosensitizer that enhances the effect of radiation on tumor cells by increasing DNA damage and inhibiting repair, thereby improving cancer treatment efficacy.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: All of the following are correct differences between normal radiography and mammography, except:
options: Radiography uses tungsten as the target, while mammography uses molybdenum
Beryllium is used as the exit window in mammography
Mammography uses Bremsstrahlung radiation for better tissue contrast
Aluminum filter is used in radiography, while molybdenum is used in mammography
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Mammography uses Bremsstrahlung radiation for better tissue contrast

Normal radiography (X-ray):

• Uses Tungsten target
• Uses Aluminum filter
• More Bremsstrahlung radiation
• Higher energy X-rays (Needs to penetrate bone, chest, abdomen etc.)
• Think of it like a “powerful beam” that has to go through thick structures.

Mammography:

• Uses Molybdenum (or Rhodium) target
• Uses Molybdenum filter (molybdenum produces X-rays at ideal energy (17–19 keV)

Lower energy X-rays (for soft tissue contrast)
• Breast is a soft tissue organ, so we need to see tiny differences (like microcalcifications)
• So we use low energy X-rays
• Uses more characteristic radiation, not mainly bremsstrahlung.
• Think of it like a “gentle, precise beam” made specially for soft tissue contrast.

Bremsstrahlung radiation?

• Bremsstrahlung = wide range of X-ray energies (mixed spectrum).
• Good for general X-rays, not for fine soft tissue contrast.

Characteristic radiation?

• Very specific energy peaks.
• In mammography, molybdenum produces X-rays at ideal energy
• This gives excellent breast tissue contrast.

Option-wise:

A) Radiography uses tungsten, mammography uses molybdenum

✔ Correct

B) Beryllium is used as exit window in mammography

✔ Correct (allows low-energy X-rays to pass)

C) Mammography uses Bremsstrahlung radiation for better tissue contrast

❌ Wrong. Mammography mainly uses characteristic radiation from molybdenum (17–19 keV) for better breast tissue contrast.

D) Aluminum filter in radiography, molybdenum filter in mammography

✔ Correct

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: All of the following are correctly paired with HU on CT except:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Fat: 0-20

Hounsfield units (HU) on CT quantify tissue density relative to water (0 HU). Fat has negative attenuation values due to low density and typically ranges from –50 to –100 HU, not 0–20 HU.

Typical CT attenuation values:

• Air: –1000 HU
• Fat: –50 to –100 HU
• Water: 0 HU
• Soft tissue/contrast: 30–130 HU
• Acute hemorrhage: 60–70 HU
• Bone/calcification: 800–1000 HU

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: All of the following radioisotopes have a half-life of less than 1 day, except:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Iodine 125

Most commonly used diagnostic radioisotopes have short half-lives (<24 hours) to minimize radiation exposure while allowing effective imaging.

• Technetium-99m: \~6 hours
• Iodine-132: \~2–3 hours
• 18F-FDG: \~110 minutes
• Iodine-125: \~60 days (long half-life)

Iodine-125 has a prolonged half-life and is mainly used in brachytherapy (e.g., prostate implants) rather than routine diagnostic imaging.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: All of the following statements about alpha radiation are correct, except:
options: Alpha particles have high ionisation ability
Alpha particles have highest molecular mass among radiations
Alpha particles are the most penetrating form of radiation
Alpha radiation is blocked by paper
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Alpha particles are the most penetrating form of radiation

• Alpha particles are heavy, positively charged particles with the highest mass and ionizing power among common radiations, causing intense local tissue damage.
• However, they have very low penetrating ability and can be stopped by a sheet of paper or the outer layer of skin.
• Penetration order of radiation: Alpha < Beta < Gamma (most penetrating).

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: All of these are causes of bilious vomiting in a neonate at birth except?
options: [Option image — not included in this edition]
[Option image — not included in this edition]
[Option image — not included in this edition]
[Option image — not included in this edition]
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. [image not included in this edition]

Bilious vomiting in a neonate indicates intestinal obstruction distal to the ampulla of Vater and is a surgical emergency.

Common causes of bilious vomiting at birth:

• Duodenal atresia (“double bubble” sign)
• Malrotation with midgut volvulus
• Jejunal/ileal atresia
• Meconium ileus

Not a cause:

• Hypertrophic pyloric stenosis (Option C image)

o Causes non-bilious projectile vomiting

o Obstruction is proximal to the ampulla

o Presents at 2–6 weeks of age, not at birth

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: An 8-year-old boy is being evaluated for seizures. A CT scan was done, and the image is given below. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Corpus callosum lipoma

A. Angiomyolipoma

• Benign renal tumor composed of blood vessels, smooth muscle, and fat
• Associated with Tuberous sclerosis
• Not an intracranial lesion causing seizures

B. Corpus callosum lipoma ✅

• Rare congenital intracranial lipoma
• CT: Well-defined homogeneous hypodense lesion (fat density: −50 to −100 HU) along the corpus callosum, often with peripheral calcification
• May present with seizures
• Frequently associated with agenesis/dysgenesis of the corpus callosum

C. Craniopharyngioma

• Typically suprasellar
• Mixed cystic-solid lesion with calcification
• Presents with headache, visual defects, growth failure, and endocrine abnormalities

D. Neurocysticercosis (NCC)

• Most common cause of acquired epilepsy in endemic regions
• CT: Ring-enhancing lesion(s), often with an eccentric scolex or calcified granuloma
• Usually multiple lesions in different stages

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: During a PET scan evaluation for suspected lymphoma, the scanner detects simultaneous 511 keV gamma photons arriving at two opposite detectors. This phenomenon is essential because it:
options: Improves spatial resolution by eliminating Compton scatter
Determines tracer distribution using time-of-flight coincidence detection
Measures the half-life of the radionuclide
Produces functional images by detecting β+ particles directly
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Determines tracer distribution using time-of-flight coincidence detection

• Positron emission tomography (PET) detects pairs of 511 keV gamma photons produced when a positron emitted from a radionuclide annihilates with an electron.
• These photons travel in opposite directions and are detected simultaneously by opposing detectors (coincidence detection).
• This simultaneous detection allows accurate localization of the radiotracer using time-of-flight and coincidence principles, enabling reconstruction of tracer distribution and generation of functional metabolic images.
• PET does not directly detect positrons or measure radionuclide half-life; instead, it maps tissue metabolism based on coincident gamma photon detection.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: Eggshell calcification is seen in all the following, except?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Metastatic lymph nodes

• Eggshell calcification refers to thin, peripheral rim-like calcification of lymph nodes, most commonly seen in silicosis and can also be seen in sarcoidosis and occasionally in post-radiation treated lymph nodes.
• It is not typical of metastatic lymph nodes, which more commonly show irregular, central, or amorphous calcifications rather than the classic thin peripheral “eggshell” pattern.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: Empty thecal sac sign on MRI is seen in:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Arachnoiditis

• The “empty thecal sac sign” on MRI I: characteristic of arachnoiditis . (thecal sac is the fluid-filled sac in the spine that contains: CSF and Cauda equina nerve roots)
• Arachnoiditis: inflammation of arachnoid matter. It may commonly seen after spinal surgery, infection, trauma, or intrathecal injections.

Normally on MRI, you see:

• Bright CSF
• Dark nerve roots floating freely inside (i.e., in the centre).

In Arachnoiditis, Because of inflammation:

• Nerve roots stick together and clump
• They move to the periphery and the center looks empty

TO RULE OUT OTHER OPTIONS:

B. Discitis → Infection of disc space (not nerve root clumping)

C. Vertebral osteomyelitis → Infection of bone

D. Tethered cord → Low-lying cord, not empty sac

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: Functional MRI (fMRI) works on which of the following principles?
options: T1 shortening due to gadolinium uptake
Changes in proton density of neuronal tissue
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Blood Oxygen Level–Dependent (BOLD) contrast

• Functional MRI (fMRI) is based on Blood Oxygen Level–Dependent (BOLD) contrast, which detects changes in regional cerebral blood flow and oxygenation associated with neuronal activity.
• Active brain areas consume more oxygen, leading to local changes in oxyhemoglobin/deoxyhemoglobin ratio that alter magnetic properties and signal intensity on MRI, allowing mapping of functional brain activity without contrast injection.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: Identify the correct pair:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. B - P1 PCA

On MR angiography of the Circle of Willis, the P1 segment of the posterior cerebral artery (PCA) is the portion that extends from the basilar artery bifurcation to the posterior communicating artery (PCoA). Correct identification of vascular segments is essential for localizing aneurysms, arterial occlusions, and stroke territories.

Correct identification:

• A → A2 segment of ACA
• B → P1 segment of PCA (correct option in question)
• C → Basilar artery
• D → Superficial temporal artery

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: Identify the image.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Orbital cellulitis

Orbital cellulitis = infection posterior to the orbital septum

CT findings:

• Diffuse inflammatory fat stranding
• Thickened extraocular muscles
• Proptosis
• No discrete abscess cavity

Why NOT subperiosteal abscess?

A subperiosteal abscess would show:

• A well-defined crescent/lentiform fluid collection
• Clear periosteal elevation along lamina papyracea
• Often rim enhancement

Here, the inflammation appears diffuse rather than loculated.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: Identify the nerve block given at the point shown:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Pudendal nerve

A nerve block given near the ischial spine targets the pudendal nerve.

Anatomical basis:

• Pudendal nerve (S2–S4) exits pelvis via greater sciatic foramen,
• Wraps around ischial spine/sacrospinous ligament,
• Re-enters via lesser sciatic foramen into pudendal canal (Alcock’s canal).

Clinical use of pudendal nerve block:

• Obstetric analgesia (second stage of labor)
• Episiotomy repair
• Perineal procedures
• Hemorrhoid surgery

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: Identify the radiological procedure shown below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Enteroclysis

Enteroclysis is a specialized fluoroscopic study of the small intestine in which contrast is directly infused into the jejunum via a nasojejunal tube, providing detailed evaluation of small bowel mucosa, distensibility, and transit. It is superior to a routine barium meal follow-through for detecting subtle mucosal lesions, strictures, adhesions, and early inflammatory bowel disease (especially Crohn disease), as it provides uniform bowel distension and better mucosal visualization.

Why not others:

B. Proctography: Studies rectum during defecation → no small bowel loops or NJ tube.

C. Barium enema: Contrast via rectum to visualize colon → shows large bowel, not small intestine.

D. Barium meal follow-through: Oral contrast, no nasojejunal tube; less uniform small bowel distension.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: Identify the rib in the X-ray shown below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Right posterior end of 6th rib

On a PA chest X-ray, posterior ribs are more horizontal and clearly visualized, while anterior ribs slope downward toward the sternum and are less distinct.

To localize a rib fracture:

• Identify the rib level by counting posterior ribs (which are easier to count).
• Use the inferior angle of scapula (\~7th rib posteriorly) and vertebral alignment as landmarks.
• Fractures near the vertebral column correspond to the posterior end of ribs.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: In patients with renal failure, which imaging technique is appropriate for visualizing vessels without causing further renal impairment?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Time-of-flight MRI angiography

In patients with renal failure, non-contrast vascular imaging is preferred to avoid contrast-induced nephropathy (iodinated contrast in CT/DSA) and nephrogenic systemic fibrosis (gadolinium in contrast MRI). Time-of-flight (TOF) MR angiography is a non-contrast technique that visualizes blood vessels using flow-related enhancement and is safest for evaluating vasculature in renal impairment.

Key Points:

• CT angiography & DSA: Use iodinated contrast → risk of contrast-induced nephropathy
• Contrast MRI angiography: Uses gadolinium → risk of nephrogenic systemic fibrosis in renal failure
• TOF MR angiography: No contrast required → safest option

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: Match the following radionuclide tracers with their most appropriate clinical application. Choose the correct match:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. A-5, B-4, C-1, D-3, E-2

Newer radionuclide tracers used in PET imaging are molecularly targeted, and their clinical application depends on the specific biological pathway or receptor they bind.

Key high-yield associations:

• Ga-68 PSMA → targets PSMA receptor → primary & recurrent prostate cancer
• C-11 choline → reflects cell membrane turnover → prostate cancer metastasis/recurrence
• F-18 florbetaben/florbetapir/flutemetamol → bind β-amyloid → Alzheimer’s disease imaging
• Co-64 DOTATATE → binds somatostatin receptors → neuroendocrine tumors
• N-13 ammonia / Rb-82 → myocardial perfusion imaging

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: Radiologically, pulmonary plethora is indicated by all of the following except:
options: Diameter of peripheral arteries > accompanying bronchiole
More than 6 blood vessels in outer 1/3rd
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Kerley B lines

• Pulmonary plethora refers to increased pulmonary vascularity due to increased pulmonary blood flow (e.g., left-to-right shunts like ASD, VSD, PDA).
• Radiological signs include enlarged central pulmonary arteries, prominent peripheral vessels extending to the lung periphery (>6 vessels in outer one-third), and peripheral arteries larger than accompanying bronchi.
• Kerley B lines indicate interstitial pulmonary edema from pulmonary venous hypertension (e.g., left heart failure), not pulmonary plethora; therefore, they are not a feature of increased pulmonary blood flow.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: The imaging shows a detailed cross-sectional view of the esophageal wall and surrounding structures. All of the following are uses of this imaging modality except:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Evaluation of gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD)

The image represents Endoscopic Ultrasound (EUS), which provides high-resolution cross-sectional imaging of the GI wall and adjacent structures.

• Circular cross-sectional view, Central echoendoscope, Layered wall structure of the esophagus clearly visible

EUS is actually used for:

✅ A. Biliary microlithiasis

• Detects tiny stones/sludge not seen on USG

✅ B. Staging of esophageal cancer

• Best modality to assess depth of invasion (T staging)

✅ C. Drainage of pancreatic pseudocyst

• EUS-guided cystogastrostomy is standard

❌ D. Evaluation of GERD

• GERD evaluation is done by: Endoscopy, 24-hour pH monitoring, Manometry
• EUS has no role GERD diagnosis.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: The intravenous pyelogram of a patient is shown below. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Medullary sponge kidney

Medullary sponge kidney is a congenital disorder characterized by cystic dilatation of the collecting ducts in the renal medulla and papillae.

Characteristic IVP finding

• Paintbrush appearance
• Bouquet of flowers appearance
• Linear or punctate contrast collections in the renal papillae

Clinical associations

• Recurrent renal stones
• Hematuria
• Recurrent urinary tract infections
• Nephrocalcinosis
• Distal renal tubular acidosis may occur

Why the other options are incorrect?

A. Retrocaval ureter

• Typically affects the right ureter
• IVP may show a reverse J-shaped or fish-hook deformity

B. Horseshoe kidney

• Fusion of the lower poles of both kidneys
• Kidneys lie lower than normal with medially directed lower calyces

C. Duplicated collecting system

• Shows two pelvicalyceal systems or duplicated ureters
• May be associated with the drooping lily sign

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: What is the likely diagnosis based on the given image?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Xanthogranulomatous pyelonephritis

CT showing an enlarged kidney replaced by multiple low-attenuation areas with a central staghorn calculus (“bear paw sign”) is characteristic of xanthogranulomatous pyelonephritis (XGP).

• Chronic suppurative infection of the kidney
• Commonly associated with obstruction by staghorn calculus
• Renal parenchyma replaced by lipid-laden macrophages (foamy histiocytes)
• Presents with flank pain, fever, weight loss, recurrent UTIs
• Management: often nephrectomy

Differentials:

A. ADPKD → Bilateral multiple cysts

B. PUJ obstruction → Dilated pelvis without destructive inflammatory pattern

D. Putty kidney → Calcified non-functioning kidney in renal TB

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: What is the likely diagnosis in the given patient showing the “bare orbit sign”?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Sphenoid wing dysplasia

The “bare orbit sign” on skull radiograph/CT refers to absence or thinning of the greater wing of sphenoid, classically seen in sphenoid wing dysplasia, a hallmark feature of Neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1). Leads to enlarged orbital cavity and pulsatile proptosis. May show herniation of temporal lobe into orbit

Differentials:

B. Orbital blow-out fracture → floor defect, not sphenoid absence

C. Sphenoid fracture → traumatic irregular margins

D. Orbital apex syndrome → neurological deficits without bony dysplasia

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: What is the likely diagnosis in the image shown below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Crossed fused ectopia

Crossed fused renal ectopia is a congenital anomaly in which both kidneys are located on the same side and fused together, with one ureter crossing the midline to enter the bladder at its normal position. It is the second most common renal fusion anomaly after horseshoe kidney.

Differentiation:

A. Pancake kidney: Complete fusion in pelvis

B. Ectopic kidney: Single kidney in abnormal location, not fused

C. Horseshoe kidney: Fusion at lower poles across midline with isthmus

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Bladder neck hypertrophy

The imaging is consistent with bladder neck hypertrophy (bladder neck obstruction), characterized by hypertrophy of the bladder neck causing bladder outlet obstruction.

Imaging findings (VCUG)

• Narrowing at the bladder neck during voiding
• Dilated posterior urethra may be seen
• Incomplete bladder emptying
• Trabeculated bladder in chronic cases

Clinical features

• Hesitancy
• Poor urinary stream
• Straining to void
• Incomplete emptying
• Increased post-void residual urine
• May mimic benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH)

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: What is the minimum amount of fluid to be detected by this X-ray?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 25ml

On a lateral decubitus chest X-ray, as little as \~25 mL of pleural fluid can be detected because fluid layers dependently between the lung and chest wall, making this view the most sensitive plain radiographic method for small pleural effusions.

Minimum pleural fluid detectable:

• Lateral decubitus view: \~25 mL (most sensitive X-ray view)
• PA erect chest X-ray: \~200 mL
• Blunting of costophrenic angle: \~175–200 mL
• Supine X-ray: Often misses small effusions

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: What is the most likely cause of the condition depicted in the HRCT below?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Aspergillus fumigatus

On HRCT of paranasal sinuses, allergic fungal rhinosinusitis (AFRS) typically shows hyperdense sinus opacification with heterogenous areas (“double density” sign) due to fungal concretions. The most common causative organism is Aspergillus fumigatus.

Key Radiologic Clue:

• Heterogeneous hyperattenuating material within expanded sinuses
• Possible sinus expansion with bone remodeling (not frank destruction)

Microbiology Correlation:

• Aspergillus fumigatus → Most common cause of allergic fungal sinusitis
• Aspergillus niger → More commonly causes otomycosis
• Staphylococcus aureus → Acute bacterial sinusitis
• Candida albicans → Rare cause of sinus fungal ball

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: What is the most likely diagnosis according to the given image in a 35 year old male presenting post-RTA?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Carotid-cavernous fistula

Carotid–cavernous fistula is an abnormal high-flow communication between the cavernous segment of the internal carotid artery and cavernous sinus, most commonly due to head trauma.

• Post-traumatic pulsatile exophthalmos
• Chemosis, orbital bruit
• Cranial nerve III, IV, VI palsies → diplopia
• Angiography: early filling of cavernous sinus and dilated ophthalmic veins

Why not other options:

• B. Pseudoaneurysm of internal carotid artery → Shows a localized contrast-filled outpouching from artery, not early filling of cavernous sinus or venous channels.
• C. Tumor blush of angiofibroma → Seen in nasopharyngeal tumor, with feeding vessels from maxillary artery and tumor vascular blush, not cavernous sinus communication.
• D. Extensive head & neck hemangioma → Shows diffuse vascular channels/soft tissue mass, no direct ICA–cavernous sinus fistula or early venous filling.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Community-acquired pneumonia

Chest X-ray in community-acquired pneumonia (CAP) typically shows lobar or segmental consolidation with homogeneous opacity, often with air bronchograms and loss of normal lung markings in the affected area.

This contrasts with:

• Bronchopneumonia: Patchy, multifocal peribronchial opacities involving multiple lobes
• Interstitial pneumonia: Reticular or ground-glass interstitial pattern
• Pulmonary TB: Upper lobe infiltrates, cavitation, fibrosis, or nodular lesions

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: What should be done to improve the contrast of an X-ray film in a morbidly obese patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Increase both KvP and mAs

In morbidly obese patients, greater tissue thickness causes increased X-ray absorption and scatter, leading to poor penetration and low image quality. To obtain an optimal radiograph:

• Increase kVp → improves beam penetration through thick tissues
• Increase mAs → increases number of photons reaching detector, improving image density

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: Which of the following findings are seen in a high-resolution CT scan of fungal pneumonia?
options: Cavitatory lesions with surrounding ground glass opacities
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Cavitatory lesions with surrounding ground glass opacities

On HRCT, invasive fungal pneumonia (especially Aspergillus) classically shows:

• Nodules or cavitary lesions
• Surrounding ground-glass opacity → “Halo sign” (due to hemorrhage around lesion)

This is highly suggestive of invasive fungal infection, particularly in immunocompromised patients.

Why not others?

A. Kerley lines: Seen in interstitial pulmonary edema (CHF), not fungal infection.

B. Hilar lymph nodes: Common in TB, lymphoma, sarcoidosis, not typical for invasive fungal pneumonia.

C. Pleural effusion: May occur but is non-specific and not characteristic.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: Which of the following investigations does not use ionizing radiation?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. FAST

• FAST (Focused Assessment with Sonography in Trauma) uses ultrasound, which is a non-ionizing imaging modality and does not expose patients to radiation.
• In contrast, scintigraphy, intravenous pyelography (IVP), and digital subtraction angiography (DSA) all involve ionizing radiation—either from radiotracers or X-rays.
• Ultrasound and MRI are the primary imaging modalities that avoid ionizing radiation and are preferred when radiation exposure must be minimized (e.g., in pregnancy or repeated imaging).

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: Which of the following is not a true statement about CT?
options: The higher the pitch, the lower will be the CT quality
Helical CT is faster than non-helical CT
The higher the pitch, the higher will be the radiation dose
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. The higher the pitch, the higher will be the radiation dose

In CT imaging, pitch refers to table movement per gantry rotation relative to beam width.

Imagine CT scan table is like a moving conveyor belt.

• Low pitch → Table moves slowly
• High pitch → Table moves fast

When the table moves slowly:

• X-rays overlap more
• Patient gets more radiation

When the table moves faster (high pitch):

• X-rays overlap less
• Patient gets less radiation

So:

• High pitch = Faster scan = Less overlap = Less radiation dose
• That’s why option D is wrong.

Simple rule to remember:

📌 Higher pitch → lower dose → slightly lower image quality

Thus:

• Higher pitch → faster scan, lower radiation dose, slightly lower image quality
• Lower pitch → slower scan, higher radiation dose, better image quality

Multidetector CT (MDCT) enables rapid acquisition and superior 3D reconstruction compared with conventional CT.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: Which of the following is the best investigation to calculate ejection fraction of the heart?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Cardiac MRI

Cardiac MRI is the gold standard non-invasive modality for accurate measurement of left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) because it provides high-resolution, three-dimensional volumetric assessment without geometric assumptions. It allows precise calculation of end-diastolic and end-systolic volumes and is highly reproducible, making it superior to nuclear scans for EF quantification.

Why not other options:

A. Thallium MPI: Assesses myocardial perfusion and ischemia; EF can be estimated but is less accurate than cardiac MRI.

B. 18-FDG PET: Evaluates myocardial viability and metabolism, not routinely used to calculate ejection fraction.

D. Pyrophosphate scan: Used mainly for cardiac amyloidosis detection, not for measuring EF.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: Which of the following isn't considered a benefit of USG compared to Mammography?
options: Can be used for screening mammographically undetectable or clinically non palpable breast mass
Useful in young females with dense breast
Differentiates between solid and Cystic lesions in the Breast
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Can be used for screening mammographically undetectable or clinically non palpable breast mass

• Breast ultrasonography (USG) is primarily a diagnostic adjunct to mammography—not a primary screening tool.
• It is especially useful in young women with dense breasts,
• But not routinely used for screening clinically non-palpable or mammographically occult breast masses due lower sensitivity for microcalcifications.
• Not recommended as routine screening in average-risk women.

✅ Correct answer: A

B. Useful in young females with dense breasts

✔ Correct — Mammography sensitivity decreases in dense breasts. USG performs better in dense tissue.

C. Differentiates solid vs cystic lesions

✔ Classic advantage of USG. Mammography cannot reliably do this.

D. Guided biopsy can be done

✔ Real-time imaging allows USG-guided FNAC/core biopsy.

TAKEAWAY

• Mammography = screening tool.
• Ultrasound = problem-solving tool (one step after screening)

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: Which of the following statements are false regarding X-rays?
options: Loss of soft tissue planes is the earliest X-ray change of infection
Glass pieces can be seen as radiopaque in X- ray images
Cartilage is not visualized on X-ray.
Live bone is more radio-opaque than dead bone on X- ray images
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Live bone is more radio-opaque than dead bone on X- ray images

On X-ray, dead bone (sequestrum) appears more radiopaque (whiter) than living bone because it loses its blood supply and undergoes increased mineralization, while surrounding living bone becomes osteopenic due to inflammation. Therefore, the statement that live bone is more radiopaque than dead bone is false.

Key Radiology Points:

• Earliest sign of infection on X-ray: Loss of soft tissue planes/swelling
• Glass pieces: Radiopaque and visible on X-ray
• Cartilage: Not visualized on X-ray (radiolucent)
• Sequestrum (dead bone): More radiopaque than viable bone

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: Which of the following will be avid on FDG PET scan?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Atypical carcinoid

FDG PET scan detects high glucose metabolism.

So tumors that have higher metabolic activity will show high FDG uptake (FDG avid).

Typical carcinoid:

• Low-grade tumor
• Slow growing
• Low metabolism
• Usually NOT very FDG avid

Atypical carcinoid:

• More aggressive
• Higher mitotic activity
• Higher metabolism
• ✅FDG avid

Mucinous adenocarcinoma:

• Has lots of mucin
• Low cellularity
• Often low FDG uptake
• Not strongly avid

Calcified TB granuloma:

• Old healed lesion
• No active metabolism
• Not FDG avid

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: While performing a HIDA scan in a patient with gallstones, the gallbladder was not visualized. What could be the possible diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Acute cholecystitis

• In a HIDA (hepatobiliary iminodiacetic acid) scan, non-visualization of the gallbladder indicates cystic duct obstruction, most commonly due to a gallstone, which is diagnostic of acute cholecystitis.
• In acute cholecystitis, the radiotracer enters the liver and bile ducts but cannot fill the gallbladder due to cystic duct blockage, leading to persistent non-visualization even on delayed images.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: 33 yr old female with fever, weight loss, elevated levels of ACE levels presented with chest X-ray as below. What is the probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Sarcoidosis

The clinical scenario with elevated ACE levels and bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy is suggestive of sarcoidosis.

Depending on the stage of sarcoidosis radiological features can range from a normal chest radiograph to pulmonary fibrosis.

Pulmonary sarcoidosis can be classified on a chest radiograph into 5 stages:

* Stage 0: Normal chest radiograph.

* Stage I: Hilar or mediastinal nodal enlargement only.

* Stage II: Nodal enlargement and parenchymal disease

* Stage III: Parenchymal disease only

* Stage IV: End-stage lung (pulmonary fibrosis)

Radiographic features are variable depending on the stage of the disease.

Stage 0: Normal chest radiograph.
Stage I: Hilar or mediastinal nodal enlargement only.

Stage II: Nodal enlargement and parenchymal disease.

Stage III: Parenchymal disease only.

Stage IV: End-stage lung (pulmonary fibrosis)

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A 45-year-old female presents for a follow-up of her disease and her chest X-ray is as shown below. What does the X-ray show?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Post mastectomy of right side

The chest x-ray shows a post-right-sided mastectomy image. The right hemithorax is more lucent (darker) than the left because the patient had previously undergone a right radical mastectomy in which the breast and the pectoralis muscles were removed. We can also see the multiple metallic clips from the surgery.

Mastectomy -

Indications for mastectomy include -

* Inflammatory breast cancer.

* Multicentric disease with more than two primary tumors in different quadrants of the breast.

* Diffuse suspicious microcalcifications on mammography, where the extent is not visible.

* Patients who received chest radiation previously and cannot receive more radiotherapy.

* Pregnancy where breast irradiation is contraindicated.

* Persistently positive resection margins.

* Tumors very large in relation to breast size.

* Patient preference

The radical mastectomy(Halstead's mastectomy) is no longer indicated due to higher morbidity with no survival benefit. The modified radical(Patey's)  mastectomy is done now instead.

Boundaries of Patey's mastectomy

* Laterally -  anterior margin of the latissimus dorsi

* Medially -  midline of the sternum

* Superiorly -  subclavius muscle

* Inferiorly -  2 to 3 cm inferior to the inframammary fold

Structures removed in Patey's mastectomy are -

* The whole breast

* The skin over the tumor and nipple

* All of the fat, fascia, and lymph nodes in the axilla

The pectoralis minor divided/retracted to access the upper axilla. The axillary vein and nerves to the serratus anterior and latissimus dorsi are preserved. The intercostal brachial nerves are usually divided and sensation changes may be present postoperatively.

Conservative breast surgery

Referred to as wide local excision. Involves removing the tumor and a margin of normal breast tissue. The term lumpectomy is reserved for when a large amount of normal breast tissue is not resected and it is called quadrantectomy is when an entire segment of the breast is removed.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A 45-year-old male with a history of heart surgery now presents with the chest X-ray shown below. What is the finding indicated by the '?' on the X-ray?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Prosthetic mitral valve

The structure marked in the image shows a prosthetic mitral valve and a pacemaker also in place.

Prosthetic heart valves are common. The most commonly replaced are aortic and mitral valves.

Replacements may be tissue or metallic valves.

In recent times, aortic valves in select circumstances are being replaced via a transcatheter approach, called transcatheter aortic valve implantation (TAVI) from a femoral artery approach.

Prosthetic valves are subdivided into two categories -mechanical and bioprosthetic

* Mechanical valves

* ball cage valves

* tilting disk valves

* Bioprosthetic valves

* homografts

* heterografts

* stented

* stentless

Transesophageal echocardiography is the modality of choice to assess the status of a prosthetic heart valve after placement of a valve.

Complications:

* Obstruction

* maybe due to thrombus or pannus

* Infective endocarditis

* with or without valvular vegetation or paravalvular abscess

* Paravalvular regurgitation

* Valve failure

* mechanical failure in mechanical valves

* degeneration of a biological valve

* Hemolytic anemia

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A 48-year-old patient, with HIV presented to the casualty with shortness of breath, and fever with chills. On examination, there was marked hepatosplenomegaly and diffuse rales were auscultated in all lung fields.The chest X-ray is shown below. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Miliary TB

The history, clinical features, and chest X-Ray point towards a diagnosis of miliary tuberculosis.

There is widespread dissemination of M. tuberculosis, via the hematogenous route that leads to the seeding of bacteria in various organs (hepatosplenomegaly).

It is a form of disseminated pulmonary tuberculosis, not extrapulmonary.

The risk factors of miliary TB include-

* Extremes of age

* Alcohol use

* Malignancy

* HIV

* Corticosteroids

* Connective tissue disease

* Renal failure

* Diabetes, and pregnancy

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A 50 -year-old woman presents with a gradual loss of visual acuity in the right eye. A CT head post-contrast reveals thickening of the the structure marked in the picture as a 'tram-track' appearance. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Optic nerve sheath Meningioma

The CT with contrast shows optic nerve thickening and the charachteristic finding of 'tram track appearance' is seen in optic nerve meningioma.

* Axial post contrast T1 weighted image showing the optic nerve involvement and compressed by a contrast enhanced circumferential mass surrounding the optic nerve sheath (tram track sign).

* Optic nerve meningioma is benign tumor arising from the arachnoid cap cells of the optic nerve sheath.

* CT or MRI shows tram track sign.

* The tram-track sign is useful in the differentiation between optic nerve sheath meningioma and optic nerve gliomas.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A 51-year-old man complains of abdominal pain and blood stained stools. The barium enema study of his intestines shows the following finding. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Intussusception

The given clinical scenario and the radiological image of the claw sign/pincer sign in barium enema is suggestive of intussusception.

Intussusception occurs when a portion of the alimentary tract is telescoped into an adjacent segment. It is the most common cause of intestinal obstruction between 5 months and 3 years of age. The most common location of intussusception is ileocolic.

The combination of paroxysmal abdominal pain, vomiting, and a palpable abdominal mass is a highly characteristic clinical presentation; the presence of associated rectal bleeding invariably confirms the diagnosis. Palpation of the abdomen usually reveals a slightly tender, "sausage-shaped" mass, sometimes ill-defined, which might increase in size during an episode of pain and is most often in the right upper abdomen, with its longitudinal axis cephalocaudal. However, approximately 30% of patients do not have a palpable mass.

Barium contrast enemas demonstrate a filling defect or cupping in the head of the contrast media where its advance is obstructed by the intussusceptum. This is known as the claw sign (shown below). A central linear column of contrast media may be visible in the compressed lumen of the intussusceptum, and a thin rim of contrast may be seen trapped around the invaginating intestine in the folds of mucosa within the intussuscipiens (coiled-spring sign). The intussusception appears as a sausage-shaped mass in a longitudinal plane or a target mass in the transverse plane on CT and USG.

Ultrasound signs include:

* Target sign -also known as the doughnut sign

* Pseudokidney sign: this is seen in the longitudinal section of the bowel:

* The edematous bowel resembles renal parenchyma and

* the mesentery, which is dragged into the intussusception, resembles the renal hilum.

* Crescent in a doughnut sign.

Other options:

Option B: Volvulus presents with constipation, abdominal bloating, nausea and/or vomiting. It shows a coffee bean sign.

Option C: Barium enema radiograph in colonic diverticulitis shows multiple barium-coated outpouchings from the colonic wall and gives the appearance of a saw-tooth. In cases of severe abdominal pain, a CT scan is preferred to avoid the risk of intestinal perforation.

Option D: Ulcerative colitis causes lead pipe appearance.

Pearl PF1800: Barium Studies

Barium swallow: Used to assess the pharynx, esophagus, and stomach. (Barium paste is used)

The image below is a barium swallow showing eosinophilic esophagitis and associated stricture:

Barium meal: Used to assess stomach and duodenum. (95% BaSO4 is used)

Barium meal followthrough: Used to assess the small intestine (50% BaSO4 is used)

Barium enema: Used to assess the large intestine (25% BaSO4 is used)

Pearl PF1850: Radiological findings in various GI disorders

Duodenal atresia: Double bubble sign

Jejunal and ileal atresia: Multiple air-fluid levels (plain erect X-ray abdomen) presenting as triple bubble sign.

Congenital hypertrophic pyloric stenosis: Single enlarged gastric gas bubble - single bubble sign

Sigmoid volvulus: Coffee bean sign

Achalasia cardia: Bird-beak sign

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A patient with head and neck cancer was told by his oncologist that needs radiotherapy at a total dose of 70 Gy over a 7 week period for his tumor. He was scheduled to receive a dose of 1.8-2Gy per fraction, once daily over 5 days a week, for 7 weeks. What is this type of radiotherapy called as?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Regular Fractionated radiotherapy

Since the patient needs 70Gy in total for his tumour and his dose per fraction is at 1.8-2.0 Gy, 5 days a week, for 7 weeks, it is called Regular/Conventional Fractionated Radiotherapy.

Radiotherapy:

The total dose of radiation needed for a tumour is usually given as fractions over the entire treatment period as it maximises the effects of the radiation on the malignant cells and minimises the damage on the healthy cells.

The reasons for this are due to :

1. Re-distribution: Cells are more resistant to damage in the late S2 phase while sensitive in the M and G2 phase. Only some tumour cells will be in the sensitive phase of the cell cycle when the radiation is given. Hence, giving another dose at a later time helps in killing the other cells who were in the resistant part of the cell cycle, thus increasing the success rate of the therapy.

2. Re-oxygenation: Hypoxic cells are less sensitive to the indirect effects of radiation. The tumour cells which are closer to oxygen sources are killed first and in the intervening time, the other relatively hypoxic cells can improve their oxygenation so that the next fraction of radiation is effective on them.

3. Repair: The ability to repair DNA is more for healthy cells than malignant cells and thus when a radiation dose has been received, the healthy cells repair their DNA faster than the malignant cells. The malignant cells whose DNA is not fully repaired are highly susceptible to the next dose of radiation.

Types of fractionation:

* In the case of Head and neck cancer, the conventional schedule of radiotherapy involves the delivery of 70 Gy in 1.8-2 Gy fractions(total around 35-36 fractions) over 7 weeks, treating 5 days per week.

* However, this dose can be delivered at 1.10-1.25 Gy/fraction for 56 fractions over the same time period of 7 weeks which is called hyperfractionation(Option B). This delivers a lower dose with more fractions and the efficacy improves as the healthy cells have more ability to repair themselves in the intervening time.

* Accelerated fractionation(Option C) is when the same 70 Gy, is given at around 1.6-1.8 Gy/fraction but it is delivered more than once daily, decreasing the total treatment time to around 6 weeks. These aim to decrease tumor proliferation which can lead to failure of the therapy.

Note:

* Shorter schedules remain useful for small-volume treatments: 50 Gy in 16 fractions over 3 weeks or 55 Gy in 20 fractions over 4 weeks.

* Accelerated schedules although is easier to implement than hyperfractionation result in a lesser survival gain.

Option D: Brachytherapy is a method of treatment in which sealed radioactive sources are used to deliver radiation at a short distance by interstitial, intracavitary, or surface application.

The following isotopes are used in brachytherapy:

* I-125 and Iridium-192 - are used in low-dose rate (LDR) brachytherapy.

* Cobalt-60 - is used for high-dose rate (HDR) brachytherapy.

Afterloading is the process of placing the radioactive material into the target region. This is either done manually by the oncologist, or by using remote afterloading devices.

Remote afterloading devices enable us to eliminate direct contact with radioactive sources while administration. It provides protection from radiation exposure to healthcare professionals by securing the radiation source in a shielded safe manner.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: Following appearance in IVP is caused by ______
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Ureterocoele

The image depicts cobra head/ adder head deformity in an IVP of bilateral ureteroceles.

* Ureterocoeles represent congenital dilatation of the distal-most portion of the ureter. The dilated portion of the ureter may herniate into the bladder secondary to the abnormal structure of vesicoureteric junction (VUJ).

* The cobra head sign (or spring onion sign) refers to dilatation of the distal ureter, surrounded by a thin lucent line, which is seen in patients with an adult-type ureterocoele. The cobra head appearance indicates an uncomplicated ureterocele.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: Identify the labelled structure in the image?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Midbrain

The labeled structure is the midbrain.

The midbrain develops from the midbrain vesicle, the cavity of which becomes much reduced to form the cerebral aqueduct or aqueduct of Sylvius.

The midbrain:

* Is of small size and is completely surrounded by cerebrospinal fluid in the subarachnoid space

* Has a cavity called the cerebral aqueduct, which opens above into the third ventricle

* Is located in the posterior cranial fossa

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: Identify the marked structure in the USG of liver given below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Portal vein

The marked structure is the portal vein.

Normal liver parenchyma echotexture is homogeneous and more reflective than the adjacent renal cortex.

Portal veins typically have hyperechoic walls (as they are invested by the Glisson capsule), and thus appear bright, while hepatic veins do not have reflective walls.

In color doppler, the portal vein waveform is normally continuous and may vary slightly with respiration and the cardiac cycle.

Hepatic veins converge on the IVC and right atrium and have walls indistinguishable from the adjacent parenchyma.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: Identify the Xray
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Hydro pneumothorax

The chest xray shows hydropneumothorax.

Chest radiography shows hydro pneumothorax with a collapsed right lung and an adjacent thoracic air–liquid level.

Hydro pneumothorax is a term given to the concurrent presence of a pneumothorax as well as a hydrothorax (i.e. air and fluid) in the pleural space.

On an erect chest radiograph, recognition of hydro pneumothorax can be rather easy and is classically shown as an air-fluid level.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: Xray of a 2 year old child is given, what is the possible diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Pneumoperitoneum

The X-ray shows "football sign" which is seen in the pneumoperitoneum.

Football sign-the abdominal cavity is outlined by gas from a perforated viscus, seen in massive pneumoperitoneum.

Causes of pneumoperitoneum include:

* Bowel perforation

* Peptic ulcer

* Ischemic bowel

* Necrotizing enterocolitis

* Small bowel perforation

* Trauma

* Penetrating injuries

* During surgery/laparoscopy

Radiological signs in pneumoperitoneum include:

* Bowel related signs

* Double-wall sign (also known as Rigler's sign): Both the outer and inner walls of the bowel are visible.

* Telltale triangle sign (also known as triangle sign): A radiolucent triangle of gas between three loops of bowel or between two loops of bowel and the abdominal wall.

* Peritoneal ligament related signs

* Football sign -the abdominal cavity is outlined by gas from a perforated viscus, seen in massive pneumoperitoneum.

* Falciform ligament sign - Falciform or medial umbilical ligaments may be seen due to free gas on either side of the ligaments.

* Lateral umbilical ligament sign (also known as inverted "V" sign) - Free gas routines the lateral umbilical ligament.

* Urachus sign

* Right upper quadrant signs

* Morison's pouch sign - a triangular area of gas in the right upper quadrant, usually bound by the 11th rib in the right upper quadrant in the area of Morrison's pouch.

* Cupola sign - Gas under the right and left hemidiaphragm joining in the midline. Seen on chest X-ray.

* Fissure for ligamentum teres sign

* Hepatic edge sign

* Lucent liver sign

* Periportal free gas sign

Rigler's sign-

Falciform ligament sign.

Cupola sign-

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A 13-year old boy with presents to you with limitation of abduction and internal rotation of the left hip. The X-ray appearance of his left hip joint is shown in the below image. What is the diagnosis of this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Slipped capital femoral epiphysis

The given clinical scenario and trethowan's sign seen in the x-ray are suggestive of slipped capital femoral epiphysis (SCFE).

The Klein line is a line along the superior aspect of the femoral neck which normally intersects the epiphysis. In SCFE, Klein's line does not intersect the epiphysis and passes superior to it. This is known as Trethowan's sign.

Slipped femoral capital epiphysis:

SCFE occurs during the period of rapid growth with the average age of presentation around 12 years.

Risk factors: Obesity, hypothyroidism, growth hormone excess, and chronic renal failure are all-important associations of SCFE.

Clinical features:

* Patients with SCFE typically present in the rapid growth phase of adolescence with pain in the thigh, groin, or knee.

* On examination, the affected limb is shortened and externally rotated.

* There is a limitation in abduction, flexion, and internal rotation on the affected side.

* Flexion of the hip might lead to obligate external rotation and abduction - positive Drehmann’s sign.

* Patients may have an antalgic or Trendelenburg gait.

Other radiological findings include:

* Wide or irregular physis with loss of the anterior head-neck concavity

* Sharp metaphyseal border of the head

* Loss of total epiphyseal height

* Steel sign (Metaphyseal blanch sign) - The posteriorly displaced femoral epiphysis overlaps over the metaphysis causing a crescent-shaped area of increased density on the AP radiograph.

* Capener’s sign –the metaphysis displaces laterally, worsening the slip and causes a reduction in the double-density crescent created by the overlap of the posterior acetabulum and proximal metaphysis on the AP radiograph.

* Southwick angle – The angle between the line drawn perpendicular to the physis and a line parallel to the femoral shaft. As slip worsens, the Southwick angle will increase. It is measured on the frog lateral X-ray view.

Other options:

Perthes disease:

It is characterized by idiopathic avascular necrosis of the proximal femoral epiphysis. This condition commonly affects children of 4-8 years of age. The child has pain in the hip while performing passive movements. The radiograph shows features of bone necrosis followed by remodeling.

Developmental Dysplasia of the hip: It is characterized by spontaneous dislocation of the hip joint before, during, or shortly after birth. This condition is more common in females. Children with this condition have a waddling gait and on examination abduction and lateral rotation of the hip are decreased. X-ray shows a broken Shenton's line and the femoral head lies in the upper and outer quadrants formed by Hilgenreiner’s line and Perkin’s line.

The image given below shows the vertical Perkin's line and the horizontal Hilgenreiner's line. Normally the femoral head lies in the inner and lower quadrant formed by these lines. But in DDH the femoral head is in the upper and outer quadrant.

Ankylosing spondylitis: It is a chronic progressive inflammatory condition affecting the sacroiliac joints and the axial skeleton. It is commonly seen in young male adults and they typically present with an insidious onset back pain that improves with exercise. The earliest radiological finding is erosion and fuzziness of the sacroiliac joints and the characteristic late sign is the bamboo-spine appearance.

X-ray showing bamboo-spine appearance-

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A 20-year-old male came with complaints of pain over the left flank associated with fever and chills. On examination, the patient had pain on the passive extension of the hip over the left side. Lab investigations reveal leucocytosis. CT scan shows findings as shown. What is the most probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Psoas Abscess

The clinical vignette of a patient with flank pain, fever, leucocytosis, positive psoas sign, and the CT scan showing a mass in the psoas muscle lateral to the vertebral column is diagnostic of a psoas abscess.

Psoas Abscess -

Commonly presents in males > females. In developed countries, the age of presentation is between 44 - 58 years and in developing countries <20 years of age.

Clinical features include fever, pain in the back or flank region, mass in the inguinal region, anorexia, and unintentional weight reduction. "Psoas sign" is pain brought on by extension of the hip.

Lab investigation - Leucocytosis, increased ESR, and mild anemia may be seen.

Diagnosis - Commonly confirmed using a CT scan. Blood culture and abscess material should be obtained in all cases to guide therapy.

Treatment - Percutaneous or surgical drainage plus Antibiotics

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A 36-year-old farmer came to the clinic with cough, chest pain for one week, and fatigue for a month, and his Chest X-ray was taken which is shown below. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Hydatid cyst

The chronic history, the frequent exposure to animals as he is a farmer, and the chest x-ray which shows a cystic lesion in the right lung are suggestive of Hydatid disease.

* The causative organism of hydatid disease is Echinococcus granulosus and it belongs to the class cestodes.

* It is a tape-like, segmented worm. It infects man accidentally, giving rise to hydatid cysts.

* Dogs are the definitive hosts of E. granulosus.

* Sheep are the usual intermediate hosts, but humans are accidental intermediate hosts. Humans are end-stage hosts of the parasite since there is no human to human transmission

The hydatid cyst wall consists of 3 layers:

* Pericyst- the outer dense fibrous capsule that is formed as a result of host inflammatory response.

* Ectocyst- the intermediate layer consisting of acellular, chitinous, laminated hyaline material.

* Endocyst- the inner germinal layer that is cellular and consists of a number of nuclei embedded in protoplasmic mass and is extremely thin. It is the vital layer of the cyst and it is the site of asexual reproduction giving rise to brood capsules with scolices.

The clinical features of hydatid disease of the lung are breathlessness, cough, hemoptysis, and chest pain.

Treatment includes wedge resection or lobectomy and administration of albendazole.

Other options:

* Asbestosis presents as pleural plaques, irregular opacities, ground-glass appearance particularly present at the lower lung fields. HRCT will show the presence of pleural plaque, subpleural curvilinear lines 5–10 mm in length that appears to be parallel to the pleura.

* Silicosis is an occupational disease and is caused by exposure to silica. It is seen in people who work in mining, stone cutting, sandblasting, and quarrying. It presents as small rounded opacities in the upper lobe. There may be calcification of hilar lymph nodes which leads to the appearance of eggshell calcification. HRCT will show a characteristic crazy paving pattern.

* Byssinosis is an occupational disease due to chronic exposure to cotton dust as in yarns of textile and rope-making industries. In the early stage of the disease, patients complain of occasional chest tightness towards the end of the first day of the workweek termed as monday chest tightness. As the day progress, the chest tightness may recur or persist throughout the week. Chest X-ray shows hyperlucency, diaphragmatic flattening, and emphysema. A chest CT demonstrates ground glass opacities largely distributed in then basal fashion with centrilobular nodules.

Pearl PF1538: Indications and contraindications of puncture, aspiration, injection, and re-aspiration (PAIR) in hydatid cyst

Indications:

* Relapse cyst, infected cyst, cyst >5 cm in different liver segments

* Patients who refuse surgery or where surgery is contraindicated

* Pregnant women, children < 3 years of age

* WHO - type CE1 and type CE3a.

Contraindications:

* Cysts in lung

* Cysts communicating with bile duct

* Cysts with multiple septae—honeycomb cysts

* Inaccessible cysts

* Hyperechogenic cysts

* Calcified cysts

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: Identify the diagnostic investigation shown below that is considered the preferred method for evaluating distal small bowel tumors.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Enteroclysis

Enteroclysis, which is the investigation of choice in patients with small bowel tumors.

Enteroclysis is a barium study in which the contrast agent is put directly into the duodenum through a nasogastric tube.

Continued infusion of 500 to 1000 mL of thin barium sulfate and methylcellulose suspension is done and then viewed continuously with the use of either fluoroscopy or radiographs taken at frequent intervals. This technique is a double-contrast procedure that allows detailed imaging of the entire small intestine.

Enteroclysis has a sensitivity of over 90% in the detection of small bowel tumors and is the investigation of choice, particularly for tumors located in the distal small bowel.

Advantages of enteroclysis:

* The contrast is administered at a controlled rate directly in the small bowel, bypassing the regulatory action of the pylorus.

* The entire small bowel is demonstrated in a distended state, allowing better diagnosis. As a result of the dilatation, the following can be visualized:

* Mild strictures

* Small sinus tracts and fistulas

* Minimal extrinsic compressions

* Skip lesions

* Proximal and distal extent of diffuse diseases.

* The examination can be completed in 15–30 minutes, thus reducing patient waiting time.

Pearl PF1589: Barium Studies

Barium swallow: Used to assess the pharynx, esophagus, and stomach.

The image below is a barium swallow showing eosinophilic esophagitis and associated stricture:

Barium meal: Used to assess stomach and duodenum.

Barium meal followthrough: Used to assess the small intestine

Barium enema: Used to assess the large intestine

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: Identify the heart chamber marked in the given CT image.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Left atrium

The structure marked in the above CT image is the left atrium.

Transverse CT images are to be observed from the foot end of the supine patient, as if we are sitting at the patient's feet. So the right-hand side of the observer corresponds to the left-hand side in the CT.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: In which condition is popcorn calcification seen ?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Pulmonary hamartoma

Popcorn calcification is seen in pulmonary hamartoma.
