Popcorn calcification is defined as a pattern of calcification in rings and arcs that resembles popped corn kernels.

The presence of fat in a well-circumscribed solitary pulmonary nodule which does not demonstrate significant growth is pathognomonic of a pulmonary hamartoma.

Chest x-ray showing pulmonary hamartoma:

Amorphous calcifications with rings and arcs which resemble popped corn kernels in appearance are known as pop-corn calcification.

It may be seen in

* Chondroid lesions like chondrosarcoma

* Fibrous dysplasia

* Pulmonary hamartomas

* Fibroadenoma breast

* Calcified uterine fibroid

* Metaphyses and epiphyses of long bones of children with osteogenesis imperfecta.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: The characteristic appearance of oesophagus on barium swallow, as shown in the image below, is seen in which of the following conditions?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Diffuse esophageal spasm

The corkscrew appearance of the esophagus is seen in diffuse esophageal spasm.

* Diffuse/distal esophageal spasm (DES) is a motility disorder of the esophagus.

* On barium swallow, DES may appear as a corkscrew or rosary bead esophagus, but this is uncommon.

* Manometry is the gold-standard diagnostic test.

Achalasia is a primary esophageal motility disorder characterised by the absence of esophageal peristalsis and impaired relaxation of the lower esophageal sphincter (LES) in response to swallowing.

In achalasia single contrast esophagogram shows, dilatation of the esophagus with a bird beak deformity near the gastroesophageal junction.

In esophageal carcinoma barium study will show irregular narrowing, mucosal destruction and shouldered margins.

Double-contrast esophagram shows a large, flat ulceration (arrow) in the distal esophagus in a patient with CMV esophagitis.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: What are the imaging modality being used and the diagnosis in the given image below of the kidneys?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. MRI of Polycystic kidney disease

As the bones and vertebrae appear white in a CT image while in an MRI the bones are seen as black, this is an MRI image. The given image is of an MRI with multiple cysts in the kidney and is suggestive of Polycystic kidney disease, mostly ADPKD( Adult polycystic kidney disease).

ADPKD is inherited as an autosomal dominant trait with mutations in the PKD1(chromosome 16) and PKD2 genes (chromosome 4).

The disease does not usually manifest before 30 years of age, and in some patients, it is never diagnosed. The progression of renal failure in this disease is faster in males.

Hypertension is the most common presentation. Renal manifestations of ADPKD include:

* Flank/loin pain -  either due to hemorrhage inside cysts or due to renal stones (most commonly uric acid stones)

* Irregular upper quadrant renal mass

* Hematuria

* Renal failure (seen in 10-15% of the patients who receive hemodialysis)

It is associated with a number of extrarenal manifestations like polycystic liver disease, where cysts are usually asymptomatic but symptoms may occur due to mass effect of cysts, intracranial berry aneurysms are seen in approximately 10% of patients with ADPKD and mitral valve prolapse, the most common valvular abnormality observed in patients with ADPKD can be diagnosed by echocardiography.

Intravenous pyelography shows a characteristic spider leg pattern, as a result of narrowed and stretched calyces and elongated, compressed renal pelvis.

Treatment includes management of hypertension using ACE inhibitors like lisinopril or angiotensin receptor blockers like telmisartan. Narcotic analgesics should be limited to episodes of acute pain. V2 receptor antagonists like Tolvaptan have been observed to slow the decline in renal function over a 3 year period.

USG-guided CT aspiration is both diagnostic and therapeutic; surgical unroofing of multiple or large cysts may alleviate symptoms of pain. Nephrectomy is indicated for symptomatic patients with end-stage renal disease (ESRD).

Note:

Horseshoe kidney is a common congenital anomaly in which there is a fusion of the inferior poles of both kidneys. It is common in patients with Turner's syndrome. Stone disease and hydronephrosis can occur as complications due to blockage of the ureteropelvic junction.

The image shown below shows the appearance of the horseshoe kidney on a CT scan.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A cancer patient undergoing radiotherapy is given a dose of 1.8 to 2 Gy once daily for 5 days per week for a duration of 6 to 8 weeks. What is this type of brachytherapy called?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Regular Fractionated radiotherapy

Since the patient is given a dose of 1.8-2.0 Gy per day for 5 days a week, for 6 to 8 weeks, it is called Regular/Conventional Fractionated Radiotherapy.

Radiotherapy:

The total dose of radiation needed for a tumor is usually given as fractions over the entire treatment period as it maximizes the effects of the radiation on the malignant cells and minimizes the damage to the healthy cells.

The reasons for this are due to :

1. Re-distribution: Cells are more resistant to damage in the late S2 phase while sensitive in the M and G2 phase. Only some tumor cells will be in the sensitive phase of the cell cycle when the radiation is given. Hence, giving another dose at a later time helps in killing the other cells that were in the resistant part of the cell cycle, thus increasing the success rate of the therapy.

2. Re-oxygenation: Hypoxic cells are less sensitive to the indirect effects of radiation. The tumor cells which are closer to oxygen sources are killed first and in the intervening time, the other relatively hypoxic cells can improve their oxygenation so that the next fraction of radiation is effective on them.

3. Repair: The ability to repair DNA is more for healthy cells than malignant cells and thus when a radiation dose has been received, the healthy cells repair their DNA faster than the malignant cells. The malignant cells whose DNA is not fully repaired are highly susceptible to the next dose of radiation.

Types of fractionation:

Standard Fractionation: Radiotherapy(RT) is given once daily for 5 days/week, not more than 2 Gy/fraction.

Accelerated Fractionation:(Option C) Any fractionation schedule that gives >10 Gy/week. Subtypes include:

* Pure accelerated fractionation (2 Gy/fraction, 6–7 fractions/week)

* Accelerated hypofractionation (>3 Gy/fraction)

* Accelerated hyperfractionation (>1 fraction/day)

Hypofractionation: Increased fraction size, with or without a decreased number of fractions/week.

* Stereotactic Radiation (SRS/SBRT/SABR): RT delivered with stereotactic localization techniques in five fractions or less.

* Fractionated Stereotactic RT (FSRT): RT delivered with stereotactic techniques and more than five fractions.

Hyperfractionation: Decreased fraction size with more than one fraction per day (BID or TID). (Option B)

Concomitant Boost (CB): Two fractions per day with one fraction to a large field and the other to a boost volume.

Simultaneous Integrated Boost (SIB): One fraction per day with a higher dose to a boost volume and a lower dose to the large field.

Note: Brachytherapy(Option D) is a method of treatment in which sealed radioactive sources are used to deliver radiation at a short distance by interstitial, intracavitary, or surface application.

Correct answer: A. V

The liver segment highlighted in green in this CT section is segment V. The section of the CT given is taken below the portal vein as the cross-section of the portal vein before its bifurcation can be viewed.

A horizontal plane known as the portal plane divides the liver where the portal vein bifurcates and becomes horizontal. This divides each section of the liver into superior and inferior segments:

* Left lateral section: segment II above and segment III below the portal plane

* Left medial section: segment IVa above and segment IVb below the portal plane

* Right anterior (or medial) section: segment VIII above and segment V below the portal plane

* Right posterior (or lateral) section: segment VII above and segment VI below the portal plane

Shown below is a section from below the portal plane.

Couinaud classification is the commonly used classification of the liver. It divides the liver is divided into eight segments. It is based on the distribution of portal venous branches in the liver parenchyma. Each segment has its own vascular supply, biliary drainage, and lymphatic drainage.

The Couinaud's liver segments are as follows:

* Based on the distribution of hepatic portal venous branches in the parenchyma

* Each segment has its own dual vascular inflow, biliary drainage and lymphatic drainage

Segment I corresponds to the gross anatomical caudate lobe and is considered as posterior segment.

questions.text: Identify the structure marked in the image given below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Internal capsule

The structure marked in the MRI of the brain is the Internal capsule.

The image below shows parts of the brain in an axial section of an MRI.

The internal capsule is a component of the white matter of the brain. They contain projection fibers. It can be divided into the following parts:

* Anterior limb

* Genu

* Posterior limb

* Retrolenticular/retrolentiform portion

* Sublenticular/sublentiform portion

The anterior limb of the internal capsule carries the fronto-pontine fibers, a lesion here produces confusion, impaired attention, agitation, and dysarthria.

Genu carries fibers of the corticonuclear tract.

The posterior limb of the internal capsule carries cortico-spinal motor fibers in the anterior part and the lesion here produces contralateral hemiparesis. The posterior part of the posterior limb carries sensory fibers and lesions here may produce contralateral hemi-sensory deficits.

The retro-lenticular part carries fibers mainly from optic radiation. A lesion here produces homonymous hemianopia, superior quadrantanopia, or inferior quadrantanopia.

The sub-lenticular part contains temporopontine and some parietopontine fibers.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: Whole-body CT scan protocol for a trauma patient includes all, except ______.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. CT Limbs

The whole-body CT of a trauma patient does not include CT limbs.

Whole-body CT or trauma CT or pans can is increasingly being used in the context of trauma patients with a dangerous mechanism of injury:

* Non-contrast CT of head

* Non-contrast CT of neck

* Contrast-enhanced CT of chest (arterial phase)

* Contrast-enhanced CT of abdomen (portal venous phase)

The purpose of the scan is to rapidly evaluate life-threatening injuries and accurately diagnose known and unknown injuries.

While limb injuries can certainly occur in trauma cases, they are usually assessed through physical examination, X-rays, or targeted CT scans if there is suspicion of a specific injury. Including limb imaging as part of the standard whole-body CT scan protocol would increase the scan time and radiation exposure for the patient without significantly impacting the detection of life-threatening injuries.

Therefore, CT limbs is the exception and is not typically included in the whole-body CT scan protocol for trauma patients.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A patient was brought to the emergency department after a road traffic accident. His CT scan is shown below. What is the most probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Subdural hemorrhage

The given CT image shows a crescent-shaped lesion that crosses suture lines and is indicative of acute subdural hematoma/hemorrhage.

Subdural hemorrhage (SDH) is a collection of blood between the dura and the arachnoid layers of the meninges. Most commonly, it results from the rupture of cortical bridging veins. Non-contrast CT is the investigation of choice.

Radiographic features of subdural hemorrhages:

* Crescent-like distribution around the periphery of the brain.

* They are not limited by sutures.

* Crescent-shaped hypodense lesion on axial CT: Chronic subdural hemorrhage

* Crescent-shaped hyperdense collections on CT: Acute subdural hemorrhage.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: Identify the correct anatomies from the CT scan given below:
options: A- Kidney, B- Liver, C- Pancreas
A- Liver, B- Pancreas, C- Spleen
A- Spleen, B- Kidney, C- Liver
A- Pancreas, B- Liver, C- Spleen
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. A- Liver, B- Pancreas, C- Spleen

The correct identification of structures marked as A, B, and C in the CT image is: A-Liver, B-Pancreas, C-Spleen.

A - Liver: The liver is an organ located in the upper right portion of the abdomen. On a CT scan, the liver has a homogeneous appearance with well-defined borders. The liver's density is higher compared to surrounding organs due to its composition of hepatocytes and blood vessels. Additionally, blood vessels such as the hepatic artery and portal vein can be seen supplying blood to the liver.

B - Pancreas: The pancreas is a glandular organ situated behind the stomach and adjacent to the first part of the small intestine (duodenum). On a CT scan, the pancreas appears as a soft tissue structure with a slightly lower density compared to the liver. It typically has a lobulated appearance and is located in the retroperitoneal space. The pancreatic duct may also be visualized, extending from the pancreas to the duodenum.

C - Spleen: The spleen is an organ located in the upper left portion of the abdomen, beneath the diaphragm and behind the stomach. On a CT scan, the spleen appears as a well-defined structure with a homogeneous density similar to the liver. It typically has a slightly lower density compared to the liver.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: Which of the following radioactive isotopes is used for teletherapy?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Cobalt-60

Cobalt-60 emits high-energy gamma rays and is commonly used in radiation therapy machines called cobalt units or teletherapy units. These units deliver radiation from outside the body, targeting the tumor.

Other options:

A) Iodine-125: This radioactive isotope is commonly used in brachytherapy for treating prostate cancer. It emits low-energy gamma rays that can effectively target and treat the cancerous tissue.

C) I-131 is a beta-emitter that is taken up by thyroid tissue as well as differentiated thyroid cancers and is used for systemic radiotherapy.

D) Iridium-192: This is a commonly used radioactive isotope in brachytherapy. It emits high-energy gamma rays and is used for treating various types of cancer, such as cervical, prostate, and breast cancer. Iridium-192 is often used in temporary brachytherapy, where the radioactive source is temporarily placed in the body and then removed after a specific period of treatment.

In summary, while Iodine-125 and Iridium-192 are commonly used in brachytherapy, Cobalt-60 is primarily used in external beam radiation therapy. Iodine-131 is used in other medical applications, such as thyroid cancer treatment and diagnostic imaging.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: Which of the following radioisotopes is used in a PET-CT scan?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 18F-FDG

18F-FDG is the radioisotope used in a PET-CT scan.

Positron emission tomography - CT (PET-CT):

* PET imaging is based on the detection of an injected positron-emitting radioactive tracer.

* It relies on the coincidence detection of the annihilation photons (γ), which are released when a positron combines with an electron.

* A glucose analogue called FDG (fluorodeoxyglucose) is used in PET imaging. FDG is taken up by metabolically active cells, where it undergoes phosphorylation to form FDG-6-phosphate. Unlike glucose, FDG-6-phosphate cannot undergo further metabolism and becomes trapped within the cell. (So, the patient must be fasted for 4-6 hrs prior to imaging).

* The trapped FDG-6-phosphate is detected by the PET scanner.

* Before injecting FDG, the blood glucose level should be measured. It should be < 150 mg/dL. Good blood glucose control is essential as FDG uptake is competitively inhibited by glucose.

* Imaging is started 60 minutes following FDG injection.

Indications of PET-CT:

* PET-CT is used in oncology imaging to detect malignant cells as they demonstrate increased glucose metabolism relative to normal tissues.

* It is indicated for the differentiation of a malignant from a benign lesion.

* It is indicated in tumour staging and evaluation of tumour recurrence.

Areas of normal physiological uptake in PET CT:

* Brain tissue

* Skeletal muscle, especially after strenuous activity, and laryngeal muscles following speech

* Myocardium

* Gastrointestinal tract, e.g. intestinal wall

* Genitourinary tract (FDG is excreted via the renal system and passes into the collecting systems)

* Brown fat (FDG accumulates here as glucose and ATP are required for heat production)

* Thymus

* Bone marrow

Other options:

Option A: 16F-FDG (Fluorodeoxyglucose) is a radiolabeled glucose analogue used in Positron Emission Tomography (PET) to assess metabolic activity in tissues. It is particularly useful for detecting cancer, and infections, and monitoring neurological disorders due to its ability to highlight areas with high glucose consumption.

Option C: Carbon-11 (C-11) is used for certain types of PET imaging, particularly in neurology and oncology.

Option D: Gallium-68 (Ga-68) is used for imaging certain types of neuroendocrine tumours and somatostatin receptor imaging.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: X-ray of a patient appears as below. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Lung collapse

In the provided X-ray image, there is evidence of complete opacification (whitening) of the left lung field, along with a shift of the mediastinum (central structure in the chest containing the heart and major blood vessels) towards the affected side. These findings are indicative of a lung collapse, also known as atelectasis.

Other Options:

Option A: Pneumonia may present with airspace opacification in the lungs, but it usually does not result in complete opacification of an entire lung field as seen in the provided image.

Option B: Pleural effusion typically appears as a blunting of the costophrenic angles or as increased opacity at the lung bases on a chest X-ray.

Option D: Hydropneumothorax refers to the presence of both fluid (hydrop) and air (pneumo) in the pleural space. While it can cause lung collapse, it typically presents with a combination of radiographic findings indicating both air and fluid in the pleural space, such as an air-fluid level or a meniscus sign.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A female patient presents with difficulty ingesting liquids more than solids. What is the most likely characteristic finding on imaging?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Rat tail appearance

The clinical scenario of a female patient having more difficulty swallowing liquids than solids suggests achalasia cardia, with the characteristic imaging finding being the Rat tail sign.

Achalasia is a primary oesophagal motility disorder. It is characterized by the absence of oesophagal peristalsis and impaired lower esophageal sphincter (LES) relaxation in response to swallowing. These abnormalities cause a functional obstruction at the gastroesophageal junction.

Esophageal manometry shows:

* Incomplete LES relaxation in response to swallowing.

* High resting LES pressure.

* Absent esophageal peristalsis.

On performing a timed barium study, barium will be retained for more than five minutes. The fluoroscopic examination will reveal a dilated oesophagus that tapers to form a bird's beak at the gastroesophageal junction as seen in the image above. Endoscopy and biopsy are usually carried out to rule out cancer. 24-hour pH monitoring is used in the diagnosis of gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD).

Medical management with sublingual nitroglycerin, nitrates, and calcium-channel blockers for symptomatic relief. Pneumatic dilatation and Botox injection

Surgical management is the treatment of choice :

* Laparoscopic Heller's myotomy is the definitive management - The major complication associated with this procedure is gastro-oesophageal reflux. So it is best to combine it with partial anterior fundoplication (Heller–Dor operation).

* Peroral endoscopic myotomy (POEM) is a recently introduced, advanced natural-orifice approach for myotomy.

* Open Esophageal Myotomy - rarely done.

Other options:

Option A: Apple core sign is characteristically seen in the barium enema of carcinoma colon as shown below.

Option B: Barium enema radiograph of diverticulosis shows multiple barium-coated outpouchings from the colonic wall and gives the appearance of a saw-tooth as shown below.

Option C: Crohn's disease is an inflammatory bowel disease that shows the string sign of Kantor on barium enema as shown below.

Pearl PF0313: Achalasia Cardia

Achalasia is a rare disease caused by the loss of ganglion cells within the esophageal myenteric plexus.

Their absence leads to increased tone of the lower esophageal sphincter, impaired relaxation of the lower esophageal sphincter (LES), and absent peristalsis.

Achalasia is the only true motility disorder of the esophagus.

Primary achalasia is due to ganglion cell degeneration and is thought to be due to an autoimmune process attributable to latent infection with human herpes simplex virus 1 (HSV1) combined with genetic susceptibility.

Secondary achalasia may arise in Chaga's disease

Clinical features:

* dysphagia (solid and liquid food)

* regurgitation

* chest pain

* weight loss

* bronchitis, pneumonia, or lung abscess from aspiration

Differential diagnosis: Diffuse esophageal spasm, Chagas’ disease, and pseudoachalasia

On barium swallow: Bird beak-appearance

Investigation of choice: Manometry (most sensitive)

Treatment: Pneumatic dilatation and Heller myotomy

Pearl PF0315: Manometric findings in oesophageal disorders

Manometric Findings in Nutcracker Esophagus

* Peristaltic esophageal contractions 2 standard deviations above normal

* Amplitude > 180 mmHg and duration > 7seconds.

* Normal peristaltic sequence

Manometric Findings in Diffuse Esophageal Spasm

* Simultaneous, multipeaked contractions of high amplitude (>120 mm Hg) or long duration (>2.5 sec)

* These erratic contractions occur after more than 20% of wet swallows.

* Intermittent normal peristalsis

Manometric Findings in Hypertensive Lower Esophageal Sphincter-

* Elevated LES pressure > 26mmHg and normal relaxation of LES

* The esophageal body may be hyper-peristaltic or normal.

Manometric findings in Achalasia Cardia

* Incomplete LES relaxation

* Aperistalsis in the esophageal body

* Elevated LES pressure ≥26 mmHg

* Increased intraesophageal baseline pressures relative to gastric baseline

Manometric findings in ineffective esophageal motility disorders

* Decreased or absent amplitude of esophageal peristalsis (<30 mmHg)

* Increased number of non-transmitted contractions

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A non-smoker patient with a history of cardiac disease suddenly develops chest pain and breathlessness. An X-ray is performed and given below. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Cardiogenic pulmonary edema

The given chest X-ray shows increased interstitial markings, vascular redistribution, and alveolar oedema in a butterfly pattern points to a diagnosis of pulmonary oedema.

Acute severe hypertension, acute myocardial infarction, or exacerbation of chronic heart failure are some of the common causes of cardiogenic pulmonary oedema. It can be precipitated by the discontinuation of medications (non-compliant patient), excessive salt intake, or tachyarrhythmias.

It presents with severe dyspnea, pink frothy sputum production, diaphoresis, and cyanosis. Auscultation reveals rales and rhonchi in all lung fields. Cardiomegaly might be seen in cases of chronic heart failure.

Management of pulmonary oedema includes the use of diuretics, nitrates, and morphine to decrease the preload. Nitroglycerin and isosorbide dinitrate have a rapid onset of action and can be given sublingually. If there is a persistence of pulmonary oedema and no hypotension, it can be administered intravenously.

Oxygen therapy to maintain a saturation of >92% is recommended. If saturation is not maintained even with supplemental oxygen, positive-pressure ventilation through a face mask or endotracheal intubation is required. A sitting position with legs hanging by the side of the bed can be used to reduce venous return in patients without hypotension.

Non-cardiac causes of pulmonary oedema are high altitude, sepsis, and disseminated intravascular coagulation.

Heart failure is a manifestation of most chronic cardiac conditions such as hypertension, valvular heart disease, and coronary artery disease. Symptoms such as shortness of breath, orthopnea, and paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea point to left heart failure due to pulmonary congestion. In contrast, symptoms such as pedal oedema, weight gain, early satiety, and hepatic congestion are characteristic of right heart failure.

Chest X-ray shows increased interstitial markings, vascular redistribution, and alveolar oedema in a bat wing/ butterfly pattern as given in the image below.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A patient with a history of breast cancer underwent tele cobalt-60 radiotherapy. She now presents with respiratory distress, and imaging shows bilateral perihilar ground glass opacities. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Radiation pneumonitis

A patient with a history of breast cancer who previously received Tele cobalt-60 radiotherapy now presents with respiratory distress. Imaging shows bilateral perihilar ground glass opacities, suggesting a likely diagnosis of radiation pneumonitis.

Radiation pneumonitis is an inflammatory reaction in the lungs that occurs as a result of radiation therapy, commonly seen in patients treated for breast cancer, lung cancer, or lymphomas. It typically develops within weeks to months after radiation exposure and presents with symptoms such as cough, fever, chest pain, and progressive shortness of breath. The condition arises due to damage to the alveolar and capillary structures, leading to increased vascular permeability, inflammatory infiltration, and pulmonary oedema. Imaging findings, particularly on CT scans, may show areas of ground-glass opacities, consolidation, or haziness, often in the radiation field.

If left untreated, radiation pneumonitis can progress to pulmonary fibrosis, causing long-term respiratory complications. Management involves corticosteroids to reduce inflammation and supportive care, including oxygen therapy if needed.

Prevention strategies include limiting the radiation dose, using advanced radiotherapy techniques to minimize lung exposure, and closely monitoring high-risk patients. Early recognition and intervention are crucial to improving outcomes and preventing long-term lung damage in affected individuals.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: Which of the following is the primary use of the given imaging modality?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Staging of esophageal cancer

The provided imaging modality is an endoscopic ultrasound of the oesophagus, primarily utilized for staging oesophagal carcinoma.

Esophageal carcinoma is more commonly seen in men. Tobacco use and alcohol are strong risk factors. Adenocarcinoma and squamous cell carcinoma of the oesophagus are the two most common types. The squamous cell variant usually affects the upper two-thirds and the adenocarcinoma variant usually affects the lower third. The incidence of adenocarcinoma is increasing.

Clinical features include:

* Dysphagia (most common)

* Regurgitation

* Vomiting

* Odynophagia

* Weight loss

In the advanced stage, there can be hoarseness of voice due to recurrent laryngeal nerve palsy, horner’s syndrome, chronic spinal pain, and diaphragmatic paralysis.

Flexible endoscopy with biopsy is preferred for confirmation of diagnosis. Other investigations include barium swallow, which shows a rat-tail appearance due to irregular narrowing or ulceration. Contrast-enhanced CT and PET can be used to assess distant metastasis. Endoscopic ultrasonography (EUS) is the investigation of choice to assess tumour invasion and lymph node metastasis.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A 20-year-old man was brought to the emergency department after a RTA. On presentation, his pulse is 110/minute, RR is 18/minute and BP is 80/60 mmhg. What is the next step in management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. eFAST

The given clinical scenario of a patient being hemodynamically unstable after a RTA indicates a probable ongoing hemorrhage and the next step in the management is to perform an eFAST.

Cardiogenic shock, hemorrhagic shock, or pneumothorax are the most likely causes of hypotension in a trauma patient. Ultrasound evaluation using eFAST to look for pericardium, pleural cavities, and abdomen in combination with plain radiographs of the chest and pelvis will usually identify the source of the bleed.

In patients with hypotension due to blunt trauma, the pelvis should be wrapped in a sheet for stabilization until radiography can be done.

eFAST stands for extended FAST and incorporates left and right thoracic views to assess for pneumothorax and haemothorax.

Limitations of eFAST are:

* Operator-dependent

* Bowel gas and subcutaneous air distort images.

* Can miss diaphragm, bowel, and pancreatic injuries

* Unreliable for assessment of the retroperitoneum

* Cannot reliably exclude injury in penetrating trauma

* May need repeating or supplementing with other investigations

FAST stands for Focussed Assessment with Sonography for Trauma. It is a rapid, non-invasive bedside test for detecting free fluid using sonography used to assess patients for potential thoracoabdominal injuries.

Technique:

* The patient is placed in a supine position and the following regions are scanned:

* Subxiphoid transverse view: assess for pericardial effusion and left lobe liver injuries

* Longitudinal view of the right upper quadrant: assess for right liver injuries, right kidney injury, and Morison pouch

* Longitudinal view of the left upper quadrant: assess for splenic injury and left kidney injury

* Transverse and longitudinal views of the suprapubic region: assess the bladder and pouch of Douglas

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A female patient presents with ambiguous genitalia and rapid virilization. She also complains of excessive facial hair growth, voice deepening, and an enlarged clitoris over the past few months. CT scan is shown below. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Congenital adrenal hyperplasia

The presented clinical scenario, along with the CT scan findings of bilaterally enlarged adrenal glands with nodules in the adrenal cortex, suggests a likely diagnosis of Congenital Adrenal Hyperplasia (CAH).

Congenital adrenal hyperplasia (CAH) is a disorder of cortisol synthesis. It has an autosomal recessive pattern of inheritance. Cortisol deficiency increases the secretion of the adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH), causing adrenal hyperplasia with the overproduction of intermediate metabolites. This child has clitoromegaly due to increased androgen synthesis. The enzyme 21-hydroxylase helps in the downstream synthesis of cortisol and aldosterone. A deficiency of aldosterone causes salt wasting that presents as low blood pressure.

The presentation depends on the enzyme that is deficient, which could result in mineralocorticoid deficiency or excess, incomplete virilization or precocious puberty in affected males, and virilization or sexual infantilism in affected females.

Given below is the pathway and enzymes involved in adrenal steroid synthesis:

Other options:

Option B: Adrenocortical carcinoma might appear as a large, irregular mass within the adrenal gland. The mass could have areas of necrosis or hemorrhage, contributing to its irregular appearance.

Option C: A pheochromocytoma typically presents as a well-defined, solid mass within the adrenal gland. It might be associated with areas of hemorrhage, leading to a heterogeneous appearance.

Option D: The adrenal glands may appear normal in size or slightly enlarged on a CT scan in case of primary hyperaldosteronism. There might not be distinct masses or nodules in the adrenal glands.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A patient presented after a road traffic accident (RTA) with a head injury. CT head is shown below. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Depressed skull fracture

The clinical history and the CT image are suggestive of a depressed skull fracture of the left frontal bone.

A depressed skull fracture occurs when a portion of the skull is pushed inward due to trauma, creating a depression in the bone. This type of fracture can occur as a result of a direct impact to the head, such as in a road traffic accident.

The management of depressed skull fractures:

* The first step is to order a CT scan to know the degree of depression and to exclude the presence of an intracranial hematoma or contusion.

* The depressed fracture is elevated and managed as an open fracture (surgery) if:

* The degree of depression is greater than the thickness of the adjacent skull

* The wound is are open and grossly contaminated

* There are focal neurological deficits

* Less severe depressed fractures are managed by the closure of the overlying scalp laceration, if present.

Other options:

Option A: Concussion refers to a temporary disturbance in brain function following head trauma and typically does not show up on CT scans.

Option B: Epidural hematoma often appears as a lens-shaped collection of blood on CT scans.

Option D: Subarachnoid hemorrhage may appear as diffuse or localized blood on imaging.

Pearl PF0368: Types of skull vault fracture

Diastatic fracture - Separation of sutures due to blow with blunt weapon or from cerebral edema. It is also called sutural fracture.

Fissured fracture/Linear fracture:

* Linear skull fractures are breaks in the bone that traverse the full thickness of the skull from the outer to inner table.

* They are usually fairly straight with no bone displacement.

* The common cause of injury is blunt force trauma where the impact energy transferred over a wide area of the skull.

Pond fracture - Occurs in children due to elasticity of bones. It is also known as indented fracture.

Depressed fracture - Caused by a heavy weapon with a small striking surface. Its shape indicates the type of weapon which is produced. So it is also called 'signature fracture'.

Comminuted fracture - It is also called spider web fracture and has a stellate appearance where there is no displacement of fracture.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A patient presented with pain and swelling of his left arm after a fall from height. An upper arm X-ray was done. Which nerve is most likely to be injured in this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Radial nerve

In the above clinical scenario, the history and radiograph suggest a closed fracture of the shaft of the humerus. The radial nerve is commonly damaged in this condition. This is because the radial nerve follows a superficial path around the humerus and can be stretched or compressed when there is significant trauma to the upper arm.

It manifests with wrist drop (inability to dorsiflex the wrist) and finger drop (inability to dorsiflex the digits). Numbness occurs on the dorsoradial aspect of the hand and the dorsal aspect of the radial 3 1/2 digits.

Management of humerus shaft fractures:

* Conservative management using a hanging cast or U-slab for 2-3 weeks followed by functional bracing

* Surgical fixation by compression plating, interlocking intramedullary nail, semi-flexible pins, or an external fixator is indicated in:

* Open fractures

* Pathological fractures

* Unstable humeral and forearm fractures (floating elbow)

* Radial nerve palsy

The below X-ray shows shaft of humerus fracture.

Other options:

* The axillary nerve is most commonly injured in shoulder dislocations or fractures of the surgical neck of the humerus.

* The ulnar nerve is more commonly injured in conditions like elbow dislocations, fractures of the medial epicondyle of the humerus, or entrapment at the elbow (cubital tunnel syndrome).

* The median nerve is more frequently associated with injuries in the forearm or wrist, such as carpal tunnel syndrome, or with certain systemic conditions like pronator teres syndrome.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: The principle of linear accelerators is used in the production of _____?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. X-rays

X-rays are the most common form of radiation used in radiotherapy. They are produced from LINAC (Linear Accelerator).

A LINAC is used in radiation therapy to deliver high-energy X-rays or electrons to target specific areas of the body, typically to treat cancerous tissues. It uses microwave technology to accelerate charged particles (such as electrons) at a high speed and then directs them into a target (usually a heavy metal) to produce X-rays. These X-rays are then carefully directed at the patient's body to deliver therapeutic radiation doses to the tumor while minimizing damage to surrounding healthy tissues.

Gamma rays: They are also a form of electromagnetic radiation used in medical imaging and radiation therapy, but linear accelerators are primarily associated with the production of X-rays for medical purposes, and gamma rays are usually produced in different ways.

Sources of radiation exposure:

* Natural:

* Cosmic rays

* Environmental - terrestrial and atmospheric

* Radioactive isotopes - of potassium (K-40) and carbon (C-14)

* Man-made:

* Medical and dental - X-rays, radioisotopes

* Occupational exposure

* Nuclear - radioactive fallout.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: The radiological imaging of choice for pheochromocytoma is ___
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. MRI

MRI is the investigation of choice for localizing the tumor in pheochromocytoma.

Pheochromocytoma is a catecholamine-secreting tumor derived from the chromaffin cells of the adrenal medulla.

Clinical features of pheochromocytoma are due to the autonomic effects of excess epinephrine and norepinephrine.

* Weight loss is due to the increase in catecholamines which increase basal metabolism.

* Pallor is due to alpha 1-mediated vasoconstriction.

* Abdominal pain with nausea and vomiting is commonly seen.

Diagnosis of pheochromocytoma requires biochemical testing followed by imaging.

* Urinary and plasma levels of catecholamines and metanephrines

* MRI is the investigation of choice for localizing the tumor

* MIBG Scintigraphy and PET Scans like Ga- DOTATE, DOPA- or FDG- PET can be used for extra-adrenal tumors and metastases

Treatment of pheochromocytoma:

Surgical resection of the tumor is the definitive treatment. Preoperatively, an alpha-receptor blocker (phenoxybenzamine) is given to control the effects produced by excess catecholamines. Beta-blockers are administered to manage tachycardia once sufficient alpha blockade has been established.This is to prevent unrestricted alpha-mediated vasoconstriction.

Following surgery, yearly follow-ups lifelong should be done.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: Which diagnostic technique is the best to assess renal perfusion?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. MAG-3 (Mercaptoacetyltriglycine)

The best diagnostic technique to assess renal perfusion is the MAG-3 (Mercaptoacetyltriglycine) or DTPA (Diethylenetriaminepentaacetic acid) scan.

These are nuclear medicine imaging tests that help evaluate the functional and perfusion aspects of the kidneys. These scans involve injecting a radiopharmaceutical into the bloodstream, which is then filtered by the kidneys. The scan tracks the movement of the radiopharmaceutical through the kidneys, allowing the medical professional to assess renal blood flow, perfusion, and overall kidney function.

Other Options:

Option B- DMSA (Dimercaptosuccinic acid) scan is used to assess renal cortical morphology and function. It is commonly used to evaluate scarring or infection in the kidneys.

Option C- RGU is a radiographic technique used to visualize the urethra and bladder. It is primarily used to diagnose urethral obstructions and other structural abnormalities of the urinary tract.

Option D- CT urography is used to visualize the urinary tract, including the kidneys, ureters, and bladder. It provides detailed anatomical information but does not focus specifically on assessing renal perfusion.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: Which of the following is true about radiotherapy?
options: Intensity is inversely proportional to squared distance
Vomiting is a late adverse reaction
Rapidly proliferating cells are most radioresistant
Radiation-induced skin changes is a reversible adverse effect
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Intensity is inversely proportional to squared distance

The intensity of radiation is inversely proportional to the squared distance from the source of radiation. This is known as the inverse square law in radiotherapy.

Inverse square law - the intensity of radiation is inversely proportional to the squared distance from the source of radiation. This principle is unsuitable for large tumors and has potential risks of radiation exposure to medical staff.

Other options:

Option B: Vomiting can be an acute (early) adverse reaction to radiation therapy, occurring shortly after treatment.

Option C: Permanent non-dividing cells are more radioresistant than rapidly proliferating cells.

Option D: Not all the adverse effects of radiation therapy are reversible. Some of the adverse effects of radiation therapy, such as fibrosis, radiation-induced skin changes, late radiation enteritis, etc are irreversible.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A 45-year-old man with a past history of tuberculosis presents to the OPD with complaints of chronic cough, occasional hemoptysis, and persistent chest pain. Chest X-ray shows the following lesion. It has been observed that when the patient's position changes, the air within the lesion changes as well. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Aspergilloma

The given clinical scenario of a patient with a past history of tuberculosis with an X-ray showing Monod's sign is suggestive of aspergilloma. The gas/air surrounding a mobile fungal ball or mycetoma (usually an aspergilloma) in an already-existing lung cavity is referred to as the Monod sign.

Aspergilloma or fungal ball is a late manifestation of chronic cavitary pulmonary aspergillosis (CPA) caused by Aspergillus species. A fungal ball is formed within the pulmonary cavity of CPA by the peeled-off inner layer of the cavity.

Patients present with chronic features of fatigue, weight loss, cough, hemoptysis, and wheezing. However, clinical features such as foul-smelling sputum and night sweats are more commonly observed in Tuberculosis which helps in differentiating the two conditions.

Chest X-ray shows a spherical or ovoid mass within a cavity. The mass is mobile. CT demonstrates a rounded mass within a cavity.

Images below show chest x-ray and CT findings in aspergilloma.

Other options:

Option A: Lung abscess typically shows a thick-walled cavity with air-fluid level as shown below.

Option B & D: Hydatid cyst and bronchogenic carcinoma can also show cavitatory lesions with air crescent but a preformed cavity from the past history of tuberculosis suggests the diagnosis of aspergilloma.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A patient underwent the following investigation for suspected malignancy. Which of the following compounds is used in this investigation?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Fluorodeoxyglucose

The image shows a positron-emission tomography (PET) scan. PET involves the use of a radiolabeled bio-compound such as 2-fluoro-2-deoxy-D-glucose (FDG), which is injected intravenously.

It is based on the principle that tumor cells have a high metabolic rate and can metabolize FDG. However, tumor cells can metabolize FDG only to FDG-6-phosphate, and no further. Hence, it accumulates in tumor cells and can be detected and quantified.

Applications of PET:

* Oncologic:

* Detection, staging, drug response

* Differentiation between radiation necrosis and recurrence

* Neurologic:

* Early diagnosis of Alzheimer's disease

* Localization of seizure focus in the interictal phase

* Localizing eloquent areas (e.g. speech, motor function)

* Cardiac:

* Identification of hibernating myocardium

The combination of PET imaging with CT (PET-CT) combines the metabolic information (PET) with the cross-sectional anatomic information (CT). PET-CT is used in oncology imaging to detect malignant cells as they demonstrate increased glucose metabolism relative to normal tissues.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: Ga-68PSMA is used to diagnose which of the following conditions?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Prostate cancer

Radio-labeled ligands- Gallium (Ga68) attached to the prostate-specific membrane antigen (PSMA)can be helpful in identifying prostatic cancer.

Prostate-specific membrane antigen (PSMA) is a specific prostate epithelial cell membrane antigen, showing increased expression in prostate cancers, which is also a potential target for monoclonal antibody therapy.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: Identify the condition shown in the given image below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Miliary tuberculosis

The above radiograph depicts the miliary pattern seen in tuberculosis.

Miliary tuberculosis is a form of disseminated pulmonary tuberculosis that occurs when organisms draining through the lymphatics enter the venous blood and circulate back to the lung. It can result from progressive primary disease, reactivation of latent foci, and iatrogenic exposure (lithotripsy, urethral catheterization, cardiac valve homograft placement, and solid organ transplantation).

The risk factors for the development of miliary TB include extremes of age, alcohol use, malignancy, HIV, corticosteroid use, connective tissue disease, renal failure, diabetes, and pregnancy.

The clinicopathological patterns of this condition include acute miliary TB (which may present as multi-organ dysfunction syndrome (MODS) and ARDS, as in this patient), late generalized TB, and anergic TB (defined histologically by the absence of granulomata). Individual lesions either microscopic or small <2 mm foci of yellow-white consolidation scattered throughout the lung parenchyma. The lesions may coalesce resulting in large areas of consolidation. Serous pleural effusions, tuberculous emyema or obliterative fibrous pleuritis may occur

Laboratory tests may show pancytopenia due to bone marrow infiltration. Other findings could include anemia, thrombocytopenia/cytosis, hyponatremia, and sterile pyuria.

Chest radiography shows a faint reticulonodular pattern distributed fairly uniformly throughout the lungs.

Histopathology shows granulomas of tuberculosis characteristically contain epithelioid macrophages, Langhans giant cells, and lymphocytes with central caseation necrosis.

Other options:

Option B: Chest x-ray appearance of acute respiratory distress syndrome varies depending on the severity and typically appears as bilateral diffuse alveolar opacities with dependent atelectasis in some cases. The opacities may have a patchy ground-glass appearance.

Option C: Allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis is a hypersensitivity reaction involving the major airways. Radiographic findings in ABPA include lobar collapse, non-segmental areas of opacities commonly involving the upper lobe, and branching thick tubular opacities due to distended bronchi filled with fungus and mucus - Finger-in-glove appearance

Option D: Pulmonary metastasis typically appears as peripheral, rounded nodules of variable size, scattered throughout both lungs (cannon-ball lesions).
The most common primaries to result in pulmonary metastases in adults include:

* Breast carcinoma

* Colorectal carcinoma

* Renal cell carcinoma

* Uterine leiomyosarcoma

* Head and neck squamous cell carcinoma

The chest radiograph given below shows cannon-ball lesions of metastatic lung cancer.

Pearl PF1056: Causes of miliary shadow in Chest X-ray

* Miliary tuberculosis

* Histoplasmosis

* Sarcoidosis

* Pneumoconiosis – coal workers pneumoconiosis and silicosis

* Healed varicella

* Long-standing MS – can lead to pulmonary hemosiderosis

* Alveolar microlithiasis

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: Identify the condition shown in the image below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Jejunal atresia

The given radiograph shows a triple bubble sign which is seen in jejunal atresia.

Jejunal atresia is a congenital anomaly which presents with bilious vomiting and abdominal distension soon after birth. A small amount of meconium may be passed despite the atresia. Plain X-ray abdomen shows multiple air-fluid levels, known as the triple bubble sign. Contrast study is the next best investigation to exclude other large bowel anomalies. In most cases, the distal end of the dilated proximal small bowel is resected and a primary end-to-end anastomosis is done. If the proximal bowel is extremely dilated, it may need to be tapered to the distal bowel before anastomosis

Other options:

Option A: Duodenal atresia occurs due to failure of vacuolization of the solid duodenum. Neonates with duodenal atresia usually present with bilious vomiting and abdominal distention. Plain X-ray shows two foci of gas, one in the stomach and the other in the duodenum, known as the double bubble sign.

Option C: Small bowel obstruction shows dilated bowel loops with multiple air fluid levels. Supine X-ray shows a row of gas bubbles trapped between the valvulae coniventes, within fluid-filled dilated small bowels, resembling a string of beads.

Option D: Congenital hypertrophic pyloric stenosis presents between 2 and 6 weeks of age with projectile, non-bilious vomiting, and abdominal distension. The hypertrophied pylorus may present as an olive-shaped mass. The diagnostic criteria for pyloric stenosis are a muscle thickness of ≥4 mm and a pyloric length of ≥16 mm in ultrasound.

Pearl PF1850: Radiological findings in various GI disorders

Duodenal atresia: Double bubble sign

Jejunal and ileal atresia: Multiple air-fluid levels (plain erect X-ray abdomen) presenting as triple bubble sign.

Congenital hypertrophic pyloric stenosis: Single enlarged gastric gas bubble - single bubble sign

Sigmoid volvulus: Coffee bean sign

Achalasia cardia: Bird-beak sign

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: Positron emission tomography is based on which of the following mechanisms?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Glucose metabolism

Positron emission tomography (PET) utilizes the mechanism of glucose metabolism.

PET imaging is based on the detection of an injected positron-emitting radioactive tracer. It relies on the coincidence detection of the annihilation photons (γ), which are released when a positron combines with an electron.

A glucose analog called fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG) is used. FDG is taken up by metabolically active cells, where it undergoes phosphorylation to form FDG-6-phosphate. Unlike glucose, FDG-6-phosphate cannot undergo further metabolism and thus accumulates within the cell. The trapped FDG-6-phosphate is detected by the PET scanner.

Before injecting FDG, the blood glucose level should be measured. It should be < 150 mg/dL. Good blood glucose control is essential as FDG uptake is competitively inhibited by glucose.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: Which of the following is the most radiosensitive organ?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Testes

Among the given options, testes is the most radiosensitive organ.

The radiosensitivity is higher in cases where the proliferation is high. In the case of the testes, it contains a high number of clonal cells since it is a reproductive organ. Thus, among the given options testes is the most radiosensitive organ.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: Which of the following statements is correct regarding the device shown below?
options: It is used to measure infrared rays emitted by red blood cells
It is used for the localisation of calcified plaque
It is used to measure systolic blood pressure
It is used to measure blood flow and detect blood flow abnormalities in the blood vessel
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. It is used to measure blood flow and detect blood flow abnormalities in the blood vessel

The given image is of a handheld doppler device. It is used to measure blood flow and detect blood flow abnormalities in the blood vessel.

The Doppler ultrasound device utilizes the doppler effect to assess the movement of red blood cells within blood vessels. The doppler effect is the change in frequency or wavelength of a wave in relation to an observer moving relative to the wave source. The device emits ultrasound waves that reflect off moving red blood cells. The frequency shift between the transmitted and received sound waves is used to calculate the velocity and direction of blood flow.

By analyzing these frequency shifts, the device can provide information about the speed and pattern of blood flow. This is particularly useful in detecting abnormalities such as blockages or stenosis.

Other options:

Option A: Doppler ultrasound does not measure infrared rays. Infrared measurements are typically related to thermal imaging or other specific applications unrelated to blood flow measurement.

Option B: Doppler ultrasound can help identify areas of reduced blood flow due to plaques, it is not specifically used for the localization of calcified plaque. Techniques like computed tomography (CT) or MRI are better suited for visualizing calcified plaques.

Option C: While Doppler can assist in certain vascular assessments, it is not a primary tool for measuring systolic or diastolic blood pressure.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A child presents with central cyanosis and a radiological image of a boot-shaped heart with oligemic lung fields. Which of the following conditions is most likely responsible for cyanosis in the child?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Tetralogy of Fallot

The image above shows a boot-shaped heart. Cyanosis, oligemic lung fields, and a boot-shaped heart (cœur en sabot in French) point towards tetralogy of Fallot (TOF)

Radiological features: "Coeur en sabot" is due to cardiac apex elevation as a result of right ventricular hypertrophy. The cardiac silhouette has been likened to that of a boot (“coeur-en sabot”). The hilar areas and lung fields are relatively clear because of diminished pulmonary blood flow or the small size of the pulmonary arteries. The aorta is usually large.

Clinical findings in TOF:

* Right ventricular hypertrophy, causing a left anterior hemithorax bulge.

* Single S2 or soft P2 because of the stenotic pulmonary valve

* Systolic thrill in the left sternal border in the 3rd and 4th parasternal spaces.

* The large 'a wave in the jugular pulse is a reflection of the forceful contraction of the right atrium at the end of diastole, as there is reduced distensibility of the hypertrophic right ventricle.

* There is a loud and harsh systolic murmur due to the right ventricular outflow tract(RVOT) obstruction. It becomes louder, longer, and harsher as obstruction increases in severity from mild to moderate.

However, in severe obstruction, especially during a tet spell, the murmur becomes less prominent as the blood is shunted towards the aortic valve and not through RVOT.

Other options:

Option B: ASD is characterised by an abnormal opening in the atrial septum, allowing communication between the right and left atria. Ostium secundum ASD is the most common type of ASD.

Option C: Ventricular Septal Defect (VSD) is the most common congenital heart defect. Commonly seen in maternal diabetes and fetal alcohol syndrome.

Option D: TGA on chest x-ray shows a classical egg on string appearance.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: An Intravenous Pyelogram (IVP) image of the child is provided. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Ureterocele

The image shown above depicts the "cobra head" sign on excretion urography in a patient with a bilateral ureterocele.

A ureterocele is the cystic enlargement of the intramural ureter. It is common in females. Clinical presentation: Children with a ureterocele usually present with infection. Adults present with renal stones.

Diagnosis: IVU shows a classical cobra head sign or ‘adder head’ sign or 'spring onion sign'. It refers to a dilated, contrast-filled distal ureter, surrounded by a thin rim of ureteric wall and bladder mucosa. On ultrasonography, it can be seen as a fluid-filled cystic mass in the bladder. Cystoscopy shows a bulging, translucent swelling involving the ureteric orifice where there is urinary stasis.

Treatment: Surgical excision with re-implantation of the ureter is the treatment of choice for a simple ureterocele.

Other Options:

Option B: Due abnormal ascent of the metanephros during embryological development leads to an ectopic kidney, increasing the risk of infection, hydronephrosis, etc.

Option C: Duplication of Ureter: Also known as Duplex Kidney, this is due to the incomplete fusion of the upper and lower poles of the kidney. The drooping lily sign is seen on Intravenous Pyelogram (IVP).

Option D: Posterior urethral valves are the most common cause of severe obstructive uropathy in children. Diagnosis is most commonly made antenatally with ultrasound (Keyhole sign is seen). Clinically, a poor urinary stream, dribbling, and palpable bladder (due to diverticula) can be present. The investigation of choice is micturating cystourethrography.

Pearl PF1667: IVU signs and associated conditions

Medullary sponge kidney

* Bouquet of flowers/ paintbrush appearance

* It refers to the cystic dilatation of the distal collecting tubules

Duplex kidney

* Drooping lily sign

* It refers to the inferolateral displacement of the lower pole due to an obstructed upper pole in a duplicated collecting system

Horseshoe kidney

* Handshake sign - due to the position of the lower poles closer to the spine, and the lower calyces closer to each other

* Flower vase sign - due to medially rotated calyces

Retroperitoneal fibrosis

* Maiden waist deformity

* It refers to the medially drawn ureters caused by fibrosis at the lumbosacral junction

Retrocaval ureter

* Fish hook / Reverse J deformity

* Right ureter hooks behind the IVC as it passes posterior to it

Ureterocele

* Cobra/ Adder head appearance

* It refers to the dilation of the distal ureter

Transitional cell carcinoma of the ureter

* Goblet sign

* It is due to the focal dilation of the ureter by an intraluminal mass

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: Identify the investigation shown in the image below?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Mammography

The image shown above is of mammography.

The mammogram is an X-ray picture of the breast. The anode in the X-ray tube is made up of molybdenum. The X-ray film used is a single-sided coated film.

The views used are two types: Craniocaudal and Mediolateral oblique

Uses of the mammogram:

* Routine screening for (ductal carcinoma in situ) DCIS.

* The most important sign of malignancy in a mammogram is clustered microcalcification (more than 5 particles in 1 cm², 3 particles of less than 0.5 mm size)

Radiological findings in other diseases of the breast:

* Popcorn calcification is seen in fibroadenoma.

* Broken-needle type of calcification is seen in duct ectasia.

* Tea-cup calcification is seen in fibrocystic disease.

Differences between mammography and conventional radiography:

* Mammography involves the use of low-energy and high-amperage waves.

* The target anode is made of a tungsten disc in conventional X-ray tubes and molybdenum in mammography X-ray tubes.

* Most mammography tubes use beryllium exit windows between the evacuated tube and the atmosphere.

* The conventional X-ray tube has an aluminum filter, but in mammography, a molybdenum filter is used.

Some indications for mammography:

* Evaluation of breast signs and symptoms like masses, skin changes, deformities, nipple retraction, discharge, and eczema

* Breast cancer screening

* Follow-up for patients treated for breast cancer

* Localization of lesions not visible on ultrasound

Pearl PF1991: Breast Cancer Screening

Breast Cancer Screening*

Individuals are encouraged to conduct a risk assessment by 25 years of age. This helps classify them into average risk or increased risk groups.

Recommendations:

* Average-risk (no known genetic or family history of breast cancer)

* 25-39 years of age: clinical breast examination every 1-3 years;

* ≥ 40 years of age: clinical breast examination and mammogram annually

* Increased risk (positive family or genetic history of breast cancer)

* Consult a healthcare professional every 6-12 months after 21 years of age

* Annual mammogram or MRI from 25 years of age or 10 years prior to the age at which the youngest family member was diagnosed with breast cancer (whichever is earliest)

* Asymptomatic women with previously treated breast cancer

* Consult a healthcare professional every 6-12 months

* Annual mammogram

* Annual MRI to be considered

* Mammogram and USG are not contraindicated in pregnant and breastfeeding women

High-risk patients for breast cancer:

* Women (or a first-degree relative) with a known BRCA1 or BRCA2 mutation or TP53 or PTEN genes

* Two first-degree relatives with breast cancers with or without gene mutations

* Women with a history of chest irradiation between the ages of 10 and 30

* Women with previously biopsy-proven breast cancer

* Women with ≥ 20% lifetime risk for breast cancer based on breast cancer risk models

*According to NCCN 2022 guidelines

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: Identify the tarsal bone marked by the arrow in the given X-ray of the right foot.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Navicular

The image above depicts the navicular bone, which is interposed between the head of the talus and the cuneiforms.

There are 7 tarsal bones, and they occupy the proximal half of the foot. The proximal row is made up of the talus and calcaneum. The distal row from medial to lateral contains the medial, intermediate, and lateral cuneiforms and the cuboid. Medially, the navicular bone is interposed between the head of the talus and the cuneiforms.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: The following radiological image was taken to access the urinary tract, identify the investigation shown below?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Intravenous Pyelogram (IVP)

The radiological image shown above is that of an Intravenous Pyelogram (IVP), also known as Intravenous Urography (IVU).

IVP is an X-ray with special contrast injected into the veins to visualize the kidneys, ureter, and bladder.

Normal Structure seen in IVP:

Renal arteries → Nephrogram (cortex > medulla) → Calyces (~1 min) → Pelvicalyceal system (~15 min with compression) → Ureters → Postmicturition KUB shows normal drainage.

Indications of IVP:

* Calculi: size, location

* Obstruction: level, effects on renal excretion

* Functional versus mechanical obstruction (post-diuretic IVU)

* Ureteric fistula or Ureteric stricture

* GU Tuberculosis

* Collecting system integrity: trauma/intervention

* Congenital anomalies

* Upper tract urothelial lesion

It is a cheaper, readily available alternative to CT in resource-limited settings

Other options:

Option A: X-ray KUB: It is used to specifically visualize KUB (kidney, Ureter, Bladder). The X-ray KUB image below shows a thimble bladder caused due to TB of the bladder.

Option C: Retrograde Pyelogram is an X-ray test in which a special contrast is inserted into the urethral orifice of the penis via a catheter to visualize more distal urinary tract abnormalities. It is used to diagnose urethral strictures, injuries, blockage, and diverticula ( it is for the urethra, not the ureter). RGP Image below shows a bulbar urethral stricture.

Option D: Micturating CystoUrethrogram, also known as a voiding cystourethrogram (VCU). In VCU, after injecting contrast into the bladder using a Foley's catheter, the posterior urethra (membranous urethra and prostatic urethra) is visualized during micturition. It helps diagnose posterior urethral abnormalities and bladder abnormalities. It is the investigation of choice for vesicoureteric reflux (VUR) and posterior urethral valve. The following image shows a voiding cystourethrogram in a patient with grade V VUR.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: What are the rays used in linear accelerator (LINAC) therapy for curing cancer?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. X-ray

X-rays are the most common form of radiation used in radiotherapy. They are produced from a LINAC (linear accelerator).

It is used in radiation therapy to deliver high-energy X-rays or electrons to target specific areas of the body, typically to treat cancerous tissues. It uses microwave technology to accelerate charged particles (such as electrons) at a high speed and then directs them into a target (usually a heavy metal) to produce X-rays. These X-rays are then carefully directed at the patient's body to deliver therapeutic radiation doses to the tumor while minimising damage to surrounding healthy tissues. For precise therapy, this LINAC is referred to as a CyberKnife when it is mounted on an electronic robotic arm. It is used in inoperable cranial lesions as stereotactic radiotherapy.

Other options:

Option A: Proton beams offer a therapeutic advantage of having a steep dose falloff at the end of their path. Advantages are mostly physical, not biological; however, new data suggest different genes may be induced after proton versus X-ray treatment

Option B: Neutron beams are used in visualizing soft tissue and can even provide better contrast than X-rays in some cases, but are rarely used clinically due to complex setup and limited availability.

Option D: Cobalt 60 undergoes beta-decay and emits 1.25 MeV (average) gamma rays, which penetrate deeper tissues while sparing skin, used in the Gamma Knife. The gamma knife is mainly used to treat inoperable intracranial lesions.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: What is the definition of Electron Volt (EV)?
options: The speed of an electron in a magnetic field
The force acting on an electron in an electric field
The energy gained by an electron when accelerated through a potential difference of one volt.
The kinetic energy of an electron at rest in a vacuum
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. The energy gained by an electron when accelerated through a potential difference of one volt.

An electronvolt (eV) is defined as the energy required to accelerate a single electron at rest through an electron potential difference of one volt in a vacuum. This is different from the electrical potential difference applied to the X-ray tube in terms of kilovolts (kV). However, the kV applied to an X-ray tube is approximately equal to the maximum photon energy achievable by a photon (keVmax).

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: New A patient presents with abdominal pain and distension. An X ray was taken which showed dilated bowel loops as given in the image below. Identify the segment involved.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Jejenum

The given clinical scenario and X-ray suggest intestinal obstruction with involvement of the jejunum. The obstructed bowel loops are central in location and show valvulae connivente (mucosal folds that cross the entire diameter of the bowel). The presence of valvulae connivente with gas bubbles trapped between them gives a string of beads/ ladder effect. Radiological features of bowel obstruction

* Small bowel - The involved dilated segments are straight and mostly centrally located.

* Jejunum - It is characterized by the presence of valvulae conniventes with gas bubbles trapped between them. This gives a string of beads/ ladder effect.

* Ileum - The distal ileal obstruction is usually featureless.

* Caecum - A rounded gas shadow in the right iliac fossa is suggestive of caecal obstruction.

* Large bowel - The presence of haustrations is a feature of large bowel obstruction. Haustral folds are not regular. They are not present in the caecum and do not traverse the whole diameter of the bowel.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: Obliteration of right cardiac border on chest X-Ray indicates pathology involving which of the following structures?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Right middle lobe

Right middle lobe pathology causes obliteration of right cardiac border.

The silhouette sign is the loss of clear demarcation between normal lung and soft tissue (e.g., heart, diaphragm). This occurs when the lung parenchyma is no longer filled with air and the contrast between air and soft tissue is lost.

A silhouette in a chest radiograph is the outline of a particular structure that is formed at the interface of two tissues with different tissue densities eg. cardiac silhouette between the heart and the lung. Blurring/obliteration of these normal silhouettes due to disease pathologies is known as the silhouette sign.

The silhouette can be obscured only by a pathology that is in direct anatomical contact, eg. right cardiac border will be obscured when there is right middle lobe pneumonia. Hence, the silhouette sign helps us in localizing the site of pathology.

Given below is a list of normal silhouettes on chest radiographs as seen on the PA view. Loss of these silhouettes are indicative of the site of pathology:

Obliterated silhouette
Site of pathology

Right para-tracheal stripe
Right upper lobe

Right heart border
Right middle lobe or
medial right lower lobe

Right hemidiaphragm
Right lower lobe

Aortic knuckle
Left upper lobe
(posterior segment)

Left heart border
Lingula segments of
left upper lobe

Left hemidiaphragm
or descending aorta
Left lower lobe

The left image is a normal chest radiograph with the red line indicating the silhouette of the right heart border and right middle lobe.

The right image shows the same red line delineating where the silhouette should be, but is lost due to consolidation in the right middle lobe.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: What is the most radiosensitive tissue in our body?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Bone marrow

The most radiosensitive tissue in our body is bone marrow.

The most radiosensitive:

* Tissue - bone marrow

* Blood Cell - Lymphocyte

* Stage of cell - G2-M interphase

* Cell type - Rapidly dividing cells

* Ocular structure - Lens

* Retinal structure - Rods>Cones

Least Radiosensitive:

* Tissue - nervous tissue

* Blood Cell - platelet

* Stage of cell -  S phase

* Cell type - Quiescent cells

* Ocular structure - Sclera

* Retinal Layer - Ganglion cell layer

Pearl PF1484: Radiosensitive and Radioresistant Tumors

Highly radiosensitive tumors are

* Lymphoma

* Seminoma

* Myeloma

* Ewing’s sarcoma

* Wilm’s tumour

Highly radioresistant tumors are

* Melanoma

* Osteosarcoma

* Pancreatic carcinoma

* Hepatic carcinoma

* Renal cell carcinoma

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: Which of the following MRI imaging techniques is shown in the image below?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. T2 MRI

The MRI shows CSF as bright/hyperintense while white matter is dark and grey matter is white, hence this is a T2 weighted MRI image.

T1 weighted image

* It is one of the basic MRI pulse sequences.

* The difference in the appearance of various tissues is due to their different T1 relaxation times.

* CSF has a long T1 time and appears dark.

T2 weighted images:

* It is also a basic MRI pulse sequence.

* It is based on the T2 relaxation time of the tissues.

* CSF appears bright in these images.

Short tau inversion recovery(STIR):

* It is a form of inversion recovery sequence.

* It is used to selectively null signals from fat.

* The imaging sequence is identified by observing the fat tissues and fluid-filled spaces.

* Fluids like CSF appear bright and fat appears dark.

Fluid attenuated inversion recovery(FLAIR):

* It is also a form of inversion recovery sequence.

* It is used to selectively null signals from fluids.

* Fluids like CSF appear dark and pathological processes appear bright.

* It would appear as a fluid suppressed T2 image.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: 74 year old gentleman presents to the OPD with history of significant unintentional weight loss, loss of appetite and iron deficiency anemia. A chest x-ray was done and is given below. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Metastasis

The above scenario indicates the patient may be suffering from colon carcinoma. The X-ray depicts cannon ball appearance classical of lung metastasis.
Pulmonary metastasis typically appears as peripheral, rounded nodules of variable size, scattered throughout both lungs. The most common primaries to result in pulmonary metastases in adults include:

* Breast carcinoma

* Colorectal carcinoma

* Renal cell carcinoma

* Uterine leiomyosarcoma

* Head and neck squamous cell carcinoma

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A newborn is seen to have an abnormal lump in the lower back. Identify the condition from the MRI given below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Meningocele

The MRI given represents meningocele.

Meningocele involves the midline protrusion of the meninges. A fluctuant midline mass, that may transilluminate is present in the lower back along the vertebral column. Meningomyelocele involves the protrusion of the spinal cord with the meningeal covering. Neurological dysfunction is more common in these open defects.

Spina bifida occulta refers to fusion defects of the posterior part of the vertebral body. There is no associated protrusion of the spinal cord or meninges. These neonates are usually asymptomatic, without any neurological signs. They present only with a tuft of hair over the lower back.

The image below shows (from left to right) spina bifida occulta, meningocele, and meningomyelocele-

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: What does the following X-ray depict?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Pleural effusion

The given X-ray depicts left-sided pleural effusion.

The CXR shows:

* Obliteration of costophrenic angle: due to accumulation of fluid on the affected side

* Air-fluid interface

Features of chest radiograph in pleural effusion:

* Presence of free pleural fluid

* Blunting of costophrenic angle

* Ellis-S curve – This is a radiological illusion and occurs as a medial radiological density due to the presence of partially aerated lung between the anterior and posterior fluid layers, whereas laterally the density is higher due to the presence of fluid only. The actual fluid level is horizontal.

The image below depicts pleural effusion in chest X-ray PA view.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: Which of the following radioactive isotopes is not used for brachytherapy?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Iodine-131

I-131 is a beta-emitter that is taken up by thyroid tissue as well as differentiated thyroid cancers and is used for systemic radiotherapy.

Brachytherapy is a form of radiation therapy in which a radioactive source is placed directly into or near the target tissue to deliver localized radiation treatment. It is commonly used for treating various types of cancer.

Other options:

A) Iodine-125: This radioactive isotope is commonly used in brachytherapy for treating prostate cancer. It emits low-energy gamma rays that can effectively target and treat the cancerous tissue.

C) Cobalt-60: This isotope is not typically used in brachytherapy but rather in external beam radiation therapy. Cobalt-60 emits high-energy gamma rays and is commonly used in radiation therapy machines called cobalt units or teletherapy units. These units deliver radiation from outside the body, targeting the tumor.

D) Iridium-192: This is a commonly used radioactive isotope in brachytherapy. It emits high-energy gamma rays and is used for treating various types of cancer, such as cervical, prostate, and breast cancer. Iridium-192 is often used in temporary brachytherapy, where the radioactive source is temporarily placed in the body and then removed after a specific period of treatment.

In summary, while Iodine-125 and Iridium-192 are commonly used in brachytherapy, Cobalt-60 is primarily used in external beam radiation therapy. Iodine-131 is not typically used in brachytherapy but has other medical applications, such as thyroid cancer treatment and diagnostic imaging.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: 40-year-old female with acute flank pain, no fever, no flank tenderness. Most appropriate imaging approach:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. X-ray followed by NCCT

For suspected ureteric calculus: X-ray KUB is done followed by Non-contrast CT (NCCT), which is investigation of choice.

NCCT is the Best for:

• Detecting stones
• Stone size/location
• Hydronephrosis

*Slightly controversial since in practice, we do USG and X-ray KUB followed by NCCT if both the initial investigations are inconclusive. USG is better for detecting renal and proximal ureteric stones, rather than distal ureteric stones since ureter is located in the retroperitoneum. Hence we are choosing X-ray over USG in this case.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A 12-year-old boy is brought with respiratory symptoms. You suspect an upper respiratory tract infection. No other complication is present. Which radiological investigation is required?
options: CT scan of neck and chest
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. No radiological investigation required

Upper respiratory tract infections (URTIs) are primarily diagnosed clinically and do not require routine imaging in uncomplicated cases. Radiological investigations should be reserved for patients with suspected complications, severe disease, atypical presentations, or an alternative diagnosis.

• An otherwise healthy 12-year-old with uncomplicated URTI does not require any radiological investigation.
• Management is based on clinical assessment and supportive care.

Why not the other options?

• A. Plain chest radiograph: Indicated only if lower respiratory tract involvement (e.g., pneumonia) or complications are suspected.
• B. CT scan of neck and chest: Reserved for suspected deep neck space infections, abscesses, or airway compromise.
• C. HRCT: Used for chronic or diffuse parenchymal lung diseases, not routine URTI evaluation.

questions.subject: Radiology
