questions.text: A child presents to the emergency following ingestion of around 20 mL of kerosene oil about 40 minutes back. The child appears stable. Which one of the following measures should be done for the management of the child?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Radiography

Kerosene poisoning is a hydrocarbon aspiration hazard. In a stable child, gastric lavage and induced vomiting are contraindicated because they increase the risk of aspiration pneumonitis. The child should be observed, and a chest radiograph (usually after 4–6 hours or earlier if respiratory symptoms develop) is performed to detect aspiration.

Why not the other options?

• A. Gastric lavage: Contraindicated due to the high risk of aspiration.
• B. Oxygen therapy: Given only if hypoxia or respiratory distress is present; not routinely in an asymptomatic child.
• C. Intravenous steroids: No proven benefit; not routinely recommended.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A patient with chronic diarrhea shows the following CT appearance. Diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Ulcerative colitis

Why is this CT suggestive of Ulcerative Colitis?

The key imaging feature is a featureless, shortened colon with loss of haustrations, producing the classic:

"Lead-pipe colon" appearance

• Normal colon has sacculations called haustra.
• Chronic inflammation in UC causes:

• Mucosal ulceration
• Muscular hypertrophy
• Fibrosis
• Loss of haustra

• The colon becomes smooth, rigid, and tubular → Lead-pipe appearance.

This is a classic radiological sign of chronic ulcerative colitis.

Why not the other options?

B. Tubercular Colitis

CT usually shows:

• Ileocecal involvement (most common)
• Asymmetric wall thickening
• Necrotic mesenteric lymph nodes
• Pulled-up contracted cecum

Loss of haustra involving long segments of colon is not typical.

C. Crohn's Disease

CT findings:

• Skip lesions
• Terminal ileal involvement
• Cobblestone appearance
• Fistulas and sinus tracts
• Creeping fat
• String sign

Crohn's causes segmental disease, whereas UC causes continuous colonic involvement.

D. Pseudomembranous Colitis

CT shows:

• Marked colonic wall thickening
• Accordion sign
• Thumbprinting
• Toxic megacolon in severe cases
•

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A radiologist notices significant artefacts on MRI brain images obtained in a newly constructed imaging suite. The biomedical engineer reports that external radiofrequency signals from nearby equipment are interfering with the scanner. To prevent both ingress of external RF signals and containment of RF signals generated by the scanner itself, which shielding system must be installed around the MRI room?
options: Maxwell cage — uses magnetic field cancellation coils arranged around the room
Faraday cage — a conductive enclosure that blocks external electromagnetic fields and contains internal RF emissions
Edison cage — an insulated enclosure that dissipates static electrical charge buildup
Ohm cage — a resistive barrier that attenuates high-frequency electrical noise through impedance matching
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Faraday cage — a conductive enclosure that blocks external electromagnetic fields and contains internal RF emissions

A Faraday cage is a conductive enclosure (typically copper or aluminium lining) that redistributes electromagnetic charges on its surface, effectively cancelling external RF fields inside and preventing internal RF from escaping. MRI rooms require this because the scanner operates at specific radiofrequency ranges (Larmor frequency) and any external EM interference degrades the signal-to-noise ratio of images. The other options are distractors — Maxwell, Edison, and Ohm cages are not real shielding systems used in radiology.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A radiopaque density may be noticed in poisoning by which of the following agents?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Chloral hydrate

Certain drugs and toxins are radiopaque and can be visualized on a plain abdominal X-ray after ingestion. Chloral hydrate is one of these radiopaque substances and may appear as a radiopaque density in the gastrointestinal tract following overdose or poisoning.

Why not the other options?

• A. Phenazopyridine: Not reliably radiopaque.
• B. Ethylene glycol: A colorless liquid; not radiopaque on X-ray.
• C. Chloroquine: Not consistently radiopaque and cannot be relied upon for radiographic detection.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: ACR class 2 MRI contrast agents can be safely given in which conditions? 1. 30-year-old without renal function tests 2. 12-year-old child with normal renal tests 3. 60-year-old without renal function tests 4. 50-year-old with eGFR <50
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 1, 2, 3, 4

ACR Group/Class II gadolinium agents:

• Macrocyclic gadolinium compounds
• Very low risk of NSF

Examples:

• Gadobutrol
• Gadoterate
• Gadoteridol

They are considered relatively safe even in reduced renal function. They are relatively contraindicated in patients where eGFR <30mL/min per 1.73 m2.

| ACR Classification of Gadolinium-Based Contrast Agents According to Risk of NSF

| -------------------------------------------------------------------------------

| Group I: Associated with greatest number of NSF cases

• Gadodiamide (Omniscan®)
• Gadopentetate (Magnevist®)
• Gadoversetamide (OptiMark®)

| Group II: Associated with few, if any, unconfounded cases

• Gadobenate (MultiHance®)
• Gadobutrol (Gadovist®)
• Gadoterate (Dotarem®/Clariscan®)
• Gadoteridol (ProHance®)

| Group III: Limited data, but no reported cases of NSF

• Gadoxetate (Eovist®)
• Gadopiclenol (Vueway®)

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: All of the following are true about X-Ray Film, Except: (NEET PG 2017)
options: Most common photosensitive material is Silver Bromide
Photosensitive material lies in the base
Total thickness of the film is about 0.25 mm
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Photosensitive material lies in the base

X-ray film is made of silver halide (AgBr), which is the photosensitive material. This material is contained in the emulsion layer, not in the base of the film. The base serves as a support structure for the emulsion layer containing the photosensitive silver bromide.

Other Option:

Option A. Typically made of 4 layers - This option is true. While the exact number of layers isn't explicitly stated\, this would be consistent with standard X-ray film construction which typically includes a base\, adhesive layer\, emulsion layer(s)\, and protective coating.

Option B. Most common photosensitive material is Silver Bromide - This option is true. Silver bromide (AgBr) is the photosensitive material used in X-ray films as mentioned in the description of film composition.

Option C. Photosensitive material lies in the base - This option is false. The photosensitive material (silver bromide) is contained in the emulsion layer of the film\, not in the base layer. The base serves as the supporting structure for the film.

Option D. Total thickness of the film is about 0.25 mm - This option is likely true based on standard X-ray film properties\, though the exact measurement isn't explicitly provided.

Educational Objective:

X-ray film construction consists of multiple layers with the photosensitive silver halide (AgBr) contained in the emulsion layer, not in the base layer which primarily provides structural support for the film.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: All of the following statements about the Piezoelectric Effect are true, except:
options: Transducers produce waves by piezoelectric effect
Transducers receive waves by reverse piezoelectric effect
Lead Zirconate Titanate (PZT) has marked piezoelectric effect
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Used in USG and MRI

• Piezoelectric effect is the ability of certain crystals to generate an electric charge when mechanically stressed.
• In ultrasonography (USG), piezoelectric crystals are used in the transducer:

• Direct piezoelectric effect: returning echoes deform the crystal and generate electrical signals.
• Reverse piezoelectric effect: applied electrical energy causes the crystal to vibrate and produce ultrasound waves.

• Lead Zirconate Titanate (PZT) is the most commonly used piezoelectric material in ultrasound transducers.
• MRI does not use the piezoelectric effect for image generation; it is based on magnetic fields and radiofrequency pulses.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: Identify the image.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Fluoroscopy

Fluoroscopy is a dynamic X-ray imaging technique used to visualize the motion of the pharynx and esophagus during swallowing. It provides real-time assessment, unlike a static barium swallow.

Fluoroscopy

• Dynamic imaging (real-time)
• Used with contrast (e.g., barium)
• Shows:

• Swallowing
• Peristalsis
• Reflux

• Appears like a continuous sequence rather than a single image

| Application | Example

| ----------- | -------

| GI studies | Barium swallow, meal, enema

| Interventions | Angiography, catheter placement

| Orthopedics | C-arm guidance

| Urology | MCU (micturating cystourethrogram)

| Option | Type | Key Feature

| ------ | ---- | -----------

| Fluoroscopy | Modality | Real-time imaging

| Barium swallow | Procedure | Uses fluoroscopy

| Acid ingestion | Disease | Coagulative necrosis

| Alkali ingestion | Disease | Liquefactive necrosis

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: Identify the marked ligament on knee MRI.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. PCL

The arrow points to the posterior cruciate ligament attaching to posterior tibial condyle. ACL lies anteriorly, menisci are cartilaginous pads, and MCL is medial extracapsular.

Signature Clues:

• Location: Posterior to ACL
• Shape: Thick, C-shaped / curved band
• Signal: Uniformly low signal (dark)
• Attachment: From tibia → medial femoral condyle

| Ligament | Function

| -------- | --------

| PCL | Prevents posterior displacement of tibia

| ACL | Prevents anterior displacement

| Structure | Appearance

| --------- | ----------

| PCL | Thick, dark, curved

| ACL | Thin, oblique

| Meniscus | Triangular

| MCL | Linear (medial side)

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: Identify the radiological investigation shown in the image below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Mammography

Mammography is identified by standard CC and MLO projection views showing compressed breast tissue with characteristic fibroglandular (white) and fatty (dark) tissue patterns using specialized low-energy X-rays.

Key Visual Clues:

• Compressed breast between plates
• Fibroglandular densities (white)
• Fat appears dark
• Views:

• CC (Craniocaudal)
• MLO (Mediolateral oblique)

| Modality | Radiation | Use | Key Feature

| -------- | --------- | --- | -----------

| Mammography | Low-dose X-ray | Screening breast cancer | Microcalcifications

| Ultrasound | No radiation | Cyst vs solid | Real-time

| MRI | No radiation | High-risk screening | Contrast enhancement

| CT | High radiation | Not routine for breast | Cross-sectional

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: Match the following. Choose the correct option:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. A–1, B–2, C–4, D–3

• A. CT → Pancreatic pseudocyst

• Best initial cross-sectional imaging.

• B. PSMA PET → Prostate carcinoma

• Used for:

• Staging
• Recurrence detection

• C. MRCP → Obstructive jaundice

• Excellent for biliary tree evaluation.

• D. FNAC → Thyroid nodule

• Standard diagnostic investigation.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: On a color Doppler, the blue color typically represents: (NEET Pg 2016)
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Flow away from the transducer

On color Doppler ultrasound, the color assignment follows a standardized convention where blue color represents blood flow moving away from the transducer. This color coding is based on the Doppler effect principles and not on the oxygenation status of blood or vessel type.

Other Options:

Option A. Deoxygenated blood flow - INCORRECT. Color Doppler doesn't distinguish between oxygenated and deoxygenated blood. The colors represent direction of flow relative to the transducer position\, not blood oxygenation.

Option C. Flow towards the transducer - INCORRECT. Flow toward the transducer is conventionally displayed as red on color Doppler\, not blue. This is a fundamental convention in vascular ultrasound.

Option D. Venous flow pattern - INCORRECT. While venous flow often appears blue (because veins typically carry blood away from superficial transducer positions)\, the color assignment is based on direction of flow relative to the transducer\, not vessel type. Arteries can also appear blue if blood is flowing away from the transducer.

Educational Objective:

In color Doppler ultrasound, blue color specifically indicates flow moving away from the transducer, while red indicates flow moving toward the transducer - this convention is standardized across ultrasound systems regardless of vessel type or blood oxygenation.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: On the provided X-ray of the foot, identify the bone marked with red arrow.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Navicular

The navicular bone is a boat-shaped tarsal bone located medially in the midfoot between the talus proximally and three cuneiforms distally, serving as the keystone of the medial longitudinal arch.

| Option | Verdict | Why

| ------ | ------- | ---

| A. Talus | ❌ | Superior bone, forms ankle joint

| B. Navicular | ✅ | Medial midfoot, anterior to talus

| C. Lateral calcaneus | ❌ | Calcaneus is posterior (heel), not midfoot

| D. Medial calcaneus | ❌ | Calcaneus doesn’t have medial/lateral distinction

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: What is the full form of the radiation safety principle “ALARA”?
options: As Low As Required for Assessment
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. As Low As Reasonably Achievable

ALARA (As Low As Reasonably Achievable) is the fundamental principle of radiation protection, which states that radiation exposure should be kept as low as reasonably achievable while obtaining the necessary diagnostic or therapeutic benefit. It is based on the assumption that there is no completely safe dose of ionizing radiation, and therefore unnecessary exposure should always be minimized.

The ALARA principle emphasizes:

• Minimizing radiation exposure to patients, healthcare workers, and the public
• Achieving this by balancing clinical benefit against radiation risk
• Applying practical measures without compromising diagnostic quality or treatment efficacy

Why not the other options?

• A. As Long As Radiation Allows – Incorrect expansion.
• C. As Little As Radiation Accepted – Not the accepted terminology.
• D. As Low As Required for Assessment – Incorrect expansion; the standard term is Reasonably Achievable.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: Which contrast agent is safe in a patient with renal failure?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. USG contrast agents

USG contrast agents, such as SONOVUE (sulfur hexafluoride microbubbles), are the only contrast agents safe for use in patients with renal failure, as they are excreted via the lungs and do not rely on renal clearance.

Composition: Microbubbles (gas-filled)

Excretion:

• Eliminated via lungs (exhaled air)
• NOT dependent on kidneys

So: No renal burden → safe in renal failure

| Contrast Type | Modality | Risk in Renal Failure

| ------------- | -------- | ---------------------

| USG contrast | Ultrasound | ✅ SAFE

| MRI contrast (Gadolinium) | MRI | NSF risk

| Iodinated contrast | CT | ❌ Contrast nephropathy

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: Which imaging modality is contraindicated in pregnancy?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. CT

CT uses ionizing radiation, harmful to fetus, hence contraindicated. CT is contraindicated because-

Risks to fetus:

• DNA damage
• Congenital malformations
• Growth retardation
• Increased cancer risk later in life

Especially dangerous in: First trimester

USG, MRI, and Doppler are safe as they do not involve radiation.

| Modality | Radiation | Safe in Pregnancy

| -------- | --------- | -----------------

| USG | No | Safe

| MRI | No | Safe (avoid contrast)

| CT | Yes | Avoid

| Doppler | No | Safe

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: Which of the following is an example of non-ionizing radiation? (NEET PG 2015)
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Infrared Rays

Infrared rays are classified as non-ionizing radiation. Non-ionizing radiation has lower energy levels that are insufficient to remove electrons from atoms or molecules, thus not creating ions. Ultrasonography is another example of non-ionizing radiation, which is why it's often preferred for certain applications like pregnancy imaging where radiation safety is paramount.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: Which of the following mechanism is involved in X-ray production?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Bremsstrahlung radiation

Bremsstrahlung (“braking”) radiation is the principal mechanism of X-ray production. It occurs when high-speed electrons from the cathode are decelerated or deflected by the electric field of the tungsten target nucleus (anode), causing loss of kinetic energy that is emitted as X-ray photons. It accounts for approximately 85–90% of diagnostic X-rays.

The remaining 10–15% of X-rays are produced by characteristic radiation, which results from electron transitions between atomic shells after inner-shell ionization.

Why not the other options?

• A. Photoelectric effect: Interaction of X-rays with matter causing complete absorption of the photon; responsible for image contrast, not X-ray production.
• B. Compton effect: Scattering of X-rays by outer-shell electrons; a major source of image degradation and radiation exposure, not production.
• C. Pair production: Occurs only with high-energy photons (>1.02 MeV) and is not involved in diagnostic X-ray generation.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: Which of the following statements is not true about T1-weighted MRI images? (NEET Pg 2016)
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Fluid appears bright

On T1-weighted MRI sequences, fluid appears dark (hypointense), not bright. This fundamental principle of MRI physics is demonstrated throughout clinical imaging, where cerebrospinal fluid in the ventricles and spinal canal appears dark on T1-weighted images, providing natural contrast against the brighter surrounding tissues.

Other Options:

Option A. Short TR - T1-weighted sequences utilize a short TR (repetition time). The repetition time between radiofrequency pulses is deliberately kept short to emphasize T1 relaxation properties of tissues.

Option B. Short TE - T1-weighted sequences utilize a short TE (echo time). The brief interval between the pulse and the resultant echo minimizes T2 effects and maximizes T1 contrast.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: Which one of the following imaging modalities imparts the highest dose of ionizing radiation to the patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. CT head and neck

The amount of ionizing radiation varies considerably among imaging modalities:

• (a) Ultrasound — Incorrect: Uses sound waves and therefore involves no ionizing radiation.
• (b) Chest X-ray — Incorrect: Uses ionizing radiation, but the dose is relatively low.
• (c) Screening mammography — Incorrect: Uses X-rays, but the radiation dose is generally lower than that of CT.
• (d) CT head and neck — Correct: CT uses multiple X-ray exposures and therefore delivers a substantially higher radiation dose than conventional X-rays or mammography.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: Which type of X-ray film is most commonly used for high-detail imaging in Mammography? (NEET PG 2016)
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Single Screen-Single Emulsion

Mammographic X-ray tubes have specific characteristics that differentiate them from normal X-ray tubes. The entire mammography system is designed for high-detail imaging of breast tissue. Single Screen-Single Emulsion films are used in mammography because they provide the highest spatial resolution required for detecting small microcalcifications and subtle tissue changes.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A 22-year-old male presents with left-sided chest pain and breathlessness after a road traffic accident. Examination reveals absent left-sided breath sounds. CT Chest image is shown below. What is the diagnosis of this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Bowel loops herniation

The patient has blunt thoracic trauma followed by left-sided breathlessness and absent breath sounds. The CT shows bowel loops occupying the left hemithorax, consistent with traumatic diaphragmatic rupture with herniation of abdominal viscera into the thorax.

Why not the other options?

• A. Pneumothorax: CT would show air in the pleural space with collapse of the lung, not bowel loops within the thorax.
• B. Pleural effusion: Would appear as fluid density in the pleural cavity.
• C. Lung cavity: Would be an air-filled lesion within the lung itself, not bowel loops with characteristic bowel-wall appearances.
• D. Bowel loops herniation: Correct — traumatic diaphragmatic rupture allows abdominal bowel to enter the thoracic cavity.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A 26-year-old male presents with chronic abdominal pain, recurrent episodes of non-bloody diarrhea, significant weight loss, low-grade fever for 8 months, occasional perianal discomfort. On examination, mild pallor and tenderness in the right lower quadrant are noted. Laboratory investigations reveal anemia, raised ESR, and hypoalbuminemia. CECT abdomen shows segmental bowel wall thickening of the terminal ileum with engorged mesenteric vessels. Biopsy reveals non-caseating granulomas. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Crohn's disease

Crohn’s disease is a chronic, relapsing inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) characterized by transmural granulomatous inflammation that can affect any part of the gastrointestinal tract, with a predilection for the terminal ileum.

The diagnosis is suggested by:

• Chronic abdominal pain
• Chronic non-bloody diarrhea
• Weight loss
• Low-grade fever
• Perianal disease
• Terminal ileal involvement
• Non-caseating granulomas on biopsy

Key differentiating features:

• Intestinal tuberculosis:

• Usually ileocecal region
• Caseating granulomas
• Confluent granulomas with acid-fast bacilli may be seen
• Necrotic lymph nodes and ascites are common

• Ulcerative colitis:

• Begins in the rectum with continuous proximal spread
• Inflammation limited to mucosa and submucosa
• No skip lesions or transmural involvement

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A 38-year-old HIV-positive male presents with fever, right upper abdominal pain, and a sense of fullness in the abdomen for the past 2 weeks. On examination, there is tender hepatomegaly. Contrast-enhanced CT abdomen shows a well-defined hypodense lesion in the liver with peripheral rim enhancement. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Liver abscess

A liver abscess should be suspected in a patient presenting with fever, right upper quadrant pain, tender hepatomegaly, and a hypodense lesion with peripheral rim enhancement (“ring-enhancing lesion”) on contrast-enhanced CT. Immunocompromised patients, including those with HIV, are at increased risk of pyogenic liver abscesses.

The diagnosis is suggested by:

• Fever and RUQ pain
• Tender hepatomegaly
• CT showing a hypodense lesion with peripheral rim enhancement
• Possible presence of air within the abscess cavity (gas-forming organisms), if seen#

Why not the other options?

• B. Hepatocellular carcinoma: Usually shows arterial phase hyperenhancement with portal venous washout, often in cirrhotic patients.
• C. Hydatid cyst: Characteristic daughter cysts, calcified wall, or water-lily sign rather than rim enhancement.
• D. Cirrhosis: Causes diffuse liver architectural changes, not a focal ring-enhancing lesion.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A 38-year-old woman presents with vague right-sided chest discomfort and intermittent postprandial fullness for the past few months. She has no significant respiratory symptoms and denies any prior trauma. On examination, bowel sounds are faintly audible over the right lower chest. A chest X-ray, done as part of a routine pre-operative workup, incidentally reveals an air-fluid level within a well-defined anterior mediastinal opacity, with no obvious bowel loops seen above the diaphragmatic contour. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Morgagni hernia

• Morgagni hernia is often congenital in origin but tends to remain clinically silent for decades because the defect is small and the herniated contents (usually omentum, sometimes transverse colon) are limited in volume.
• It's classically discovered incidentally in adulthood — frequently in obese patients, where raised intra-abdominal pressure over time is thought to promote herniation through the pre-existing defect.
• Presentation, when symptomatic, tends to be nonspecific: mild chest discomfort, postprandial fullness, or vague GI complaints, rather than the dramatic respiratory distress seen in Bochdalek hernia, which is essentially always seen in neonates.

Why not the others?

• A. Bochdalek hernia — Almost always presents in the neonatal period with severe respiratory distress; an adult presentation would be exceptionally rare and would show obvious bowel loops in the thorax.
• C. Eventration of the diaphragm — No true defect or herniation; bowel sounds wouldn't be heard in the chest.
• D. Diaphragmatic paralysis — Due to phrenic nerve dysfunction; causes elevated hemidiaphragm, not a mediastinal air-fluid opacity.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A 48-year-old male with a 15-year history of alcohol use disorder presents with abdominal distension and fatigue. On examination, he has a distended abdomen with a fluid thrill, mild jaundice, and dilated superficial veins radiating from the umbilicus (caput medusae). LFTs show elevated bilirubin, low albumin, and raised INR. An abdominal ultrasound with Doppler is performed. Which of the following ultrasound findings is the most specific for portal hypertension?
options: Portal vein diameter >13 mm on grey-scale ultrasound
Splenomegaly with splenic vein diameter >10 mm
Free fluid in the hepatorenal pouch and pelvis
A patent tubular structure in the falciform ligament with hepatofugal flow on Doppler
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. A patent tubular structure in the falciform ligament with hepatofugal flow on Doppler

This describes a recanalized paraumbilical vein (umbilical vein recanalisation) — the most specific sonographic sign of portal hypertension.

The umbilical vein normally closes at birth and becomes the ligamentum teres. When portal pressure rises significantly, this vessel reopens to shunt blood from the left portal vein → paraumbilical vein → umbilical region → systemic veins. On Doppler, flow is hepatofugal (away from the liver), confirming portosystemic shunting. This is a direct pathophysiological consequence of raised portal pressure and does not occur in any other condition — making it highly specific.

Why the other options lack specificity:

| Finding | Seen in Portal HTN? | Problem with Specificity

| ------- | ------------------- | ------------------------

| Portal vein >13 mm (A) | Yes | Varies with respiration, body habitus, meals; absent in \~30% of confirmed cases

| Splenomegaly (B) | Yes | Also seen in haematological malignancy, infections, infiltrative disorders

| Ascites (C) | Yes | Also seen in CCF, hypoalbuminaemia, nephrotic syndrome, peritoneal malignancy

| Recanalized umbilical vein (D) | Yes | Unique to portal hypertension — pathognomonic

Doppler findings in portal hypertension to know:

• Hepatofugal flow in the portal vein — reversal of normal direction; indicates severe portal hypertension
• Recanalized paraumbilical vein — most specific sign
• Reduced portal vein velocity (<16 cm/s) — sensitive but non-specific
• Spontaneous splenorenal or gastrorenal collaterals — seen in advanced disease

High-yield pearl: The clinical correlate of a recanalized umbilical vein on ultrasound is caput medusae on examination — both represent the same portosystemic collateral pathway made visible by different means. Caput medusae radiates from the umbilicus; a Cruveilhier–Baumgarten murmur (venous hum at the umbilicus) may also be audible.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A 48-year-old man presents with colicky abdominal pain, progressive abdominal distension, vomiting, and inability to pass flatus for the past 24 hours. An erect abdominal X-ray is shown. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Small bowel obstruction

The patient’s symptoms of colicky abdominal pain, progressive abdominal distension, vomiting, and absolute constipation (failure to pass flatus) are classic for acute intestinal obstruction. The erect abdominal X-ray shows multiple air bubbles called as string of pearls sign, which is characteristic of small bowel obstruction (SBO).

The clinical presentation and X-ray demonstrate:

• Multiple central dilated bowel loops
• Valvulae conniventes traversing the full width of the bowel
• Multiple air-fluid levels (“step-ladder” appearance)

These are classic radiographic findings of small bowel obstruction.

Why not the other options?

• A. Large bowel obstruction – Typically shows peripherally located, markedly dilated colon with haustra that do not extend across the entire lumen.
• C. Pancreatitis – May show a sentinel loop or colon cut-off sign, but not multiple step-ladder air-fluid levels.
• D. Volvulus – Usually demonstrates a coffee-bean sign (sigmoid volvulus) or massively dilated cecum (cecal volvulus), which is not seen here.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A 56-year-old female patient presented with progressive dysphagia. A barium swallow done is given below. What is the most probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Carcinoma esophagus

The given clinical history of an elderly female presenting with symptoms such as progressive dysphagia, loss of appetite and weight loss along with the given barium study which shows irregular narrowing, mucosal destruction and shouldered margins. These findings are suggestive of Carcinoma Esophagus.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A 6-week-old child was brought to the emergency department with complaints of recurrent projectile vomiting. USG of the child is shown below. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. CHPS (Congenital Hypertrophic Pyloric Stenosis)

CHPS presents with projectile non-bilious vomiting and USG shows thickened pylorus (>4 mm, canal >16 mm). Atresias cause bilious vomiting, volvulus shows corkscrew sign.

Key USG Signs:

• “Target sign” / “Donut sign”  (transverse view)
• Elongated pyloric canal (longitudinal view)
• Thickened pyloric muscle

| Parameter | Cutoff

| --------- | ------

| Muscle thickness | > 4 mm ⭐

| Pyloric canal length | > 16 mm ⭐

| Feature | CHPS | Duodenal Atresia | Jejunal Atresia | Volvulus

| ------- | ---- | ---------------- | --------------- | --------

| Age | 2–8 weeks | Birth | Birth | Neonate

| Vomiting | Projectile, non-bilious | Bilious | Bilious | Bilious

| Imaging | USG | X-ray | X-ray | USG / contrast

| Key sign | Target sign | Double bubble | Multiple levels | Whirlpool

| Level of obstruction | Gastric outlet | Proximal | Mid bowel | Twisting

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A sigmoid configuration along with tapering beak-like deformity at the lower esophageal sphincter on barium swallow is a feature of:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Achalasia cardia

Achalasia cardia is a primary esophageal motility disorder characterized by failure of the lower esophageal sphincter (LES) to relax and absence of normal esophageal peristalsis, resulting from degeneration of inhibitory neurons in the myenteric (Auerbach) plexus.

Characteristic barium swallow findings:

• Dilated esophagus with a sigmoid (S-shaped) configuration in advanced disease.
• Smooth, tapering “bird’s beak (beak-like)” narrowing at the lower esophageal sphincter (LES).
• Delayed emptying of contrast into the stomach.

Diagnostic evaluation:

• Gold standard: High-resolution esophageal manometry showing:

• Incomplete LES relaxation
• Increased LES resting pressure
• Absent peristalsis

• Upper GI endoscopy: Performed to exclude pseudoachalasia (e.g., malignancy).

Why not the other options?

• A. Diffuse esophageal spasm: Barium swallow shows corkscrew (rosary bead) esophagus.
• B. Squamous cell carcinoma of the esophagus: Produces an irregular, shouldered narrowing, not a smooth bird’s beak appearance.
• D. Barrett’s esophagus: Diagnosed endoscopically by specialized intestinal metaplasia, not by a bird’s beak deformity.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: An 88-year-old male presented to the emergency department with the sudden onset of severe epigastric pain. On physical examination, she had a temperature of 101.44° F, a pulse of 115 bpm and a blood pressure of 125/72 mm of Hg. Abdomen was tender & rigid. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Pneumoperitoneum

The presence of free gas under the right diaphragm in the X-ray. This is suggestive of pneumoperitoneum.

·        C/F: Acute abdominal pain, rigidity, tenderness, guarding.

·        Most sensitive X-ray: CXR-PA erect.

·        Most sensitive Ix: CECT with oral contrast.

·        Next step: Resuscitation with IV fluids, Exploratory laparotomy.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: An elderly man with dysphagia and halitosis for 7 months undergoes barium swallow. Most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Zenker’s diverticulum

Zenker’s diverticulum is a pharyngoesophageal pouch at Killian’s dehiscence, presenting with dysphagia, regurgitation, and bad breath.

Hallmark Imaging Features:

• Posterior outpouching
• At pharyngoesophageal junction (Killian’s dehiscence)
• Barium-filled sac
• May retain food → explains halitosis

Cricopharyngeal dysfunction

↓

↑ Intraluminal pressure

↓

Weak area (Killian’s dehiscence)

↓

Posterior mucosal herniation

↓

Zenker’s diverticulum

↓

Food retention → halitosis

Achalasia shows bird‑beak, diffuse spasm shows corkscrew, neoplasia causes progressive obstruction.

| Condition | Key Feature | Imaging

| --------- | ----------- | -------

| Zenker’s diverticulum | Halitosis | Posterior pouch

| Achalasia | Bird beak | Distal narrowing

| Esophageal cancer | Irregular narrowing | Shouldering

| Diffuse spasm | Corkscrew esophagus | Multiple contractions

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: Based on the CT images provided, which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. GB mass

Gallbladder carcinoma presents as a heterogeneous mass in the gallbladder fossa with direct liver invasion and loss of fat planes, distinguishable from other abdominal masses by its characteristic location and infiltrative growth pattern.

Key Imaging Clues:

• Mass in gallbladder fossa
• Irregular wall thickening or polypoidal lesion
• Loss of normal GB outline
• Direct liver invasion
• Possible biliary obstruction

| Feature | GB Mass | HCC | RCC | Retroperitoneal Tumor

| ------- | ------- | --- | --- | ---------------------

| Origin | Gallbladder | Liver | Kidney | Retroperitoneum

| Location | GB fossa | Intrahepatic | Renal | Posterior

| Enhancement | Heterogeneous | Arterial + washout | Strong enhancement | Variable

| Liver invasion | Common | Primary site | Rare | Displacement

| Key clue | Replaces GB | Cirrhosis background | Renal mass | Organ displacement

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: Identify the sign.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Double ring sign

The term double ring sign (also called the halo sign) is seen on an AP neck/chest X-ray when a child swallows a button battery lodged in the esophagus.

Why does it occur?

A button battery has a bilaminar structure:

• Outer metallic casing
• Inner recessed compartment

On X-ray, this produces two concentric circular densities, giving the appearance of a double ring (halo).

How is it different from a coin?

| Feature | Coin | Button Battery

| ------- | ---- | --------------

| AP view | Single uniform circular opacity | Double ring / halo sign

| Lateral view | Uniform thickness | Step-off sign (one side appears recessed)

| Urgency | Usually non-emergent | Surgical emergency

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: Identify the structure marked by the arrow?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Superior mesenteric vein

None

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: In which of the following conditions is the given X-ray finding seen?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Reflux esophagitis

The given image is a barium swallow X-ray showing a feline esophagus suggestive of eosinophilic esophagitis seen in asthma and GERD.

Other important barium swallow signs:

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: Match the following: A. ERCP B. MRCP C. HIDA D. PTC
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. A-3, B-1, C-4, D-2

• A. ERCP → 3
• B. MRCP → 1
• C. HIDA Scan → 4
• D. Percutaneous Transhepatic Cholangiography (PTC) → 2

Educational Objective:

Different imaging modalities are used to evaluate the hepatobiliary and pancreatic system, each with distinct indications and techniques.

• ERCP (Endoscopic Retrograde Cholangiopancreatography) is an endoscopic fluoroscopic procedure used for both diagnosis and therapy (stone extraction, sphincterotomy, biliary stenting).
• MRCP (Magnetic Resonance Cholangiopancreatography) is a non-invasive MRI technique that provides excellent visualization of the biliary and pancreatic ducts without contrast injection or radiation.
• HIDA (Hepatobiliary Iminodiacetic Acid) scan is a nuclear medicine study that evaluates gallbladder function and biliary patency.
• Percutaneous Transhepatic Cholangiography (PTC) is an invasive fluoroscopic procedure in which contrast is injected directly into the intrahepatic bile ducts through a percutaneous transhepatic needle, commonly used when ERCP is not feasible.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: The earliest detectable sign on a Barium Enema in patients with Ulcerative Colitis is: (NEET Pg 2016)
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Mucosal Granularity

Diffuse mucosal granularity is the earliest radiographic sign of ulcerative colitis on barium studies. This subtle finding represents the initial inflammatory changes that occur in the mucosa before more advanced signs develop. Mucosal granularity appears as fine irregularities on the normally smooth mucosal surface and is best visualized on double-contrast barium enema examinations.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: The following appearance in IVP is caused by:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Retroperitoneal fibrosis

Key Finding in this IVP:

The image shows medial deviation of the ureters — the classic hallmark of retroperitoneal fibrosis (RPF)

Classic IVP Findings in Retroperitoneal Fibrosis:

| Feature | Description

| ------- | -----------

| Medial deviation of ureters | Most characteristic — ureters pulled medially at L4-L5 level

| Hydronephrosis | Due to ureteric obstruction

| Tapering obstruction | Smooth extrinsic compression of ureters

| Level of obstruction | Typically at L4-L5 (mid-ureter)

| Bilateral involvement | Common

Causes of RPF:

• Idiopathic (most common — Ormond's disease)
• Methysergide use
• Aortic aneurysm
• Malignancy
• Radiation fibrosis

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: The following scan is of a young woman on oral contraceptives. The most likely diagnosis is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Hepatic adenoma

The image given is of hepatic adenoma which is the most frequent hepatic tumor in young women on oral contraceptive pills. Hepatic adenomas are benign liver tumors, predisposed in patients on OCPs and glycogen storage disorders with a predilection for hemorrhage. They are enhancing lesions on the arterial phase.

·        Liver tumors - IOC: Triple phase CT

·        Typical appearance of hemangioma

·        Other options

·        Option A: Hepatocellular carcinoma: More commonly associated with chronic liver disease and hepatitis B or C infections.

·        Typical appearance of HCC:

·        Option B: Metastatic infiltrates: Typically appear as multiple lesions with variable enhancement patterns depending on the primary cancer's nature.

·        Option D: Hemangioma: The most common benign liver tumor, characterized by its classic "light bulb" bright enhancement on T2-weighted MRI images, not typically associated with oral contraceptive use.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Chronic pancreatitis

Chronic pancreatitis shows pancreatic calcifications. Wolman disease affects adrenals, acute pancreatitis lacks calcification, TB rarely involves pancreas.

Key Radiological Features:

• Pancreatic calcifications
• Dilated irregular pancreatic duct (“chain of lakes”)
• Gland atrophy
• Possible pseudocysts

| Feature | Chronic Pancreatitis | Acute Pancreatitis | Wolman Disease | TB

| ------- | -------------------- | ------------------ | -------------- | ---

| Calcification | Present ⭐ | Absent | Adrenal | Rare

| Pancreas size | Atrophic | Enlarged | Normal | Variable

| Duct | Dilated, irregular | Normal | Normal | Variable

| Age | Adults | Any | Infants | Any

| Key clue | Calcified pancreas | Edema | Adrenal calcification | Nodes/ascites

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: What is the likely diagnosis based on the MRCP image?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Choledochal cyst

Type 1 choledochal cyst shows fusiform CBD dilatation. Caroli disease affects intrahepatic ducts, cholangiocarcinoma shows mass, choledocholithiasis shows signal voids.

Key Imaging Features:

• Fusiform or cystic dilatation of CBD
• Smooth contour
• Continuity with biliary tree
• No obstructing lesion

| Type | Description

| ---- | -----------

| Type I | Fusiform dilatation of CBD ⭐ (most common)

| Type II | Diverticulum

| Type III | Choledochocele

| Type IV | Multiple intra + extrahepatic

| Type V | Caroli disease

| Feature | Choledochal Cyst | Cholangiocarcinoma | Caroli Disease | Choledocholithiasis

| ------- | ---------------- | ------------------ | -------------- | -------------------

| Nature | Cystic dilatation | Stricture | Intrahepatic dilation | Stone

| Contour | Smooth | Irregular | Saccular | Filling defect

| Location | CBD (extrahepatic) | Anywhere | Intrahepatic | CBD

| Key sign | Fusiform dilation | Cutoff | Central dot | Signal void

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: Which investigation is shown below?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. X ray Defecography

X‑ray defecography uses rectal barium and lateral X‑ray to assess anorectal function. X-ray Defecography-

A functional imaging test to evaluate:

• Defecation mechanics
• Coordination of pelvic floor muscles
• Structural abnormalities
•

Hallmark Clues:

• Dynamic fluoroscopy (patient is asked to strain/defecate)
• Barium paste in rectum
• Visualization of anorectal angle
• Shows pelvic floor descent / prolapse / rectocele

| Condition | Finding

| --------- | -------

| Rectocele | Anterior bulge

| Rectal prolapse | Descent of rectum

| Dyssynergia | Failure of relaxation

| Enterocele | Small bowel herniation

MR defecography uses MRI, barium swallow evaluates esophagus, follow‑through studies small bowel.

| Feature | X-ray Defecography | MR Defecography

| ------- | ------------------ | ---------------

| Modality | Fluoroscopy | MRI

| Radiation | Yes | No

| Soft tissue detail | Less | Excellent

| Availability | Widely available | Limited

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: Which of the following investigations is shown in the radiograph?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Barium meal

The given image is a barium meal. This study is used to examine the stomach and proximal duodenum.

Visual Cues: The image shows the distribution of barium within the stomach, outlining its contours and revealing its internal structure, which is typical in a barium meal examination.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A 28-year-old man presents with headache and visual disturbances. MRI brain reveals a cerebellar hemangioblastoma. On further evaluation, abdominal imaging shows a solid renal mass suggestive of clear cell renal carcinoma. Family history reveals that his father and paternal aunt had similar CNS and renal tumors at a young age. Which of the following genetic mutations is most likely responsible for this condition?
options: Loss of function of TSC1/TSC2 gene
Mutation in VHL tumor suppressor gene
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Mutation in VHL tumor suppressor gene

Familial occurrence of renal tumors with CNS tumors suggests von Hippel–Lindau (VHL) disease.

VHL gene mutations predispose to renal cell carcinoma, hemangioblastomas of the brain and retina, and pheochromocytoma.

Mutation:

VHL loss

↓

↑ HIF accumulation

↓

↑ VEGF, PDGF

↓

Tumor formation (highly vascular)

Tumors in VHL-

| Organ | Tumor

| ----- | -----

| Kidney | Clear cell renal cell carcinoma

| Brain (CNS) | Hemangioblastoma (cerebellum)

| Retina | Retinal hemangioblastoma

| Adrenal | Pheochromocytoma

| Pancreas | Cysts / tumors

RET is linked to MEN2, TSC causes hamartomas, and Li–Fraumeni involves diverse early-onset cancers.

| Syndrome | Gene | Key Tumors

| -------- | ---- | ----------

| VHL | VHL (3p) | RCC, hemangioblastoma

| MEN2 | RET | Thyroid, pheochromocytoma

| TSC | TSC1/2 | Hamartomas

| Li-Fraumeni | TP53 | Multiple malignancies

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A 5-year-old child has recurrent urinary tract infections, a weak urinary stream, and intermittent incontinence. The radiological image demonstrates the characteristic findings. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Ureterocele

Ureteroceles appear as smooth, round "cobra head" filling defects at the ureterovesical junction, causing obstruction, recurrent UTIs, poor stream, and incontinence in children.

Key Radiological Sign:

• Round filling defect in bladder
• Surrounded by contrast → looks like cobra head

| Option | | Why

| ------ | --- | ---

| A. Ureterocele | ✅ | Cystic dilation + cobra head sign + obstruction symptoms

| B. Duplicated collecting system | ❌ | May coexist, but alone doesn’t give cobra head sign

| C. Posterior urethral valves (PUV) | ❌ | Seen in male infants, shows dilated posterior urethra

| D. Vesicoureteric reflux (VUR) | ❌ | Reflux of urine, not cystic lesion

| Condition | Key Feature | Imaging Finding

| --------- | ----------- | ---------------

| Ureterocele | Distal ureter dilation | Cobra head sign

| PUV | Male infant obstruction | Dilated posterior urethra

| VUR | Reflux of urine | Contrast going upward

| Duplicated system | Two ureters | Double collecting system

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A 65-year-old postmenopausal woman presents with vaginal bleeding. What is the most likely diagnosis based on the image provided?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Adenomyosis

Adenomyosis is characterized on MRI by thickening of the junctional zone (>12 mm) with a heterogeneous “salt and pepper” appearance due to ectopic endometrial tissue and small cystic foci within the myometrium.

Signature Imaging Features:

• Thickened junctional zone (>12 mm)
• Heterogeneous myometrium
• Small myometrial cysts (T2 bright)
• Globular enlarged uterus

Endometrial tissue invades myometrium

↓

Repeated bleeding inside muscle

↓

Inflammation + fibrosis

↓

Junctional zone thickening

↓

Adenomyosis appearance on MRI

| Feature | Adenomyosis | Fibroid

| ------- | ----------- | -------

| Borders | Ill-defined | Well-defined

| Pattern | Diffuse | Focal

| MRI | Junctional zone thickening | Mass lesion

| Cysts | Present | Absent

MRI showing multiple intramural fibroids in the uterus

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A full-term male newborn is noted to have the following appearance. Which of the following best describes the associated abnormalities in this congenital condition?
options: Urinary tract anomalies with undescended testes
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Urinary tract anomalies with undescended testes

Prune Belly syndrome (Eagle–Barrett syndrome) is a rare congenital disorder characterized by the classic triad of:

1. Partial or complete absence of the anterior abdominal wall muscles → wrinkled, "prune-like" abdomen
2. Urinary tract anomalies → dilated ureters, megacystis, hydronephrosis, posterior urethral obstruction, vesicoureteral reflux
3. Bilateral cryptorchidism (undescended testes)

It occurs almost exclusively in male infants. Urinary tract abnormalities may lead to recurrent urinary tract infections, renal dysplasia, and chronic kidney disease.

Why not the other options?

• A. Acute subpubic angle: Incorrect. This is a pelvic anatomical feature and is not a characteristic finding of Prune Belly syndrome.
• C. Bilateral undescended ovaries: Incorrect. Ovaries do not descend into the inguinal canal like testes. The syndrome is classically associated with bilateral cryptorchidism in males.
• D. Tracheoesophageal fistula: Incorrect. This is a separate congenital anomaly, commonly associated with esophageal atresia, and is unrelated to Prune Belly syndrome.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A patient presented with abdominal pain and sterile pyuria, and the x-ray showed the following features. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Putty kidney

Putty kidney is an advanced renal pathology often resulting from chronic infections such as tuberculosis, leading to extensive calcification and renal dysfunction. This condition is distinguishable on imaging by its irregular, extensive calcifications throughout the kidney, associated with clinical symptoms like abdominal pain and sterile pyuria.

Key Radiological Features:

• Diffuse, dense calcification replacing kidney
• Kidney outline may be preserved
• Appears like a chalky/putty-like structure
• Represents end-stage TB kidney (autonephrectomy)

| Feature | Putty Kidney | Nephrocalcinosis | Staghorn Calculus | Psoas Calcification

| ------- | ------------ | ---------------- | ----------------- | -------------------

| Location | Whole kidney | Medulla | Pelvis/calyces | Muscle

| Pattern | Diffuse dense ⭐ | Speckled | Branching | Linear

| Cause | TB | Metabolic | Infection/stone | Soft tissue

| Function | Non-functioning | Preserved | Obstructed | Normal kidney

| Key clue | Sterile pyuria | Bilateral | Stone shape | Outside kidney

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A patient presents with ureteric colic. Examination is normal. What is the best imaging to diagnose?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. NCCT KUB

Non‑contrast CT KUB is the gold standard for detecting urinary stones, highly sensitive and specific. NCCT KUB shows-

• Stone = hyperdense focus
• Exact location (PUJ, mid-ureter, VUJ)
• Size & number (guides management)
• Hydroureter / hydronephrosis
• Alternative diagnoses (appendicitis, diverticulitis) if no stone

| CT Finding | Meaning

| ---------- | -------

| Hyperdense dot in ureter | Calculus

| Perinephric stranding | Inflammation from obstruction

| Dilated pelvis/ureter | Upstream obstruction

| “Soft tissue rim sign” | Ureteral wall edema around stone

MRI is poor for stones, ureteroscopy is therapeutic, and CECT is unnecessary for stone detection.

| Modality | Role | Limitations

| -------- | ---- | -----------

| NCCT KUB | Gold standard, detects all stones | Radiation

| USG KUB | Screening, pregnancy | Misses ureteric stones

| CECT KUB | Tumors/vascular | Masks stones

| MRI | Rare role | Poor for stones

| Ureteroscopy | Diagnostic + therapeutic | Invasive, not first-line

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: An imaging study was performed to assess the urinary tract. Which radiological modality is shown in the image?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. IVP

IVP (Intravenous Pyelography) demonstrates bilateral simultaneous opacification of the entire urinary collecting system from calyces to bladder following IV contrast administration.

Key Visual Clues:

• Bright contrast in renal pelvis & calyces
• Ureters outlined like thin white tubes
• Contrast filling urinary bladder

| Option | Verdict | Why

| ------ | ------- | ---

| A. IVP | ✅ | Shows entire urinary tract with IV contrast excretion

| B. RGU (Retrograde urethrogram) | ❌ | Only urethra, contrast injected via urethral meatus

| C. MCU (Micturating cystourethrogram) | ❌ | Focuses on bladder + reflux during voiding

| D. Plain X-ray | ❌ | No contrast → cannot outline urinary tract

| Feature | IVP | RGU | MCU

| ------- | --- | --- | ---

| Contrast route | Intravenous | Urethral | Bladder catheter

| Structures seen | Kidneys → ureters → bladder | Urethra | Bladder + urethra

| Main use | Stones, obstruction | Urethral injury/stricture | Vesicoureteral reflux

| Phase | Excretory | Retrograde | Voiding phase

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: Best diagnostic investigation for suspected ureteric stone?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. NCCT KUB

Non‑contrast CT KUB is gold standard for ureteric stones, detecting all types except indinavir.

What NCCT shows:

• Stone = hyperdense (bright white)
• Hydroureter / hydronephrosis
• Exact location + size
• Detects even radiolucent stones (e.g., uric acid)

| Modality | Role | Limitation

| -------- | ---- | ----------

| NCCT KUB | Best diagnostic test | Radiation

| USG KUB | Screening (pregnancy) | Misses ureteric stones

| CECT KUB | Tumor evaluation | Masks stones

| Ureteroscopy | Diagnostic + therapeutic | Invasive

USG may miss stones, CECT obscures them, ureteroscopy is therapeutic not diagnostic.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: In which of the following pathologies is the cobra-head appearance seen on an IVU, as shown in the image below?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Ureterocele

The cobra-head (adder-head) sign on Intravenous Urography (IVU) is the classic radiological appearance of a ureterocele.

A ureterocele is a cystic dilatation of the distal intravesical ureter caused by congenital stenosis of the ureteric orifice. On IVU, contrast fills the dilated distal ureter, producing a round contrast-filled sac surrounded by a thin radiolucent halo, giving the characteristic cobra-head appearance.

Why not the other options?

• A. Vesicoureteric reflux (VUR): Diagnosed by MCU/VCUG, showing retrograde reflux of contrast into the ureter.
• B. Posterior urethral valves (PUV): MCU shows a dilated posterior urethra (“keyhole sign”).
• C. Duplication of ureter: May be associated with ureterocele but does not itself produce the cobra-head sign.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: The clinical condition shown in the image is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Horseshoe kidney

The image shows fusion of the lower poles of both kidneys by an isthmus, producing the characteristic U-shaped configuration of a horseshoe kidney.

Key features:

• Usually fusion of the lower poles
• Kidneys are often malrotated
• The fused kidney typically lies lower than normal
• The inferior mesenteric artery commonly prevents normal ascent

Why not the other options?

• (a) Malrotated kidney: Abnormal orientation of the renal hilum without fusion.
• (b) Malascended kidney: Kidney remains abnormally low but is not necessarily fused.
• (c) Doughnut kidney: Usually refers to complete fusion of the kidneys, forming a ring-like configuration.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: What is the diagnosis based on the CT image?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. PUJO

Pelviureteric junction obstruction causes massive pelvis dilatation with parenchymal thinning. ADPKD shows multiple cysts, renal cyst is solitary, horseshoe kidney is fused poles.

Key Radiological Features:

• Dilated renal pelvis + calyces
• Abrupt narrowing at PUJ
• Normal ureter (key differentiator!)
• Kidney may appear enlarged

| Feature | PUJO | Renal Cyst | ADPKD | Horseshoe Kidney

| ------- | ---- | ---------- | ----- | ----------------

| Pelvis | Dilated | Normal | Distorted | Normal

| Ureter | Normal | Normal | Normal | Normal

| Cysts | No | Single | Multiple bilateral | No

| Shape | Ballooned pelvis | Round lesion | Enlarged kidneys | Fused kidneys

| Key clue | Hydronephrosis only | Simple cyst | Many cysts | Fusion anomaly

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: What is the diagnosis based on the given image?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Unicornuate uterus

The given image shows the HSG of a Unicornuate uterus. The endometrial cavity forms a fusiform (banana type) shape, tapering at the apex and draining into a single fallopian tube. The uterus is generally shifted off the midline.

Other Options:

Option A: Uterus didelphys is a type of Müllerian duct anomaly where there is a complete duplication of uterine horns as well as duplication of the cervix, with no communication between them.

Option B: Bicornuate uterus is due to incomplete fusion of the mullerian ducts and is characterized by the presence of a cleft in the external contour of the uterine fundus.

Option C: Septate uterus is the result of partial or complete failure of resorption of the uterovaginal septum after fusion of the paramesonephric ducts.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: Which of the following statements is true regarding the investigation shown below?
options: Non-invasive and can diagnose pelviureteric junction obstruction
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Non-invasive and can diagnose pelviureteric junction obstruction

Intravenous pyelography (IVP) is a non-invasive radiographic examination that can effectively diagnose pelviureteric junction obstruction through visualization of contrast excretion by the kidneys.

IVP showing PUJO:

Cystoscopy is the gold standard for bladder carcinoma, IVP may just show a filling defect.

There is no percutaneous component, only IV contrast needs to be injected.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A 45-year-old patient presented with vague abdominal pain. On USG, he was found to have a renal cyst of Bosniak class III. CECT was done, as shown below. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Renal angiomyolipoma

The CT image showing renal lesions that has hypoattenuating components consistent with macroscopic fat is highly suggestive of renal angiomyolipoma.

Imaging in renal angiomyolipoma: Demonstration of macroscopic fat is the main part of making a diagnosis. USG may show hyperechoic lesions in the cortex with posterior acoustic shadowing. In patients with tuberous sclerosis, the entire kidney is affected, producing an echogenic appearance with loss of normal corticomedullary junction.

CT findings:

• Cortical lesions that demonstrate macroscopic fat (less than -20 HU)
• Absence of ossification or calcification
• The presence of macroscopic fat is strongly suggestive of this condition, but not pathognomonic as RCC may rarely demonstrate macroscopic fat.
• Approximately 5% may be fat poor.

MRI: It is an excellent tool to demonstrate intramural fat components. Two sequences are used:

• Fat-saturated techniques
• Phase-in and phase-out imaging that shows India ink artifact at the junction between fat and non-fat components.

Digital subtraction angiography: They are hypervascular lesions showing 'sunburst appearance' in the arterial phase and 'onion peel appearance' in the venous phase.

Angiomyolipomas are benign tumors that occur sporadically or in association with tuberous sclerosis. The mean age of presentation is 43 years and there is a female predilection. It can present as spontaneous retroperitoneal hemorrhage, especially with larger tumors. The patient can present with flank pain, palpable mass, hematuria, urinary tract infections, hypertension, or renal failure. They usually do not require any intervention. mTOR inhibitors like everolimus can be used to decrease the size of the lesion.

Bosniak classification:

It classifies the renal cystic lesions mainly into four classes based on the CT characteristics.

Class I and II are benign and do not require follow-up imaging or surgery.

Class IIF requires follow-up for about 5 years to exclude malignancy.

Class III needs to be biopsied or surgically explored due to a higher risk of malignancy.

Class IV lesions are clearly malignant and need appropriate treatment.

Other options:

Renal cell carcinoma (RCC): It is the most common malignant tumor of the kidney. It usually occurs in the age group 50-70 years and macroscopic hematuria is seen in about 60% of the cases. It is a differential for angiomyolipoma but it is important to note that macroscopic fat is almost always associated with ossification or calcification.

Renal oncocytoma: They are relatively benign in nature and usually present in the 6th to 7th decade. An important point regarding this tumor is its similarity with RCC and hence it is very difficult to differentiate between them preoperatively. A sharp central stellate scar may be seen in one-third of the cases. But RCC may also show this stellate scar appearance in some cases.

Renal cyst: It is a broader term that includes the cystic lesions of the kidney. They can be simple cysts that are benign. Complex or complicated cystic lesions need evaluation and can be malignant. Bosniak classification of renal cysts is given above.

Image showing a simple renal cyst:

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A woman presented with confusion, constipation, and headache. Serum calcium was 13.1mg/dL and ALP was elevated. She was diagnosed with primary hyperparathyroidism. Which of the following is the imaging of choice?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Sestamibi scan

Sestamibi scan is the imaging of choice to delineate parathyroid abnormalities.

Sestamibi is a monovalent lipophilic cation. It shows passive diffusion across cell membranes and accumulates in mitochondria. Because of its accumulation in the mitochondria, there is a difference in the rate at which it gets washed out depending upon the number of mitochondria in each tissue.

In parathyroid adenomas, there is a high concentration of oxyphilic cells with high mitochondrial content. The three protocols for sestamibi scanning are:

• Single-isotope dual-phase scan
• Dual-isotope subtraction imaging
• Single-photon emission computed tomography (SPECT).

SPECT is commonly used because of its improved spatial resolution. Sestamibi combined with CT can be used to detect smaller parathyroid tissues.

Other imaging modalities for parathyroid localization:

• Ultrasonography:

• It is inexpensive and noninvasive
• Mediastinal parathyroid tissue cannot be detected because USG cannot penetrate the sternum or clavicles.

• Four-dimensional CT:

• It has a very high sensitivity
• Increased radiation exposure than other routine modalities is a potential disadvantage

• Selective venous sampling for PTH can be used for the exact localization of adenomas

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A young child presented with mild intermittent upper abdominal pain. X-ray is given below. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Morgagni hernia

The clinical features and the chest X-ray showing an opacity in the right cardiophrenic angle are suggestive of Morgagni hernia.

Congenital diaphragmatic hernia(CDH) of anteromedial location is the Morgagni hernia. Here the defect is anterior and retrosternal. It is rarer than bochdalek hernia and accounts for only 2-5% of CDH. About 90% of the cases occur on the right side.

It is less symptomatic than bochdalek hernia and the diagnosis is usually delayed until childhood. The patient presents with respiratory or upper GI symptoms. Respiratory symptoms like distress, tachypnea, and recurrent pulmonary infections are common in children. Other symptoms are abdominal pain, dyspnea, flatulence, and indigestion.

Radiographic findings:

• Radiolucent paracardiac shadow may be seen retrosternally on lateral chest x-ray if there is bowel herniation.
• Rounded opacity in the right cardiophrenic angle may be seen if there is herniation of omentum or solid organs.
• A CT scan may be used to confirm the diagnosis.

Surgical repair is indicated in all cases either by a thoracic or abdominal approach.

Other options:

Bochdalek hernia: It is more common than Morgagni hernia. Here the defect is posterolateral in location. Respiratory distress is experienced by most infants. In the pediatric age group, symptoms are predominantly respiratory due to pulmonary hypoplasia. In adults, it is usually asymptomatic and is incidentally found. About 85% of the cases are left-sided.

Gastric volvulus: This is an uncommon condition and presents with the characteristic Borchardt triad which includes:

• Sudden-onset severe upper abdominal pain
• Recurrent retching with the production of little vomitus
• Inability to pass a nasogastric (NG) tube

It can be organoaxial or mesentroaxial. Chest X-ray may show intrathoracic upside-down stomach and retrosternal or mediastinal air-fluid level.

Image showing intrathoracic gastric volvulus with mediastinal gastric bubble-

Eventration of the diaphragm: It refers to the abnormal contour of the dome of the diaphragm without any disruption to the diaphragmatic continuity. It usually involves a segment of the hemidiaphragm. It can cause respiratory distress in newborns and is usually asymptomatic in adults.

Radiographic findings: The affected portion of the hemidiaphragm is elevated and is seen as a smooth hump, while the normal contour is seen in the remaining part. 'Double diaphragmatic contour' may be seen in frontal view and is confirmed with a lateral X-ray.

Image showing eventration of the right dome of the diaphragm-

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: Double bleb sign seen in early pregnancy is due to _______.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Yolk sac and amniotic sac

The double bleb sign is due to the yolk sac and amniotic sac.

On ultrasonographic examination, a gestational sac may contain the yolk sac and amniotic sac, appearing like two small bubbles. This is known as the double bleb sign. The embryonic disc is located between the yolk sac and the amniotic sac. It is an important feature of an intrauterine pregnancy.

Other options:

In a twin pregnancy, the chorionicity of the placenta is best diagnosed with the help of an ultrasound examination.

• In dichorionic gestation, the twins are separated by amniotic membranes and an intervening chorion. So, a thicker twin peak sign or lambda (λ) sign is formed at the point at which the amnions meet the placenta.

• In monochorionic diamniotic gestation, the twins are separated only by the two amniotic membranes with no intervening chorion. So, a thin T sign is formed at the point at which the amnions meet the placenta.

Heterotopic pregnancy is a condition in which a normal uterine pregnancy co-exists with an extrauterine (ectopic) pregnancy. Although heterotopic pregnancy can occur spontaneously, it is more likely after artificial reproductive technology (ART) and ovulation induction.

The below image shows heterotopic pregnancy with 2 sacs, one inside the uterus (white arrow) and the other in the cervix (black arrows).

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: During rounds, your senior was discussing the given image. The following is an image of which of the following investigations?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. CT scan

The image in the question is a CT scan as it shows the bone as a high-intensity structure (white appearance).

In CT study X-rays are applied in a circular motion and body tissue slices are recreated mathematically. Different tissues are seen with different intensities depending on the proportion of attenuation of the X-rays that pass through them.

• Air and water are displayed as low intensities (dark appearance) because they produce only little attenuation.
• Bone is displayed as a high-intensity structure (bright appearance) because of its significant attenuation.
• High density is seen with hyperemia, freshly clotted blood, and when contrast is used.
• Edema and necrosis are seen as low-intensity lesions.

Other options:

Contrast dye study: In this imaging study, a special dye or contrast is given to evaluate structures that are not identified by conventional imaging. The contrast added would be visible in the image depending on the type of contrast and tissues targeted. Intravenous pyelogram, barium studies, angiography, etc are all examples of contrast studies.

X-ray: It shows different parts of the body in varying shades of black and white. The difference in the appearance of various tissues is due to the differences in the amount of radiation absorbed by them.

• Bone appears white because calcium has high x-ray absorption.
• Fat and soft tissues appear grey due to less x-ray absorption.
• The least absorption is seen with air which appears black.

Angiography: Here a special dye or contrast is injected to highlight the blood vessels are they are not clearly identified in normal imaging. Hence vessels would be highlighted in an angiogram.

Note: A contrast study is different from a contrast-enhanced CT scan, Intravenous pyelogram, barium studies, angiography, etc are all examples of contrast studies.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text:
Identify the imaging modality given below.

USG- Ultrasonography
MRI- Magnetic resonance imaging
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. USG

The image shown in the question is the USG of the neck.

Sonographic examination of the neck shows the thyroid gland, muscles, blood vessels, bony structures or cartilages, and nerves. The thyroid of a healthy patient appears homogeneously echogenic with a uniform echotexture on USG. Lateral to the thyroid, the large blood vessels (the common carotid artery and more laterally, the internal jugular vein) can be identified. In the above image, hypoechoic areas are suggestive of the lumen of vessels seen in the neck i.e common carotid artery and internal jugular vein.

Neck ultrasonography is the preferred modality for routine radiographic evaluation of the thyroid gland, as it offers the most accurate visualization of thyroid nodular disease. It also allows for the concomitant performance of percutaneous fine-needle aspiration biopsy of thyroid lesions.

Neck ultrasound can also be used to localize parathyroid disease.

Other options:

Option B: Fluoroscopy is an imaging modality that allows real-time X-ray viewing of a patient with high resolution. During this procedure, radiologists usually use contrast material (dye) to highlight the area being examined.

Below image shows the fluoroscopy of neck.

Option C: The below image shows the X-ray appearance of neck in AP view.

Option D: Relative to the neck musculature, the thyroid is hyperintense on MRI images.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: What is the structure marked in the CT scan ?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Cribriform plate

The structure marked in the image is the cribriform plate of the ethmoid bone. The image shown is a coronal section of paranasal sinuses at the level of anterior ethmoidal cells.

The cribriform plate is identified as a bony structure that separates the nasal cavity from the anterior cranial fossa. It is part of the ethmoid bone and is a sieve-like structure as it is pierced by the olfactory nerve fibers.

Crista Galli is also a part of ethmoid bone that projects superiorly from the cribriform plate. It provides attachment for the falx cerebri.

The anterior ethmoidal canal is identified by its location below the roof of ethmoidal air cells. The anterior ethmoidal artery passes through this canal and it is important to identify this to avoid bleeding from this vessel during sinus surgeries.

The posterior ethmoid canal/foramen is an opening in the ethmoid bone through which the posterior ethmoidal artery, vein, and nerve traverse. It is not visualized in this image as it is a coronal section at the level of anterior ethmoidal cells.

The optic nerve can be identified as an oval intraorbital structure in the coronal sections.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: What type of MRI image is given below?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Susceptibility weighted image

The image shown is a susceptibility-weighted image(SWI) as it clearly demonstrates microhemorrhages as hypointense foci.

SWI is a form of MRI sequence that is especially sensitive to substances that distort the local magnetic field. Compounds with diamagnetic, paramagnetic, and ferromagnetic properties will interact with the local magnetic field and produce distraction. This would lead to a loss of signal in these areas.

Deoxyhemoglobin, hemosiderin, and ferritin are paramagnetic. Bone minerals and dystrophic calcifications are diamagnetic in nature.

The main clinical use is the identification of microhemorrhages/blood products or calcium that are not detected in other MRI sequences.

Other options:

Proton density image:

It is based on the number of nuclei in the area that is imaged. In PD-weighted image tissues with a higher density of protons produce stronger signals and appear brighter. PD weighted image can be identified by comparing fluid with the fat signal. Fluids in these images appear greyish white similar or the appearance of fat in the body.

Gradient echo sequences(GRE):

It uses gradient fields to generate transverse magnetization. In areas of hemorrhage, the iron that is present in the hemoglobin produces its own local magnetic field and dephases the spinning nuclei. This is useful to identify hemorrhagic contusions in the brain and pigmented villonodular synovitis.

Inversion recovery sequences:

This MRI sequence is used to selectively null certain tissues. It can be:

• Short tau inversion recovery(STIR) where fat is nulled. Fluids appear bright and fat appears dark in these images.
• Fluid attenuated inversion recovery(FLAIR) or double inversion recovery(DIR where fluid is nulled.- The fluid(CSF) normally appears dark and lesions appear to be brighter on these images.

FLAIR image-
