questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: This is the radiograph of a child with a foreign body in the oesophagus. What is the sign seen in this?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Double ring sign

The presence of a halo sign or double ring sign is indicative of the foreign body being a button battery.

Button batteries and sharp objects in the oesophagus and foreign bodies associated with respiratory symptoms all mandate urgent endoscopic removal.

Button batteries, in particular, are very dangerous foreign bodies, which must be expediently removed because they can cause:

• Mucosal injury in 1-hour contact time
• Involve all layers of the oesophagus in 4 hours

Injury is thought to be secondary to electrochemical burns from electrical discharge. Chemical burns from electrolyte alkali leakage and pressure necrosis also may contribute to mucosal injury.

Asymptomatic blunt objects and coins lodged in the oesophagus can be observed for up to 24 hr in anticipation of passage into the stomach.

Another AP and lateral X-ray demonstrating the presence of a button battery in the oesophagus is as shown below.

Other options

Option A: Thumb sign is seen in acute epiglottitis.

Option B: A steeple sign is seen in croup or laryngotracheobronchitis.

Option D: String sign on the barium enema is in ileocecal tuberculosis.

The image below shows the string sign of Kantor associated with Crohn's disease.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: What does this image below indicate?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Choledochal cyst

The given MRCP image showing saccular dilatation of the common bile duct suggests a diagnosis of type I choledochal cyst.

Todani classification:

• Type I- saccular dilatation of the whole (Ia) or a segment (Ib) of the common bile duct (CBD)
• Type II- diverticulum from the CBD
• Type III- choledochocele that opens into the duodenum
• Type IV- multiple cysts (both intrahepatic and extrahepatic)
• Type V- multiple cysts that are only intrahepatic (Caroli's disease)

The diagnosis is made initially with a right upper quadrant ultrasound, following which a confirmatory MRCP can be carried out to help in pre-operative planning.

Treatment is usually surgical with a Roux-en-Y hepaticojejunostomy with radical resection of all the biliary tissue. There is a risk of malignant transformation in long-standing disease, so surgical removal is usually recommended.

Other options:

Option B: Gall bladder carcinoma would show abnormal growths or masses in the gall bladder rather than cystic dilations of the bile ducts.

Option C: Cholangiocarcinoma is a malignancy of the bile ducts and would present as irregular masses or bile duct strictures rather than cystic structures.

Option D: Choledocholithiasis refers to the presence of stones in the bile duct, which would appear as filling defects within the bile ducts rather than cystic dilations.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A 10-year-old boy presents with bitemporal hemianopia. CT is shown below. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Craniopharyngioma

A calcified lesion in the suprasellar region suggests craniopharyngioma. It is derived from Rathke's pouch.

Other Options:

Option A: Pituitary adenomas are seen in the sellar region in adults. Macroadenomas are seen as snowman or figure of eight appearance.

Option B: Meningioma is a supratentorial tumor, mainly in the parasagittal region. A classical Dural tail is seen.

Option D: Oligodendroglioma is exclusively found in the cerebral hemispheres, most commonly in the frontal lobes. Up to 90% of oligodendrogliomas contain visible calcification on CT.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A 10-year-old boy presents with bitemporal hemianopia. CT is shown below. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Craniopharyngioma

A calcified lesion in the suprasellar region suggests craniopharyngioma. It is derived from Rathke's pouch.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A 2-month-old infant is brought to the OPD with a parietal swelling present since birth. An X-ray was ordered and is shown below. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Cephalhematoma

| | Cephalhematoma | Caput Succedaneum | Subgaleal hematoma | Encephalocele

| --- | -------------- | ----------------- | ------------------ | -------------

| Site | Sub periosteal | Sub cutaneous fluid collection | Between galeal aponeurosis and periosteum | Herniation of intracranial contents through defect in skull vault

| Cause | Instrumental Delivery | Normal Vaginal delivery | Trauma during delivery, particularly with vacuum | Neural tube defects

| Presentation | Focal swelling; Limited by suture line | Focal swelling; Not limited by suture line | Diffuse swelling | Neurological deficit symptoms

| Prognosis | Observation, may resolve spontaneously by 2 -3 months | Self-resolves within a few days to weeks | Transfusion if severe, monitoring for anemia, surgical drainage if necessary | Surgical repair, neurosurgical intervention as needed

| Image | | | |

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A 20-year-old male patient presented with a headache and altered sensorium. MRI was performed, which revealed multiple ring-enhancing lesions. What will be the next step to confirm the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. MR spectroscopy

MR spectroscopy detects lipid-lactate peak, distinguishing tuberculomas from NCC. CBNAAT is for meningitis, biopsy is invasive, SWI detects bleeds. MR Spectroscopy

MRS analyzes metabolites inside the lesion, helping distinguish between different causes of ring lesions.

It is:

• Non-invasive
• Highly diagnostic
• Helps avoid biopsy in many cases

| Feature | Tuberculoma | Abscess | NCC | Metastasis

| ------- | ----------- | ------- | --- | ----------

| Number | Multiple | Single/multiple | Multiple | Multiple

| Enhancement | Ring | Ring | Ring | Ring

| MRS | Lipid peak | Amino acids | Variable | ↑ Choline

| Edema | Moderate | Marked | Mild | Variable

| Key clue | India, TB endemic | Infection signs | Scolex | Primary tumor

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A 25-year-old patient was involved in a road traffic accident. He was initially conscious, but later became unconscious and subsequently died. On postmortem examination, multiple petechial hemorrhages are observed in the corpus callosum. What is the most probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Diffuse axonal injury

Diffuse axonal injury from rotational trauma presents with characteristic petechial hemorrhages in the corpus callosum, grey-white matter junctions, and brainstem, with clinical deterioration after initial consciousness.

Key Imaging Clues:

• Multiple small hemorrhagic foci
• Best seen on:

• MRI (GRE / SWI) → blooming lesions

• CT may be:

• Normal or subtle early

| Feature | DAI | Subdural Hematoma | Ischemic Injury

| ------- | --- | ----------------- | ---------------

| Mechanism | Shearing | Venous bleed | Vascular occlusion

| Location | Deep (CC, brainstem) | Extra-axial | Arterial territory

| Imaging | Tiny hemorrhages | Crescent collection | Hypodensity

| CT early | Often normal | Visible | Visible

| Best modality | MRI (GRE/SWI) | CT | MRI (DWI)

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A 28-year-old man presents with purposeless involuntary, jerky movements of the face and limbs that have gradually worsened over the past year. His family reports personality changes, irritability and progressive forgetfulness. On examination, he has choreiform movements involving both upper and lower limbs and an unsteady gait. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Huntington's disease

• Huntington’s disease presents with progressive chorea, psychiatric changes, and dementia. Mutation in HTT gene (Chromosome 4)

• CAG trinucleotide repeat expansion

• Selective degeneration of:

• Caudate nucleus
• Putamen

Result: Loss of inhibitory GABA neurons → excessive movement (chorea)

MRI shows caudate nucleus atrophy with enlarged frontal horns.

Key Radiological Sign:

“Bat-wing appearance” of lateral ventricles

• Due to caudate nucleus atrophy
• Frontal horns appear dilated

Tardive dyskinesia is drug-induced, Sydenham’s is post-streptococcal, Tourette has tics.

| Condition | Age | Movement | Key Feature | Imaging

| --------- | --- | -------- | ----------- | -------

| Huntington’s | Adult | Chorea | Dementia + psychiatric | Caudate atrophy

| Sydenham’s chorea | Child | Chorea | Rheumatic fever | Normal

| Tardive dyskinesia | Adult | Orofacial | Drug-induced | Normal

| Tourette syndrome | Childhood | Tics | Vocal + motor tics | Normal

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A 30-year-old male presents for evaluation, and his MRI brain is shown below. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Meningioma

Meningiomas are extra-axial tumors characterized by broad dural attachment, homogeneous enhancement, well-defined margins, and the "dural tail" sign on contrast-enhanced MRI.

Typical clues on MRI:

• Extra-axial location
• Broad dural attachment
• Homogeneous contrast enhancement
• “Dural tail sign”

Key Imaging Features:

• Well-defined extra-axial mass
• Broad-based dural attachment
• Dural tail sign (thickened enhancing dura)
• Mass effect with buckling of adjacent cortex
• Possible hyperostosis of adjacent skull

| Feature | Meningioma | Glioma | Ependymoma | Pilocytic Astrocytoma

| ------- | ---------- | ------ | ---------- | ---------------------

| Location | Extra-axial | Intra-axial | Ventricular | Intra-axial

| Enhancement | Homogeneous | Heterogeneous | Variable | Nodule enhances

| Special sign | Dural tail | Necrosis | CSF spread | Cyst + mural nodule

| Age | Adults | Adults | Children | Children

| Margins | Well-defined | Ill-defined | Variable | Well-defined

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A 35-year-old lady presents with sudden severe headache. CT is shown below. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. SAH

Subarachnoid hemorrhage shows blood in cisterns, often from aneurysm rupture. SDH is crescent-shaped, EDH is biconvex, pneumocephalus shows air density.

Key Imaging Findings:

• Hyperdensity in basal cisterns
• Blood in:

• Sylvian fissures
• Interhemispheric fissure

• Classic “Star sign” (blood outlining cisterns)

| Feature | SAH | SDH | EDH | Pneumocephalus

| ------- | --- | --- | --- | --------------

| Location | Subarachnoid space | Subdural | Epidural | Intracranial air

| Shape | Fills sulci/cisterns | Crescent | Biconvex | Black air

| Density | Hyperdense | Hyper/hypo | Hyperdense | Hypodense

| Key sign | Star sign | Crescent | Lens | Air pockets

| Cause | Aneurysm rupture | Vein rupture | Artery rupture | Trauma/surgery

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A 50-year-old patient presents with persistent headache, nausea, vomiting, and altered sensorium. A non-contrast CT (NCCT) brain scan shows hyperdense areas in the image given below. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Subarachnoid hemorrhage

Acute subarachnoid hemorrhage appears as hyperdensity in basal cisterns and sulci on non-contrast CT, presenting clinically with sudden severe headache, nausea, vomiting, and altered sensorium.

• Hyperdensity in:

• Basal cisterns (classic “star sign”)
• Sylvian fissures
• Interhemispheric fissure

• Blood follows CSF spaces, not brain parenchyma

| Condition | CT Appearance | Key Location

| --------- | ------------- | ------------

| SAH | Hyperdense in sulci/cisterns | Subarachnoid space

| Epidural hematoma | Biconvex (lens-shaped) | Outside dura

| Subdural hematoma | Crescent-shaped | Between dura & arachnoid

| Intracerebral bleed | Focal hyperdense area | Brain parenchyma

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A 76-year-old presents with a history of headache after a fall. A CT scan was performed. Which of the following is the likely diagnosis? (NEET PG 2017)
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Acute epidural hematoma

An epidural hematoma (EDH) is an acute collection of blood between the inner table of the skull and the dura mater. EDH typically appears as a biconvex (lenticular) shaped hyperdensity that does not cross suture lines. In the clinical context of a patient presenting with headache after a fall, an EDH represents a traumatic arterial bleed, commonly from the middle meningeal artery.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A child presents with left to right shunt and high output cardiac failure. The following is his MRI. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Vein of Galen malformation

The MRI shown is suggestive of Vein of Galen Malformation (VOGM).

VOGM:

●       C/F: Newborn with high output cardiac failure with intracranial bruit

●       Type of A-V fistula

●       Doppler - Large midline vessel seen

●       MRI – Large flow void.

●       CT angiography – Giant vein of galen draining into straight sinus.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A child with seizures has CECT as shown below. Most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Neurocysticercosis

The “scolex sign” (central dot within ring lesion) is pathognomonic for neurocysticercosis.

Signature Imaging Clues:

• Ring-enhancing lesion
• Eccentric hyperdense dot inside → scolex (the parasite’s head)
• Surrounding edema (varies by stage)
• Often small (<2 cm), sometimes multiple

Vesicular stage

(cyst + scolex, no edema)

↓

Colloidal stage ⭐

(ring enhancement + edema)

↓

Granular nodular stage

(shrinking lesion)

↓

Calcified stage

(no edema, seizures persist)

Tuberculoma and abscess lack scolex, metastases are rare in children.

| Feature | NCC | Tuberculoma | Abscess | Metastasis

| ------- | --- | ----------- | ------- | ----------

| Size | Small | Larger | Variable | Variable

| Number | Single/multiple | Often single | Single | Multiple

| Scolex | ✔️ Present | ❌ Absent | ❌ | ❌

| Edema | Mild–moderate | Marked | Marked | Variable

| Wall | Thin | Thick, irregular | Smooth | Irregular

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A patient complains of neck stiffness and severe headache. The CT image shown below is suggestive of which of the following conditions?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Subarachnoid hemorrhage

The given clinical scenario of a patient presenting with neck stiffness and severe headache with CT showing blood in the basal cistern suggests towards the diagnosis of subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH).

Subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH) is an extra axial intracranial hemorrhage and denotes the presence of blood within the subarachnoid space. NCCT shows the hyperdense “star of death” appearance.

The modified Fisher scale is a grading method for SAH as seen on non-contrast CT (NCCT). The Hunt and Hess scale is used to describe the severity of SAH and to predict survival.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: Astrocytomas are associated with all of the following syndromes, except:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Cowden’s disease

Astrocytomas are associated with several inherited tumor-predisposition syndromes:

• (a) Neurofibromatosis type 1 — Correct association

• Classically associated with optic pathway pilocytic astrocytomas.

• (b) Neurofibromatosis type 2 — Correct association

• NF2 can be associated with gliomas including astrocytomas, although vestibular schwannomas, meningiomas and ependymomas are more characteristic.

• (c) Cowden disease — Incorrect → Answer

• Cowden syndrome is caused by PTEN mutation and is classically associated with dysplastic cerebellar gangliocytoma (Lhermitte–Duclos disease) rather than astrocytoma.

• (d) Li-Fraumeni syndrome — Correct association

• Due to TP53 mutation and associated with CNS tumors including astrocytoma/glioblastoma.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: Brain MRI of a patient with movement disorder is shown below. This is most suggestive of:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Pantothenate kinase associated neurodegeneration

PKAN shows bilateral hypointensity in globus pallidus with central hyperintensity on T2 MRI, resembling a tiger’s eye. It is due to iron deposition and gliosis.

Hallmark Finding:

“Eye of the Tiger” sign

• Central T2 hyperintensity (gliosis/necrosis)
• Surrounding hypointensity (iron deposition)
• Located in globus pallidus

| Condition | MRI Finding | Key Feature

| --------- | ----------- | -----------

| PKAN | Eye of tiger sign | Iron in globus pallidus

| Wilson disease | T2 hyperintensity in basal ganglia | Copper accumulation

| Huntington | Caudate atrophy | Chorea

| Krabbe disease | White matter changes | Demyelination

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: Consider the following statements with regard to cysticercosis: 1. It may present as personality change. 2. Subcutaneous nodule may be excised for histology. 3. Cerebral signs commonly do not occur until the larvae die, 5–20 years later. 4. Praziquantel can be given for 10 days. Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 1, 2, 3 and 4

Neurocysticercosis (larval infection by Taenia solium) commonly presents with seizures, but may also cause personality changes, raised intracranial pressure, and focal neurological deficits. Symptoms usually occur when the larvae degenerate and trigger an inflammatory response.

Why are the statements correct?

• 1. It may present as personality change ✔️: Can occur in neurocysticercosis.
• 2. Subcutaneous nodule may be excised for histology ✔️: Confirms diagnosis.
• 3. Cerebral signs commonly do not occur until the larvae die, 5–20 years later ✔️: Symptoms result from inflammation around dying cysts.
• 4. Praziquantel can be given for 10 days ✔️: Accepted treatment regimen (alternative: albendazole).

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: Identify the artery marked with a blue arrow on MR angiography.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Superficial temporal artery

The superficial temporal artery is a terminal branch of the external carotid, running laterally at the temples. External carotid artery

↓

Terminal branches

↓

Superficial temporal artery

↓

Frontal + parietal branches

↓

Supplies scalp

Posterior auricular lies behind the ear, middle meningeal is intracranial, and occipital supplies the posterior scalp.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: Identify the CT image finding near the orbit.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Subperiosteal abscess

CT shows a crescent‑shaped collection between periosteum and bone, typical of subperiosteal abscess, often complicating ethmoid sinusitis.

Signature CT Clues:

• Lentiform (biconvex) collection along orbital wall
• Commonly medial orbit (next to ethmoid sinus)
• Displacement of medial rectus muscle laterally
• Often rim-enhancing
• Associated sinusitis (ethmoid)

Orbital cellulitis is diffuse, preseptal affects eyelid only, sinusitis shows mucosal thickening.

| Condition | Location | Imaging Feature

| --------- | -------- | ---------------

| Subperiosteal abscess | Between bone & periosteum | Lentiform collection

| Orbital cellulitis | Within orbit | Diffuse fat stranding

| Preseptal cellulitis | Anterior to septum | Eyelid swelling only

| Sinusitis | Sinus cavity | Mucosal thickening

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: In the given image, the white arrow is pointing to which of the following structures?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Pyriform sinus

The pyriform sinuses appear as paired lateral air-filled recesses of the hypopharynx on AP neck X-rays, serving as important landmarks for foreign body detection and swallowing assessment.

Signature Clues:

• Air-filled space
• Lateral to larynx (on both sides)
• Located in hypopharynx
• Appears as a triangular recess

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: Mt. Fuji sign is seen in:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Pneumocephalus

The Mt. Fuji sign is indicative of tension pneumocephalus and is characterized by the peaking of the frontal lobes due to intracranial air pressure.

Key Imaging Features:

• Air in subdural space
• Frontal lobes pushed apart
• Shape resembles Mount Fuji peak
• Indicates tension (pressure effect)

| Sign | Diagnosis

| ---- | ---------

|  Mt. Fuji sign | Tension pneumocephalus

|  Crescent sign | Subdural hematoma

|  Target sign | Schwannoma / lesions

|  Eye of tiger | PKAN

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: The sign shown in the image below, is typically associated with which of the following conditions?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Carotid body tumor

The Lyre sign, characterized by splaying of the internal and external carotid arteries at the bifurcation, is pathognomonic for carotid body tumor (paraganglioma).

Signature Imaging Feature:

• “Lyre sign”

• Tumor at carotid bifurcation
• Splits:

• Internal carotid artery (ICA)
• External carotid artery (ECA)

The vessels look like a lyre (string instrument)

| Condition | Imaging Feature | Key Difference

| --------- | --------------- | --------------

| Carotid body tumor | ICA & ECA splayed (Lyre sign) | Hypervascular

| Carotid aneurysm | Dilated vessel | No splaying

| Branchial cleft cyst | Cystic lesion | Non-vascular

| Jugular vein thrombosis | Venous filling defect | Posterior location

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: What is the best imaging study for diagnosis of cerebral infarct?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Diffusion weighted MRI

Diffusion-weighted MRI is the most sensitive investigation for diagnosis of cerebral ischemia.  It is particularly useful for identifying acute ischemic changes in the brain due to its ability to detect diffusion restriction of water molecules in the brain tissue.

Diffusion restriction: hyperintense on DWI and hypointense on ADC.

●       Diffusion restriction is seen with:

1.     Acute stroke

2.     Hypercellular tumors

3.     Abscess

4.     Epidermoid cyst

5.     Keratin-Craniopharyngioma/ Cholesteatoma

Other Options:

Option A: FLAIR MRI: Fluid-Attenuated Inversion Recovery (FLAIR) MRI is useful for identifying older infarcts and chronic changes but is less sensitive in the acute phase of a stroke.

Option B: Non-contrast CT: While commonly used for initial assessment due to its availability and speed, it is less sensitive in the early stages of a stroke, often not showing changes until several hours post-onset.

Option D: СECT (Contrast-Enhanced CT): Typically used to assess for complications or other causes of symptoms but not as sensitive as DWI for early detection of cerebral infarcts.

Educational Objective

Diffusion-weighted MRI is the optimal choice for early detection of cerebral infarcts, making it an indispensable tool in acute stroke management. Its ability to show diffusion restriction provides critical information that can influence therapeutic decisions.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Chronic SDH

Chronic subdural hematoma is crescent-shaped and hypodense due to old blood. EDH is biconvex, acute SDH is hyperdense.

Key Radiological Features:

• Crescent-shaped collection
• Hypodense (dark) due to old blood
• Crosses suture lines
• Causes:

• Mass effect
• Midline shift

| Feature | Chronic SDH | Acute SDH | EDH

| ------- | ----------- | --------- | ---

| Shape | Crescent | Crescent | Biconvex

| Density | Hypodense | Hyperdense | Hyperdense

| Cause | Venous | Venous | Arterial

| Cross sutures | Yes | Yes | No

| Onset | Slow | Rapid | Rapid

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Chiari malformation

Chiari I malformation shows tonsillar ectopia >5 mm below foramen magnum. Dandy Walker has posterior fossa cyst, vein of Galen is vascular, encephalocele is brain herniation.

Key Imaging Features:

• Tonsillar herniation > 5 mm below foramen magnum ⭐
• Peg-shaped cerebellar tonsils
• Crowded posterior fossa
• Often associated with:

• Syringomyelia (spinal cord cavity)

| Type | Features

| ---- | --------

| Chiari I | Tonsillar herniation (most common)

| Chiari II | With myelomeningocele (Arnold-Chiari)

| Chiari III | Rare, severe

| Chiari IV | Cerebellar hypoplasia

| Feature | Chiari | Dandy-Walker | Vein of Galen | Encephalocele

| ------- | ------ | ------------ | ------------- | -------------

| Posterior fossa | Small/crowded | Enlarged | Normal | Defect

| Key feature | Tonsillar herniation | 4th ventricle cyst | Vascular dilation | Brain outside skull

| Location | Foramen magnum | Posterior fossa | Midline vein | Skull defect

| Associated | Syringomyelia | Hydrocephalus | Cardiac failure | Neural tube defect

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Abscess

Brain abscess shows ring-enhancing lesion with diffusion restriction on DWI. Tuberculomas lack restriction, cryptococcomas show soap-bubble, NCC has scolex.

Key Imaging Features:

• Smooth, thin ring enhancement
• Central diffusion restriction
• Extensive perilesional edema
• Mass effect

| Feature | Abscess | Tuberculoma | NCC | Cryptococcoma

| ------- | ------- | ----------- | --- | -------------

| Wall | Smooth | Irregular | Thin | Minimal

| DWI | Restricted ⭐ | No | No | No

| Edema | Marked | Moderate | Mild | Minimal

| Key sign | Pus cavity | Lipid peak | Scolex | Soap bubbles

| Host | Any | TB endemic | Endemic | Immunocompromised

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Anencephaly

Anencephaly shows absent cranial vault and forebrain with frog-eye sign. Cystic hygroma is neck cyst, encephalocele is herniation, Dandy Walker shows posterior fossa cyst.

Key Radiological Signs:

• Absent calvarium (no skull vault)
• “Frog-eye sign”  (prominent orbits)
• Disorganized brain tissue
• Polyhydramnios may be present

| Feature | Anencephaly | Cystic Hygroma | Encephalocele | Dandy-Walker

| ------- | ----------- | -------------- | ------------- | ------------

| Skull vault | ❌ Absent | Present | Defect present | Present

| Brain tissue | Absent/disorganized | Normal | Herniated | Abnormal cerebellum

| Location | Whole cranial vault | Neck | Focal skull defect | Posterior fossa

| Key sign | Frog-eye | Neck cyst | Sac-like protrusion | Enlarged 4th ventricle

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: Which of the following is not a radiological feature of hypothyroidism? (NEET Pg 2016)
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Beaking of vertebra

Beaking of vertebra is not associated with hypothyroidism. This vertebral finding is characteristic of mucopolysaccharidosis conditions, with central beaking observed in Morquio's disease and antero-inferior beaking seen in Hurler disease. Hypothyroidism has several skeletal manifestations, but vertebral beaking is not among them.

Other Options:

●        Option A. Wormian bones - These accessory sutural bones can be seen in various conditions including hypothyroidism\, especially in congenital hypothyroidism or cretinism.

●        Option B. Stipulated ribs - Rib abnormalities can occur in hypothyroidism as part of the broader skeletal manifestations of the disease.

●        Option D. Epiphyseal Dysgenesis - This is a recognized skeletal manifestation in hypothyroidism\, particularly in juvenile hypothyroidism\, affecting the growth plates.

Educational Objective:

Vertebal beaking is specifically associated with mucopolysaccharidosis conditions rather than hypothyroidism, which has its own distinct pattern of skeletal manifestations.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: Which of the following statements are correct regarding a brain abscess? I. Abscesses arise when the brain is exposed directly as a result of fracture or infection of air sinus. II. Presenting features include low grade fever, confusion, seizures and focal deficits. III. MRI with contrast is the initial imaging modality of choice. IV. The aetiological agents include bacteria, fungi, protozoa and viruses. Select the answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. I, II and IV

A brain abscess is a focal intracerebral infection consisting of a collection of pus surrounded by a vascularized capsule. It usually develops due to direct spread from adjacent infections, hematogenous dissemination, or penetrating cranial trauma/neurosurgery.

The following statements are true:

• I. Abscesses arise when the brain is exposed directly as a result of fracture or infection of air sinus: Brain abscesses commonly result from:

• Direct extension from otitis media, mastoiditis, sinusitis
• Penetrating skull fractures or neurosurgery
• Hematogenous spread from distant infections

• II. Presenting features include low-grade fever, confusion, seizures and focal deficits: Common clinical features include:

• Headache (most common symptom)
• Fever (may be absent)
• Altered mental status/confusion
• Focal neurological deficits
• Seizures
• Features of raised intracranial pressure

• IV. The etiological agents include bacteria, fungi, protozoa and viruses: Although bacteria are the most common cause, brain abscess-like lesions can also occur due to:

• Fungi (Aspergillus, Candida)
• Protozoa (Toxoplasma gondii, especially in AIDS)
• Rarely viral infections can produce focal necrotizing lesions, though classic brain abscesses are predominantly bacterial.

Why is III incorrect?

• III. MRI with contrast is the initial imaging modality of choice: Contrast-enhanced CT scan is usually the initial imaging investigation because it is rapid, widely available, and useful in emergency settings.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A 20-year-old woman presented with hypertension and chest pain. A chest radiograph was taken as shown in the image below. What is the likely cause of hypertension in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Coarctation of aorta

The given clinical scenario and the chest X-ray depicting the figure of 3 sign are suggestive of coarctation of aorta to be the cause of hypertension in this patient.

Typical C/F: Brachio-femoral delay – Upper limb pulsations/BP is high; Lower limb pulsation/BP is feeble.

Radiological investigation:

• Figure of 3 signs on CXR
• Inferior rib notching – Roesler's sign

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A 22-year-old man has a history of recurrent sinus infections and chronic productive cough since childhood. High-resolution CT of the chest shows bronchiectasis, and a chest radiograph demonstrates dextrocardia with complete situs inversus. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Kartagener syndrome

Kartagener syndrome is a subtype of Primary Ciliary Dyskinesia (PCD), an autosomal recessive disorder caused by defective dynein arms of motile cilia. Impaired ciliary motility leads to defective mucociliary clearance and abnormal embryonic left-right axis determination.

The classic triad consists of:

• Chronic sinusitis
• Bronchiectasis
• Situs inversus (or dextrocardia)

Other features include:

• Recurrent otitis media
• Chronic productive cough
• Male infertility (immotile sperm)
• Female subfertility/ectopic pregnancy due to impaired fallopian tube cilia

Why not the other options?

• A. Cystic fibrosis: Also causes recurrent respiratory infections and bronchiectasis, but is associated with pancreatic insufficiency, malabsorption, elevated sweat chloride, and does not cause situs inversus.
• C. Young syndrome: Characterized by bronchiectasis with obstructive azoospermia, but ciliary function is normal and situs inversus is absent.
• D. Primary immunodeficiency: May cause recurrent sinopulmonary infections but does not produce the characteristic combination of bronchiectasis with situs inversus.

High-yield pearl

| Disorder | Key defect | Characteristic features

| -------- | ---------- | -----------------------

| Kartagener syndrome (PCD) | Defective dynein arms → impaired ciliary motility | Sinusitis + bronchiectasis + situs inversus

| Cystic fibrosis | CFTR mutation | Bronchiectasis, pancreatic insufficiency, ↑ sweat chloride

| Young syndrome | Unknown cause | Bronchiectasis + obstructive azoospermia; no situs inversus

| Primary immunodeficiency | Immune defect | Recurrent infections without laterality defects

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A 3-month-old infant is brought to the emergency department with complaints of cyanosis and difficulty breathing. A chest X-ray shows the findings given below. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Tetralogy of Fallot

Tetralogy of Fallot presents with a "boot-shaped" heart on chest X-ray due to right ventricular hypertrophy and pulmonary stenosis, with oligemic lung fields and cyanosis typically manifesting after the neonatal period.

Key Radiographic Signs:

• Boot-shaped heart (Coeur en sabot)
• Upturned cardiac apex (RV hypertrophy)
• Concave pulmonary artery segment
• Decreased pulmonary vascular markings (oligemia)

| Option | Verdict | Why

| ------ | ------- | ---

| A. Atrial septal defect (ASD) | ❌ | Acyanotic; ↑ pulmonary flow; normal/large heart, no boot shape

| B. Ventricular septal defect (VSD) | ❌ | Acyanotic initially; cardiomegaly + pulmonary plethora

| C. Tetralogy of Fallot | ✅ | Cyanotic; boot-shaped heart + oligemic lungs

| D. Transposition of great arteries (TGA) | ❌ | Shows egg-on-a-string heart, not boot-shaped

| Disease | X-ray Appearance | Pulmonary Blood Flow

| ------- | ---------------- | --------------------

| Tetralogy of Fallot |  Boot-shaped heart | ↓ Decreased

| Transposition of great arteries |  Egg-on-string | ↑ Increased

| Tricuspid atresia | Small heart | ↓ Decreased

| Total anomalous pulmonary venous return (TAPVR) | Snowman sign | ↑ Increased

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A 32-year-old woman presents with fatigue, low-grade fever, and dry cough for 2 months, along with painful red nodules on her shins. Elevated ACE levels are noted. Based on the provided chest X-ray, what is the most likely stage of the disease?
options: Stage I → Bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy only
Stage III → Pulmonary infiltration without lymphadenopathy
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Stage I → Bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy only

This patient has the classic features of sarcoidosis—dry cough, low-grade fever, erythema nodosum, elevated serum ACE levels, and a chest X-ray showing bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy (BHL) without pulmonary infiltrates, consistent with Stage I sarcoidosis.

Sarcoidosis Chest X-ray Staging

| Stage | Chest X-ray Finding

| ----- | -------------------

| Stage I | Bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy (BHL) only

| Stage II | BHL + pulmonary infiltrates

| Stage III | Pulmonary infiltrates without BHL

| Stage IV | Pulmonary fibrosis

Why not the other options?

• B. Stage II: Requires both bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy and lung parenchymal infiltrates.
• C. Stage III: Characterized by pulmonary infiltrates with resolution of hilar lymphadenopathy.
• D. Stage IV: Shows irreversible pulmonary fibrosis with volume loss and architectural distortion.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A 35 year old man presents to the emergency department with sudden onset shortness of breath. Below is the CT of the patient. What is the next best step in management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Needle thoracostomy

CT shows tension pneumothorax.

Key Radiological Signs:

• Collapsed lung
• Air in pleural space (black area)
• Mediastinal shift to opposite side
• Compression of great vessels → ↓ venous return

Air enters pleural space (one-way valve)

↓

Air accumulates → pressure increases

↓

Lung collapses

↓

Mediastinum shifts

↓

↓ Venous return to heart

↓

Shock + death (if untreated)

Immediate needle thoracostomy in 5th ICS midaxillary line is lifesaving. Chest tube follows for definitive management.

Other options are not appropriate in emergency.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A 35-year-old male presents to the trauma center after RTA with shortness of breath. The supine CXR is shown below. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Hemothorax

In a supine chest X-ray of a trauma patient, a hemothorax presents as a diffuse opacity throughout the affected hemithorax due to the gravitational spread of blood in the pleural space.

Key Radiological Clues:

• Diffuse haziness on one side (veiling opacity)
• No clear fluid level (because supine)
• Possible loss of diaphragmatic outline
• Lung may appear compressed

| Condition | CXR Feature | Key Difference

| --------- | ----------- | --------------

| Hemothorax | Diffuse haziness (supine) | Fluid

| Pneumothorax | Deep sulcus sign | Air

| Pulmonary contusion | Patchy opacities | Parenchymal

| Diaphragm injury | Elevated/irregular diaphragm | Structural

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A 50-year-old man presents with a chronic, non-productive cough, mild dyspnea, and fatigue. He has a long-standing occupational history as a construction laborer with significant exposure to dust and sand. A chest X-ray demonstrates characteristic changes, as shown in the image below. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Silicosis

Silicosis presents with bilateral upper lobe nodules and pathognomonic "eggshell calcification" of hilar lymph nodes in patients with crystalline silica exposure from construction, mining, or sandblasting work.

Key Radiological Features:

• Multiple small nodules (upper lobes)
• Upper lobe predominance
• Eggshell calcification of hilar lymph nodes
• Advanced stage → Progressive massive fibrosis (PMF)

| Option | Verdict | Why

| ------ | ------- | ---

| A. Tuberculosis | ❌ | May affect upper lobes but shows cavitation, not nodular fibrosis

| B. Asbestosis | ❌ | Lower lobe fibrosis + pleural plaques

| C. Bagassosis | ❌ | Hypersensitivity pneumonitis (sugarcane dust), diffuse pattern

| D. Silicosis | ✅ | Upper lobe nodules + eggshell calcification + occupational exposure

| Disease | Exposure | X-ray Finding | Lobe Involvement

| ------- | -------- | ------------- | ----------------

| Silicosis | Sand, stone | Nodules + eggshell calcification | Upper lobes

| Asbestosis | Asbestos | Reticular fibrosis + plaques | Lower lobes

| Coal worker’s pneumoconiosis | Coal dust | Nodules | Upper lobes

| Bagassosis | Sugarcane dust | Ground-glass, diffuse | Diffuse

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A 50-year-old presents with severe chest pain, respiratory distress, and crepitus after a fall from a roof. The X-ray image is shown. Which of the following is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Pneumomediastinum

The X-ray demonstrates air in the mediastinum (pneumomediastinum), visible as lucent streaks outlining mediastinal structures. This finding represents free air that has dissected through fascial planes into the mediastinum. Pneumomediastinum can result from trauma and typically presents with chest pain, respiratory distress, and subcutaneous emphysema (crepitus). The pattern shown matches classic pneumomediastinum signs.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A 55 year old chronic smoker presents with drooping of the right eyelid, constricted pupil, and absence of sweating on the right side of the face. He also complains of shoulder pain and tingling sensation in the right arm. The chest x-ray of the patient is given below. Which of the following is the best investigation to confirm the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. CT scan-guided biopsy

Pancoast Tumor:

• Tumor located at lung apex (superior sulcus)
• Usually non-small cell lung carcinoma (NSCLC)

It invades:

• Sympathetic chain → Horner syndrome
• Brachial plexus → arm pain/paresthesia
• Ribs/vertebrae → bone pain

The clinical picture suggests Pancoast tumor with Horner’s syndrome. CT-guided biopsy confirms diagnosis.

Classic Radiographic Findings:

• Apical opacity
• Rib destruction (sometimes)
• May be subtle → often missed on X-ray

Sputum microscopy is for infection, nerve conduction for neuropathy, ultrasound is not definitive.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A 56-year-old woman with carcinoma of the cervix is planned for intracavitary brachytherapy after external beam radiotherapy. What is the main advantage of brachytherapy?
options: It is effective in treating distant metastases
It eliminates the need for radioactive sources
It delivers a high radiation dose to the tumor while minimizing exposure to surrounding normal tissues
It is more effective than surgery for all solid tumors
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. It delivers a high radiation dose to the tumor while minimizing exposure to surrounding normal tissues

• Brachytherapy is a form of internal radiotherapy in which a radioactive source is placed within or very close to the tumor, allowing the delivery of a very high radiation dose to the target while rapidly reducing the dose to adjacent normal tissues because of the inverse square law.
• In carcinoma cervix, intracavitary brachytherapy is an essential component of definitive treatment after external beam radiotherapy (EBRT), significantly improving local tumor control and survival.

Why not the other options?

• A. It is effective in treating distant metastases – Brachytherapy is a local treatment and has no role in treating distant metastatic disease.
• B. It eliminates the need for radioactive sources – Incorrect; brachytherapy uses sealed radioactive sources (e.g., Iridium-192, Cesium-137, Cobalt-60).
• D. It is more effective than surgery for all solid tumors – False. The role of brachytherapy depends on the tumor type and stage and is not universally superior to surgery.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A 58-year-old man presents with chronic cough, weight loss, and progressive dyspnea. On evaluation, he is found to have a primary liver malignancy. A whole-body imaging study demonstrates multiple hypermetabolic lesions in both lungs, consistent with pulmonary metastases. What is the principle of the imaging investigation shown?
options: Increased glucose metabolism in tissues using ¹⁸F-fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG)
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Increased glucose metabolism in tissues using ¹⁸F-fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG)

The imaging shown is an ¹⁸F-FDG PET-CT scan, which detects increased glucose metabolism in tissues. ¹⁸F-fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG) is a radioactive glucose analog that is taken up by metabolically active cells through glucose transporters and phosphorylated by hexokinase. Because malignant cells have increased glycolytic activity (Warburg effect), they accumulate FDG and appear as hypermetabolic (“hot”) lesions on PET imaging.

Why not the other options?

• A. Tissue perfusion using iodine contrast – Principle of contrast-enhanced CT, not PET.
• B. Decreased glucose metabolism in tissues – PET identifies areas of increased, not decreased, glucose uptake in most malignancies.
• D. Water diffusion in brain tissue – Principle of diffusion-weighted MRI (DWI), mainly used in acute stroke and certain brain lesions.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A 6-year-old child presenting with recurrent respiratory infections. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. CPAM

Congenital pulmonary airway malformation shows multiple cystic air-filled spaces. Pyopneumothorax has pleural air-fluid, CDH shows bowel in chest, abscess is single cavity.

Key Radiological Features:

• Multiple cystic lucencies in lung
• Usually unilateral
• May have:

• Air-filled cysts
• Air-fluid levels (if infected)

• Commonly involves lower lobes

| Feature | CPAM | Lung Abscess | CDH | Pyopneumothorax

| ------- | ---- | ------------ | --- | ---------------

| Age | Child | Any | Neonate | Any

| Number of lesions | Multiple cysts | Single | Multiple bowel loops | Single

| Wall | Thin | Thick | Bowel wall | Pleural

| Infection | Recurrent | Acute | Early distress | Severe

| Key clue | Congenital cysts | Thick cavity | Bowel in chest | Pleural air-fluid

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A child presents with breathlessness. Chest X ray shows a radiopaque circular object with double rim. Identify?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Button battery

Button batteries show a double rim/halo on X‑ray, unlike coins or other objects. They are a medical emergency due to caustic leakage and electrical injury, requiring urgent removal.

Radiological Signs:

• Double rim / halo sign (two concentric circles)

• Usually lodged in esophagus

• On lateral view:

• Step-off sign (unequal edges)

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A child with acute lymphoblastic leukemia undergoes prophylactic irradiation prior to autologous hematopoietic stem cell transplantation. Which of the following will be the least affected?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Neurons

Neurons (Central nervous system) are the least affected by irradiation among the options given, due to their highly differentiated and non-dividing nature.

Other Options:

• Option. A. Spermatogonia: These are germ cells that continually divide and are highly sensitive to radiation, which can lead to infertility.
• Option. B. Intestinal epithelial cells: These cells have a high turnover rate, making them very sensitive to radiation, which can result in gastrointestinal toxicity.
• Option. D. Bone marrow/erythroid precursor cells: These cells are among the most sensitive to radiation due to their role in rapidly producing new blood cells, leading to potential marrow suppression.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A patient presents in OPD with a history of fever and cough for 5 days. On auscultation, crepts were heard on right side. Chest X-ray is given below. Mark the correct finding in this case?
options: Apical segment of Right lower lobe consolidation
Posterior segment of right lower lobe consolidation
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Right middle lobe consolidation

Right middle lobe consolidation is suggested by the obscuration of the right heart border and the specific location of opacity on the chest X-ray, aligned with the patient's clinical presentation of respiratory symptoms.

Key Radiological Sign → Silhouette Sign ⭐

Right heart border is obscured

This is the giveaway because-

• Right middle lobe lies adjacent to right heart border
• When it consolidates → the border disappears

| Lost Border | Diagnosis

| ----------- | ---------

| Right heart border | Right middle lobe ⭐

| Left heart border | Lingula

| Right diaphragm | Right lower lobe

| Left diaphragm | Left lower lobe

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: All of the following half-lives and radioisotopes are correctly matched, except: (NEET PG 2017)
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Technetium-99m - 6 days

Technetium-99m has a half-life of 6 hours, not 6 days as incorrectly stated in option D. Tc-99m is a metastable nuclear isomer that loses roughly half of its radioactivity in that 6-hour timeframe. This short half-life makes it particularly useful for diagnostic nuclear medicine procedures since it decays quickly after imaging is complete, minimizing radiation exposure to patients.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: Based on the image shown below, which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Congenital Diaphragmatic Hernia

| Feature | Explanation

| ------- | -----------

| Air-filled structures in chest | Indicates bowel, not lung pathology

| Mass effect | Herniated viscera compress lungs

| Neonatal distress | Due to pulmonary hypoplasia

| Left-sided predominance | Classic for Bochdalek hernia

Congenital diaphragmatic hernia is characterized on chest X-ray by the presence of bowel loops in the thoracic cavity, appearing as multiple air-filled lucencies with a "bubbly" pattern and causing contralateral mediastinal shift.

Key Findings:

• Multiple air-filled bowel loops in thorax
• Absent diaphragmatic outline
• Mediastinal shift to opposite side
• Scaphoid abdomen (clinically!)
• Sometimes nasogastric tube seen in thoracic cavity

| Feature | CDH | CPAM | Sequestration | Pneumothorax

| ------- | --- | ---- | ------------- | ------------

| Origin | Diaphragm defect | Lung | Lung (aberrant) | Pleural space

| Contents | Bowel loops | Cysts | Solid/cystic mass | Air only

| Air-fluid levels | Present | Sometimes | Rare | Absent

| Feeding vessel | No | No | Yes (aorta) | No

| Mediastinal shift | Yes | Sometimes | Sometimes | Yes

| Key clue | Bowel in chest | Lung cysts | Systemic artery | No markings

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: Consider the following statements regarding radiation enteritis and proctocolitis: 1. Diarrhoea in the acute phase should be treated with codeine or loperamide. 2. Surgery is the treatment of choice and involves resection of the injured intestine. 3. Sucralfate enemas and hyperbaric oxygen are effective treatments. 4. Small bowel strictures and rectovaginal fistulae may develop as chronic complications. Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 1, 3 and 4

Radiation enteritis and radiation proctocolitis are complications of abdominal or pelvic radiotherapy. They may present as acute (during or within 3 months of radiotherapy) or chronic (months to years later). Treatment is primarily conservative, while surgery is reserved only for severe complications.

• 1. Diarrhoea in the acute phase should be treated with codeine or loperamide ✓: Acute radiation enteritis is managed symptomatically with antidiarrheal agents (loperamide or codeine), hydration, and nutritional support.
• 2. Surgery is the treatment of choice and involves resection of the injured intestine ✗: Surgery is not the treatment of choice because irradiated bowel heals poorly and surgery has high morbidity. It is reserved only for complications such as obstruction, perforation, fistula, or refractory bleeding.
• 3. Sucralfate enemas and hyperbaric oxygen are effective treatments ✓: Sucralfate enemas are effective for chronic radiation proctitis, while hyperbaric oxygen therapy promotes healing in refractory cases.
• 4. Small bowel strictures and rectovaginal fistulae may develop as chronic complications ✓: Chronic radiation injury can cause fibrosis leading to strictures, fistulae, obstruction, and chronic bleeding.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: During evaluation of PUO, a patient's chest X-ray is as seen below. What is your diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Miliary tuberculosis

The given chest X-ray depicts miliary tuberculosis.

Miliary tuberculosis:

●       Bilateral randomly distributed nodules on HRCT.

●       Hematogenous spread.

Miliary pattern D/D:

●       Healed varicella

●       TPE/ Loeffler’s syndrome

●       Hemosiderosis

●       Silicosis

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: Identify the imaging modality given below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. PET CT

PET CT combines metabolic imaging with CT anatomy, using FDG uptake to detect malignant cells. It works on the principle of coincidence detection and annihilation reaction. It is crucial in oncology for staging and monitoring tumors.

Key Imaging Features

• Color-coded metabolic activity
• Background CT anatomy visible
• Areas of high uptake = “hot spots”
• Usually uses:

• FDG (fluorodeoxyglucose)

| Modality | Color | Functional Info | Anatomical Info | Scope

| -------- | ----- | --------------- | --------------- | -----

| PET-CT | ✅ Yes | ✅ Metabolic | ✅ CT | Whole body

| CBF scan | ❌ | Perfusion | ❌ | Brain

| Sestamibi | ❌ | Functional | ❌ | Targeted

| MDCT | ❌ | ❌ | ✅ | Whole body

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: Identify the marked structure:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Posterior rib

The posterior rib appears as a horizontal structure on a chest X-ray, distinguishing it from the more curved anterior ribs and other thoracic structures.

| Feature | Posterior Ribs | Anterior Ribs

| ------- | -------------- | -------------

| Orientation | Horizontal 🟩 | Oblique downward 🔽

| Visibility | More prominent | Less prominent

| Density | Thicker | Thinner

| Use | Count ribs (lung expansion) | Less useful

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: In radiation therapy, a Linear Accelerator is commonly used for treating cancer. Which type of energy does a linear accelerator generate to destroy malignant cells?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. X-ray

Linear accelerators (LINAC) produce high-energy X-rays through bremsstrahlung when accelerated electrons strike a tungsten target, delivering megavoltage photon beams for cancer radiotherapy.

| Modality | Source | Radiation Type | Use

| -------- | ------ | -------------- | ---

| LINAC | Accelerated electrons | X-rays (photon beam) | Most common EBRT

| Cobalt therapy | Radioisotope | Gamma rays | Older technique

| Proton therapy | Cyclotron | Proton beam | Precision therapy

| Neutron therapy | Nuclear reactions | Neutrons | Rare, specialized

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: In radiological physics, which of the following statement best describes eV?
options: The speed of an electron in a magnetic field
The force acting on an electron in an electric field
The energy gained by an electron when accelerated through a potential difference of one volt
The kinetic energy of an electron at rest in a vacuum
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. The energy gained by an electron when accelerated through a potential difference of one volt

An electron volt (eV) is the energy gained by an electron accelerated through a potential difference of one volt, equal to 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ joules, fundamental for understanding X-ray production energies.

| Quantity | Formula | Meaning

| -------- | ------- | -------

| Energy | E = eV | Energy gained by charge

| Electron charge | e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C | Constant

| Voltage | V | Potential difference

| Option | Verdict | Why

| ------ | ------- | ---

| A. Speed of electron in magnetic field | ❌ | Speed depends on energy, but eV itself is not speed

| B. Force on electron in electric field | ❌ | Force = charge × field, not energy

| C. Energy gained through 1 volt | ✅ | Exact definition of eV

| D. Kinetic energy at rest | ❌ | Electron at rest has zero kinetic energy

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: Match the following: A-SVC, B-Aorta, C-Esophagus, D-Trachea
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. A-SVC, B-Aorta, C-Trachea, D-Esophagus

SVC lies right, aorta is central arch, trachea is air-filled anterior, esophagus lies posterior. Correct match is A-SVC, B-Aorta, C-Trachea, D-Esophagus.

| Structure | Position | Density | Key Clue

| --------- | -------- | ------- | --------

| Trachea | Central | Air (black) | Round, lumen

| Esophagus | Posterior to trachea | Soft tissue | Collapsed

| SVC | Right | Soft tissue | Thin-walled vein

| Aorta | Left | Soft tissue | Thick-walled artery

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: Most sensitive investigation for parathyroid tumor imaging?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Tc Sestamibi SPECT

Sestamibi SPECT combines nuclear imaging with CT, giving 3D localization and higher sensitivity than planar sestamibi.

Key Imaging Features:

• Focal persistent uptake on delayed images
• Usually inferior to thyroid
• SPECT adds 3D localization

Tc-99m sestamibi injected

↓

Early uptake (thyroid + parathyroid)

↓

Delayed phase

↓

Thyroid washes out

↓

Parathyroid retains tracer

↓

SPECT → precise 3D localization ⭐

USG and MRI are less sensitive, PET is not routine.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: Most useful investigation for localizing a parathyroid adenoma?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Sestamibi scan

Tc‑99m sestamibi scan (especially with SPECT) is best for parathyroid adenoma localization due to functional uptake and 3D accuracy.

Why is it the best investigation:

• Highest sensitivity for localizing parathyroid adenoma
• Detects single-gland disease (the most common cause of primary hyperparathyroidism)
• Shows persistent tracer uptake on delayed images → characteristic of adenoma
• Helps plan minimally invasive parathyroidectomy (MIP)

Other investigations

• Ultrasound neck → operator-dependent, good for superficial glands
• 4D-CT → used if Sestamibi is negative or for ectopic glands
• MRI → less commonly used

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: The finding shown in the MRI is most characteristic of which condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Sacral insufficiency fracture

The Honda sign is an H‑shaped hyperintensity on sacral STIR MRI, pathognomonic for sacral insufficiency fracture. It represents bilateral sacral ala edema connected by a horizontal line.

Signature Pattern:

• H-shaped / Honda sign

• Vertical lines → both sacral alae
• Horizontal line → sacral body

• Hyperintense marrow edema on STIR/T2
• Often bilateral symmetric

It looks like a tiny scooter logo etched into the sacrum

| Condition | MRI Pattern | Key Feature

| --------- | ----------- | -----------

| Sacral insufficiency fracture | H-shaped edema | Bilateral, symmetric

| Multiple myeloma | Focal lesions | Lytic, punched-out

| Osteomyelitis | Diffuse edema + abscess | Infection signs

| Bone marrow edema (non-specific) | Patchy | No specific pattern

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: What is the earliest indicator of left atrial enlargement in cases of mitral stenosis? (NEET PG 2015)
options: Elevation of the right main bronchus
Enlargement of the left atrial appendage
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Enlargement of the left atrial appendage

In mitral stenosis, left atrial enlargement follows a predictable radiographic sequence. The left atrial appendage (left auricle) forms part of the normal left heart border between the pulmonary trunk and the left ventricle. It is the first structure to enlarge, producing straightening — or even bulging — of the left heart border, obliterating the normal concavity. This is the earliest and most sensitive plain film sign.

The sequence of progressive left atrial enlargement on CXR is:

| Stage | Radiographic Sign

| ----- | -----------------

| Earliest | Straightening of left heart border (LAA prominence)

| Intermediate | Splaying of carina (>70°), double density sign

| Late | Elevation of left main bronchus, posterior oesophageal displacement

Why the other options are wrong:

• Elevation of the right main bronchus (A) — not a feature of LA enlargement; it is the left main bronchus that is elevated and splayed as the LA expands superiorly
• Widening of the carina (C) — occurs after significant LA enlargement; an intermediate sign, not the earliest
• Oesophageal displacement (D) — seen on barium swallow or lateral CXR only after substantial posterior LA enlargement; a late sign

High-yield pearl: The four classic signs of LA enlargement in mitral stenosis on PA CXR in order — left heart border straightening → double density sign → left main bronchus elevation → splayed carina. Oesophageal displacement is best seen on lateral view with barium.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: What is the likely diagnosis based on the given image?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Aberrant right subclavian artery

An aberrant right subclavian artery is an anatomical variant where the artery arises as the fourth branch of the aortic arch and courses posterior to the esophagus, often leading to dysphagia lusoria due to esophageal compression.

Signature Imaging Clues:

• Indentation on posterior wall of esophagus
• Vessel arising distally from aortic arch
• Courses behind the esophagus (retro-esophageal)

| Condition | Imaging Feature | Key Difference

| --------- | --------------- | --------------

| ARSA | Posterior esophageal indentation | Retro-esophageal vessel

| Right-sided aortic arch | Right arch shadow | No posterior compression

| Tracheal diverticulum | Air pouch near trachea | Not vascular

| Esophageal duplication | Cystic mass | No vascular flow

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Lung Abscess

Lung abscess is a thick-walled cavity with air-fluid level. TB cavities lack air-fluid level, fungal pneumonia shows nodules, hydropneumothorax is pleural air-fluid.

Key Radiological Features:

• Thick-walled cavity
• Air–fluid level inside lung
• Surrounding consolidation
• Usually single lesion

| Feature | Interpretation

| ------- | --------------

| Thick irregular wall | Infection with necrosis

| Air-fluid level | Liquefied pus

| Location | Within lung (not pleura)

| Surrounding opacity | Inflammatory changes

| Feature | Lung Abscess | TB | Fungal Pneumonia | Hydropneumothorax

| ------- | ------------ | --- | ---------------- | -----------------

| Location | Parenchyma | Parenchyma | Parenchyma | Pleural space

| Wall | Thick | Thin | Variable | None

| Air-fluid level | Present | Rare | Rare | Straight line

| Surrounding lung | Consolidation | Fibrosis | Nodules | Collapsed lung

| Key clue | Thick cavity | Apical thin cavity | Halo sign | Pleural level

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Kartagener syndrome

Kartagener syndrome triad: situs inversus, bronchiectasis, sinusitis. Cystic fibrosis has bronchiectasis but no situs inversus. Pneumoperitoneum shows free air, not dextrocardia.

Key Imaging Clues:

• Dextrocardia (cardiac apex on right)
• Situs inversus totalis (organs reversed)
• Signs of bronchiectasis:

• Dilated bronchi
• “Tram-track” appearance

| Feature | Kartagener | CF | Pneumoperitoneum | Labelling Error

| ------- | ---------- | --- | ---------------- | ---------------

| Dextrocardia | ✅ | ❌ | ❌ | Fake

| Situs inversus | ✅ | ❌ | ❌ | ❌

| Bronchiectasis | ✅ | ✅ | ❌ | ❌

| Key cause | Ciliary defect | CFTR mutation | Perforation | Human error

| Exam clue | Mirror organs | Thick mucus | Air under diaphragm | Inconsistent findings

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: What is the minimum recommended thickness for a lead apron to protect the patient from radiation? (NEET PG 2017)
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 0.25 mm

Lead aprons used for radiation protection require a minimum thickness of 0.25 mm to provide adequate shielding from radiation exposure. This minimum standard ensures basic protection for personnel working with radiation.

While 0.25 mm represents the minimum acceptable thickness for lead aprons, most clinical facilities actually use thicker aprons of 0.5 mm for daily practice. The thickness directly correlates with the level of radiation attenuation provided by the apron.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: What is the most probable diagnosis based on the image provided?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. RUL consolidation

• There is a homogeneous opacity in the right upper zone.
• The horizontal (minor) fissure is clearly visible and maintains its normal position.
• No elevation or displacement of the fissure → no volume loss.
• Lung volume appears preserved → ribs and mediastinum are not shifted.

Why this favors consolidation over collapse

| Feature | RUL Consolidation | RUL Collapse

| ------- | ----------------- | ------------

| Horizontal fissure | Normal position | Elevated

| Volume loss | Absent | Present

| Mediastinal shift | Absent | Toward lesion

| Air bronchogram | May be present | Usually absent

The decisive point:

If it were collapse, the horizontal fissure would be pulled upward due to volume loss.

Here, it is intact and not displaced, which strongly supports consolidation.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: Which characteristic best describes an ideal therapeutic radioisotope for medical use? (NEET PG 2016)
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Strong Beta; Low Gamma emitter

An ideal therapeutic radioisotope should be a strong beta emitter with low gamma emission. Beta particles have relatively high energy and are strongly absorbed by adjacent tissue, allowing them to cause substantial damage to targeted cells (like cancer cells). Low gamma emission is preferred to minimize radiation exposure to surrounding healthy tissues and healthcare workers.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: Which of the following is not controlled by Kilovolt Peak (kVp) in X-ray imaging? (NEET Pg 2016)
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Density

Kilovolt Peak (kVp) regulates the velocity of electrons traveling from cathode to anode in the X-ray tube. KVp determines the quality and quantity of X-rays and affects penetration. The relationship is expressed as "kVp ∝ penetration" and "kVp ∝ 1/contrast." Density (film blackening) is controlled by mAs (milliamperage second), not by kVp.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: Which of the following radiopharmaceutical is most commonly used in PET imaging to detect metabolically active tissues?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Fluorodeoxyglucose (¹⁸F-FDG)

¹⁸F-Fluorodeoxyglucose (¹⁸F-FDG) is the most commonly used radiopharmaceutical in Positron Emission Tomography (PET). It is a glucose analogue that accumulates in metabolically active tissues, making it highly useful for detecting malignancy, infection, and inflammation.

After entering the cell via glucose transporters, FDG is phosphorylated but cannot undergo further metabolism, leading to intracellular trapping. Areas with increased glucose metabolism therefore show increased FDG uptake (“hot spots”) on PET imaging.

Why not the other options?

• A. Technetium-99m: Used in SPECT, bone scans, renal scans, hepatobiliary scans, and thyroid imaging; not PET.
• B. Iodine-131: Used for radioiodine therapy and thyroid imaging; emits β and γ radiation, not routinely used for PET.
• D. Gallium-67: Used for imaging infection, inflammation, and lymphoma, but with planar scintigraphy/SPECT, not PET.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: Which of the following statements about Technetium-99m (Tc-99m) is not correct? (NEET PG 2015)
options: It has a half-life of 6 hours.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. It emits Beta radiation.

Technetium-99m (Tc-99m) emits gamma radiation, not beta radiation. The "m" in Tc-99m stands for metastable, which indicates that the nucleus releases gamma rays to reach a stable state. This metastable state decays by emitting low-energy gamma rays rather than beta emission.

Other Options:

Option A. It has a half-life of 6 hours - Correct The physical half-life of Tc-99m is indeed 6 hours\, meaning it loses roughly half of its radioactivity in that time. This relatively short half-life makes it ideal for diagnostic imaging while minimizing patient radiation exposure.

Option B. It is derived from Molybdenum - Correct Tc-99m is obtained from Molybdenum-99 generators used in nuclear medicine departments\, allowing for on-site production of the radioisotope.

Option D. Its decay process is isomeric - Correct The "m" in Tc-99m stands for metastable\, indicating an isomeric transition decay process where the nucleus releases energy (gamma rays) to reach a stable state without changing the number of protons or neutrons.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: Which of the following terms describes nuclides that have identical atomic mass numbers but different atomic numbers? (NEET PG 2015)
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Isobars

Isobars are nuclides that have the same mass number (A) but different atomic numbers (Z). This means they have the same total number of protons and neutrons, but the distribution between protons and neutrons differs.

Other Options:

Option A. Isotopes - Isotopes are different forms of the same element (same atomic number/Z) with different numbers of neutrons\, resulting in different mass numbers (A). Isotopes have identical chemical properties but different physical properties due to their different masses.

Option C. Isotones - Isotones are nuclides that have the same number of neutrons but different numbers of protons. This results in different elements with different mass numbers but the same neutron count.

Option D. Isomers - Isomers are nuclides with identical atomic numbers (Z) and mass numbers (A)\, but different nuclear energy states. An example is Technetium-99m\, where the "m" denotes a metastable state with higher energy than the ground state Technetium-99.

Educational Objective:

Isobars are different elements with the same mass number but different atomic numbers, representing nuclides with the same total number of nucleons but different proton-to-neutron ratios.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: Which types of cancer are associated with exposure to ionizing radiation? 1. Leukaemia 2. Lung cancer 3. Breast cancer 4. Lymphoma Select the correct answer using the code given below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 1, 3 and 4

Ionizing radiation is a well-established carcinogen that causes DNA damage through direct strand breaks and free radical formation. The risk of malignancy depends on the radiation dose, age at exposure, and tissue radiosensitivity. Hematopoietic tissues and rapidly dividing cells are particularly susceptible.

Why is C correct?

• 1. Leukaemia ✅

• One of the earliest and best-established malignancies associated with ionizing radiation exposure, especially acute leukemia (except CLL).

• 2. Lung cancer ❌

• Although high-dose radiation can increase the risk of lung cancer, lung cancer is classically associated with smoking, radon, and asbestos, and is not considered one of the characteristic radiation-induced cancers in this context.

• 3. Breast cancer ✅

• Exposure to ionizing radiation, particularly during childhood or adolescence, significantly increases the risk of breast cancer.

• 4. Lymphoma ✅

• Ionizing radiation is associated with an increased risk of lymphomas, especially non-Hodgkin lymphoma.
